title: Remark on internal relaxation in large number qubit systems
summary: For a time $t_{c}$ of calculation in an $N$ qubit quantum computer that is much shorter than the intrinsic Heisenberg time $t_H$, $t_c\ll t_H$, the dynamics of the system is effectively irreversible and the couplings between the qubits give rise to a relaxation time scale $τ_r$. If $t_H\gg t_c >\sim τ_r$ one looses quantum coherence exponentially fast. Since $t_H$ scales exponentially with $N$ there is a threshold $N_c$ such that for $N\gg N_c$ one must be aware of possible intrinsic relaxation during calculation. As an order of magnitude estimation we find $N_c\approx \ln(τ_r/T)$ where $T$ is a typical system specific oscillation time of a single qubit. $τ_r$ can be estimated as the typical inverse transition rate between two parts of the system, one of which is treated as an environment of the other.

AI.tldr: Quantum coherence in an N-qubit quantum computer decays exponentially once the calculation time exceeds a relaxation time τ_r, but only for qubit counts above a threshold N_c ≈ ln(τ_r/T). Below that threshold intrinsic relaxation is negligible during computation.
AI.motivation: To establish whether intrinsic, unavoidable relaxation (decoherence arising from qubit-qubit couplings themselves, not external noise) can limit quantum computation, and to identify the system size at which such intrinsic decoherence becomes relevant.
AI.method: Analytical scaling argument using the Heisenberg time t_H (which grows exponentially with N) compared to computation time t_c and relaxation time τ_r; τ_r is estimated as the inverse transition rate between two subsystems, one treated as the environment of the other.
AI.result: For t_c ≪ t_H the dynamics is effectively irreversible; when t_H ≫ t_c ≳ τ_r coherence is lost exponentially fast. Because t_H scales exponentially with N, a threshold N_c ≈ ln(τ_r/T) exists (T = typical single-qubit oscillation time) beyond which intrinsic relaxation during calculation must be considered.
AI.conclusion: For N ≫ N_c intrinsic relaxation during computation cannot be neglected; the threshold grows only logarithmically with τ_r/T, providing an order-of-magnitude criterion for the scalability of qubit-based quantum computing.

title: CSS circuits are ICM circuits without magic states
summary: Gidney and Jones recently introduced ``CSS circuits'', generated by $X$, $Z$, $\MX$, $\MZ$ and CNOT, and showed that they can be sampled with $O(1)$ work per gate. They suspected that the class had been seen before. We point out that it is, up to a normal form, the initialisation--CNOT--measurement (ICM) form introduced in 2015 for compiling fault-tolerant circuits, restricted to $\ket{0}$ and $\ket{+}$ initialisations. The ICM construction answers constructively their question about ``non-CSS-ness as a resource'': every Clifford$+T$ circuit compiles to a CSS circuit acting on $\ket{Y}$ and $\ket{A}$ input states.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies Gidney-Jones "CSS circuits" as, up to normal form, the 2015 initialisation-CNOT-measurement (ICM) form restricted to |0⟩ and |+⟩ initialisations, and uses this to give a constructive answer to the "non-CSS-ness as resource" question.
AI.motivation: Gidney and Jones introduced CSS circuits (generated by X, Z, MX, MZ, CNOT) samplable with O(1) work per gate and suspected the class had been seen before. The authors aim to resolve this provenance question and to address whether non-CSS-ness is a resource.
AI.method: The authors establish an equivalence, up to normal form, between CSS circuits and a restriction of the ICM (initialisation-CNOT-measurement) compilation form to |0⟩ and |+⟩ initialisations. They then apply the ICM construction constructively.
AI.result: CSS circuits coincide (up to normal form) with the restricted ICM form. The ICM construction shows every Clifford+T circuit compiles to a CSS circuit acting on |Y⟩ and |A⟩ input states.
AI.conclusion: The previously "unknown" CSS circuit class is a known compilation form, and non-CSS-ness is constructively captured as a resource via the |Y⟩ and |A⟩ magic input states required to compile arbitrary Clifford+T circuits.

title: QEDist: Practical Exact Distance Certification for Stabilizer Codes
comment: 28 pages, 5 figures, 10 tables. Code available at https://github.com/yeon-lee/QEDist
summary: We present QEDist, a method and software package that certifies the distance of qubit stabilizer codes. Building on tree-search methods, QEDist constructs candidate logical operators one qubit at a time, using sparse parity checks, stabilizer equivalence, and verified symmetries to reduce the work. For a cutoff $W$, a completed search either finds a nontrivial logical operator of weight at most $W$ or proves that none exists. Because satisfying one check can violate another, we use both satisfied and unsatisfied checks to lower-bound the weight needed to complete a logical operator, and prune branches whose bound exceeds the remaining budget, which substantially reduces net search time. We benchmark QEDist mainly on Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes; the same formulation extends to non-CSS codes and to the fault distance of syndrome-extraction circuits. For lifted-product (LP) codes, we further exploit the product structure to replace part of the full-code search with a smaller search on a classical constituent. We establish exact distances for codes with up to several thousand qubits, including Abelian and non-Abelian LP codes whose distances were previously reported only as upper bounds. In several seconds of search on one laptop core, QEDist certifies exact distances up to 20 for many of these codes and fault distance 10 for the syndrome-extraction circuit of the $[[144,12,12]]$ code. With orders-of-magnitude speedups over the tested exact solvers, QEDist makes exact distance certification a practical tool for selecting and optimizing finite-length quantum codes.

AI.tldr: QEDist is a tree-search-based method and software that certifies exact (and fault) distances of qubit stabilizer codes, using sparse parity checks, stabilizer equivalence, verified symmetries, and dual satisfied/unsatisfied-check lower bounds for pruning, with a specialized decomposition for lifted-product codes.
AI.motivation: Exact distance certification is critical for selecting and optimizing finite-length quantum codes, but existing exact solvers are too slow to be practical, and many code distances (e.g., non-Abelian LP codes) were only known as upper bounds.
AI.method: Builds candidate logical operators one qubit at a time via tree search; for a cutoff W, either finds a nontrivial logical operator of weight ≤ W or proves none exists. Reduces work using sparse parity checks, stabilizer equivalence, and verified symmetries. Uses both satisfied and unsatisfied checks to lower-bound the weight needed to complete a logical operator, pruning branches whose bound exceeds the remaining budget. Formulation extends to non-CSS codes and fault distance of syndrome-extraction circuits; for LP codes, replaces part of the full-code search with a smaller classical constituent search.
AI.result: Establishes exact distances for codes with up to several thousand qubits, including Abelian and non-Abelian LP codes previously known only as upper bounds; certifies exact distances up to 20 for many codes and fault distance 10 for the [[144,12,12]] syndrome-extraction circuit in seconds on one laptop core; achieves orders-of-magnitude speedups over tested exact solvers.
AI.conclusion: QEDist makes exact distance certification practical for selecting and optimizing finite-length quantum codes, scaling to large codes and fault-distance certification with substantial speedups.

title: Black holes as black boxes: a query lower bound on python's lunch decoding
summary: The python's lunch conjecture relates the complexity of bulk reconstruction in holographic tensor networks to an exponential cost associated with post-selection. We establish a tight query lower bound for this decoding problem in a Haar random oracle model, with a python's lunch circuit that applies Haar random unitary $U$ to a logical input and fixed ancillas, followed by post-selection on $m$ output qubits. Given one copy of the normalized encoded state and coherent oracle access to $U$ and $U^\dagger$, including controlled queries, we prove that recovering even a single logical bit with constant average advantage requires $Ω(2^{m/2})$ queries. Together with the state-independent amplitude amplification upper bound for approximately isometric encodings, this establishes query complexity $Θ(2^{m/2})$ at constant decoding accuracy. We also comment on the decoding cost for other "admissible'" ensembles of unitaries $U$ which give rise to families of approximately isometric holographic maps.

AI.tldr: The paper proves a tight Θ(2^{m/2}) query lower bound (and matching upper bound) for decoding in a Haar random oracle model of a "python's lunch" tensor-network circuit, confirming the exponential post-selection cost conjectured for bulk reconstruction, even for recovering a single logical bit.
AI.motivation: The python's lunch conjecture posits that bulk reconstruction in holographic tensor networks incurs an exponential cost tied to post-selection. Prior work lacked a rigorous, tight complexity-theoretic characterization of this decoding cost, motivating a formal query-complexity analysis of the reconstruction/decoding problem.
AI.method: The authors model the problem in a Haar random oracle setting: a python's lunch circuit applies a Haar random unitary U to a logical input plus fixed ancillas, then post-selects on m output qubits. The decoder receives one copy of the normalized encoded state along with coherent oracle access to U and U^\dagger, including controlled queries. They derive a query lower bound via an adversary-type argument and combine it with a state-independent amplitude amplification upper bound for approximately isometric encodings; they also discuss extensions to other "admissible" unitary ensembles yielding approximately isometric holographic maps.
AI.result: Recovering even a single logical bit with constant average advantage requires Ω(2^{m/2}) queries under coherent (including controlled) oracle access. Combined with the amplitude amplification upper bound, the query complexity is Θ(2^{m/2}) at constant decoding accuracy, establishing tightness.
AI.conclusion: The exponential 2^{m/2} decoding cost underlying the python's lunch conjecture is rigorously established and tight in the query model, and the analysis extends to broader admissible ensembles of unitaries that produce approximately isometric holographic maps.

title: Contact-number hyperuniformity at glass close packing in infinite dimensions
summary: We investigate contact-number fluctuations of harmonic spheres near glass close packing (GCP), the amorphous jamming endpoint reached by compressing an ideal glass. Using replica theory, we show that the Gardner-unstable region shrinks toward jamming as the spatial dimension increases, allowing GCP to be approached along a stable one-step replica symmetry breaking branch in the high-dimensional limit. By coupling an external field to the local contact number, we derive the variance of the total contact number and the wave-number-dependent structure factor directly from the microscopic interactions. At GCP, the structure factor vanishes quadratically at small scaled wave numbers, demonstrating contact-number hyperuniformity. Upon weak compression above GCP, the structure factor develops a low-wave-number plateau whose height is proportional to the excess coordination. These results provide an analytical description of contact-number hyperuniformity and its breakdown upon compression.

AI.tldr: Using replica theory, the authors analyze contact-number fluctuations of harmonic spheres near glass close packing (GCP) and show that at GCP the structure factor vanishes quadratically at small scaled wave numbers (contact-number hyperuniformity), which breaks down into a low-wave-number plateau under weak compression.
AI.motivation: How contact-number fluctuations behave near the amorphous jamming endpoint (GCP) is unclear; the paper aims to characterize contact-number hyperuniformity and its breakdown analytically from microscopic interactions.
AI.method: Replica theory of harmonic spheres. The Gardner-unstable region is shown to shrink toward jamming with increasing spatial dimension, enabling GCP to be approached along a stable one-step replica symmetry breaking (1-RSB) branch in the high-dimensional limit. An external field is coupled to the local contact number to derive the total contact-number variance and the wave-number-dependent structure factor.
AI.result: At GCP the structure factor vanishes quadratically at small scaled wave numbers, demonstrating contact-number hyperuniformity. Upon weak compression above GCP, the structure factor develops a low-wave-number plateau whose height is proportional to the excess coordination.
AI.conclusion: The work provides an analytical description of contact-number hyperuniformity and its breakdown upon compression, linking macroscopic fluctuation statistics to microscopic interactions.

title: A Proposal for Quantum Reference Frames in Quantum Field Theory and their Experimental Exploration
summary: We construct quantum reference frames (QRFs) in quantum field theory, using localized modes of a scalar field as frames for its shift symmetry. We import tools from relativistic quantum information to explicitly compute entropies and correlation measures of relational observables, investigating their frame dependence and the new features arising from the field-theoretic character of the system. Unlike QRFs for systems with finitely many degrees of freedom, localized field-theoretic QRFs are necessarily mixed in physically relevant states and generically correlated with the subsystems they describe. These aspects of QRFs for fields affect the properties of relational observables in a subtle way. Furthermore, we put forward a proposal for testing these predictions with existing quantum simulators based on ultracold atoms and quantum fluids, thus connecting QRF physics with analogue gravity platforms.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs quantum reference frames (QRFs) from localized scalar-field modes for the field's shift symmetry, computes entropies and correlation measures of relational observables, and shows that field-theoretic QRFs are necessarily mixed and generically correlated with the described subsystems, proposing tests with ultracold-atom and quantum-fluid simulators.
AI.motivation: Existing QRF constructions treat systems with finitely many degrees of freedom; extending QRFs to quantum field theory is nontrivial because localized field modes may be mixed and entangled with other subsystems in physically relevant states, potentially altering the properties of relational observables.
AI.method: Localized modes of a scalar field are used as reference frames for the field's shift symmetry. Tools from relativistic quantum information are imported to explicitly compute entropies and correlation measures of the resulting relational observables, analyzing their frame dependence and field-theoretic features. A proposal is advanced to test the predictions with existing quantum simulators based on ultracold atoms and quantum fluids, linking QRF physics to analogue gravity platforms.
AI.result: Unlike QRFs for finite-dimensional systems, localized field-theoretic QRFs are necessarily mixed in physically relevant states and generically correlated with the subsystems they describe; these features affect the properties of relational observables in a subtle, frame-dependent way. Entropy and correlation measures are explicitly computed, and experimental tests with ultracold-atom and quantum-fluid platforms are proposed.
AI.conclusion: Field-theoretic QRFs introduce qualitatively new, mixedness- and correlation-driven behaviour in relational observables, extending QRF physics beyond finite-dimensional settings and opening a route to empirical investigation via analogue gravity quantum simulators.

title: Stochastic Dynamics of Domain Walls on a Racetrack: Impact of Inhomogeneity of Magnetic Anisotropy
summary: Racetrack memory is a spintronic technology that stores information in current-driven magnetic domain walls (DW), offering a promising route toward non-volatile, high-density, and high-speed memory devices. In ultrathin magnetic films, atomic-scale interface disorder can produce spatially inhomogeneous magnetic anisotropy, creating a complex spatially varying energy landscape that strongly influences DW motion. In this work, we model anisotropy inhomogeneities using a two-dimensional fractal Weierstrass--Mandelbrot function, which provides independent control over the disorder amplitude and characteristic spatial scale. Micromagnetic simulations reveal pronounced stochasticity of current-driven domain-wall transport even in the absence of thermal fluctuations. Transport is quantified by the transmission fraction, defined as the fraction of DWs that successfully reach a detector after propagating through a disordered racetrack. We investigate its dependence on current density, disorder amplitude, and the spatial scale of the anisotropy inhomogeneity. The resulting transmission statistics are described by Gaussian error-function profiles and exhibit a universal scaling behavior upon normalization by the corresponding median values. Statistical analysis of DW trajectories further characterizes the disorder-induced fluctuations of the propagation process. The variance of the random DW positions shows a pronounced dependence on disorder amplitude and is well described by the proposed phenomenological model. These results provide a quantitative framework for describing stochastic DW transport in structurally disordered racetracks and establish disorder-induced reliability limits in racetrack-memory devices.

AI.tldr: Current-driven domain-wall (DW) transport in racetrack memory is modeled under spatially inhomogeneous anisotropy, generated by a 2D fractal Weierstrass–Mandelbrot disorder function. Micromagnetic simulations show strong stochastic DW motion even without thermal noise, with transmission statistics collapsing onto universal curves and DW-position variance captured by a phenomenological model.
AI.motivation: In ultrathin magnetic films, atomic-scale interface disorder produces spatially inhomogeneous magnetic anisotropy, creating a complex energy landscape that strongly affects DW motion and threatens the reliability of racetrack-memory devices. A quantitative description of disorder-induced stochastic transport is lacking.
AI.method: Anisotropy inhomogeneities are modeled with a two-dimensional fractal Weierstrass–Mandelbrot function allowing independent tuning of disorder amplitude and characteristic spatial scale. Micromagnetic simulations of current-driven DW transport are performed at zero thermal fluctuation. Transport is quantified by a transmission fraction (fraction of DWs reaching a detector), analyzed versus current density, disorder amplitude, and spatial scale, complemented by statistical analysis of DW trajectories.
AI.result: Transmission statistics follow Gaussian error-function profiles and exhibit universal scaling when normalized by their median values. DW-position variance depends strongly on disorder amplitude and is well described by a proposed phenomenological model, characterizing disorder-induced fluctuations of propagation.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a quantitative framework for stochastic DW transport in structurally disordered racetracks and identifies disorder-induced reliability limits for racetrack-memory devices.

title: Restoring quantum neural network trainability through reusable calibration
summary: Quantum neural networks (QNNs) rely on measured quantum observables to guide optimization, but hardware noise can suppress the parameter-dependent signals essential for learning. Here, we develop a structure-preserving error-mitigation framework that improves QNN trainability through reusable calibration of the quantum circuit's effective noise response. By calibrating a reference circuit with the same gate architecture as the trainable circuit, we construct regularized estimators of local quantum features that remain fixed throughout training. We quantify how calibration errors and response mismatches affect the recovery of both observables and their derivatives. Numerical simulations demonstrate enhanced loss-landscape contrast, faster convergence, and improved classification performance, and an IBM Quantum experiment confirms improved closed-loop variational optimization under hardware noise. We further demonstrate calibration reuse in a modular QNN comprising 25 independent four-qubit channels, corresponding to 100 qubits in aggregate. Our results establish reusable feature calibration as a practical approach to improving noise-limited quantum machine learning without repeated calibration at every training step.

AI.tldr: A structure-preserving error-mitigation framework calibrates a reference circuit once and reuses the calibration throughout QNN training to construct regularized estimators of parameter-dependent features, improving trainability under hardware noise.
AI.motivation: QNNs rely on measured observables to guide optimization, but hardware noise suppresses the parameter-dependent signals essential for learning, degrading gradient information and trainability.
AI.method: Calibrate a reference circuit sharing the same gate architecture as the trainable circuit, obtaining the effective noise response. From this, build regularized estimators of local quantum features kept fixed during training. The authors analytically quantify how calibration errors and response mismatches affect recovery of observables and their derivatives.
AI.result: Numerical simulations show enhanced loss-landscape contrast, faster convergence, and improved classification. An IBM Quantum experiment confirms improved closed-loop variational optimization under noise. Calibration reuse is demonstrated in a modular QNN of 25 independent four-qubit channels (100 qubits aggregate).
AI.conclusion: Reusable feature calibration is a practical route to improving noise-limited quantum machine learning without recalibrating at every training step.

title: Robust Passive Quantum Memory in Three Dimensions, Part I: Thermal and Zero-Temperature Perturbative Stability
summary: Whether a three-dimensional quantum many-body system with geometrically local, bounded-degree interactions can passively protect encoded quantum information has remained a central open question since Kitaev introduced topological quantum computation. Passive protection requires stability against both thermal noise at nonzero temperature and generic static Hamiltonian perturbations Balasubramanian, Davydova, and Lin (BDL) recently established unperturbed three-dimensional thermal self-correction using a recursively defined family of stabilizer Hamiltonians. However, they left open whether their construction remains stable against quantum perturbations, even at zero temperature. In this paper, we show that a slight variant of the BDL code family achieves stability along both boundary axes of the perturbation-temperature phase diagram as the system size grows. Following BDL, in the absence of perturbation it is thermally stable below a critical temperature, achieving a stretched-exponentially long memory lifetime when coupled to any local Markovian thermal bath generated by single-site system-bath interactions satisfying detailed balance with bounded coupling rates. At zero temperature under arbitrary weak, superpolynomially decaying quantum perturbations, the family maintains a uniform bulk spectral gap, superpolynomially small ground-space splitting, and a superpolynomially long closed-system unitary memory lifetime for quasi-locally dressed logical observables. To prove this zero-temperature stability, we establish local topological quantum order across the multiscale hierarchy using a linearly dilated relaxation of the usual Bravyi-Hastings-Michalakis criteria. In the companion paper, we combine the tools developed here with finite-temperature worldline cluster expansions to establish passive self-correction throughout the phase diagram's positive-temperature perturbed interior.

AI.tldr: A slight variant of the BDL three-dimensional stabilizer code family achieves passive quantum memory stability against both thermal noise and weak quantum perturbations as system size grows.
AI.motivation: Passive protection of encoded quantum information in a three-dimensional, geometrically local, bounded-degree quantum many-body system has been open since Kitaev's topological quantum computation. BDL established unperturbed 3D thermal self-correction but left open stability against quantum Hamiltonian perturbations, even at zero temperature.
AI.method: The authors introduce a variant of the BDL recursively defined stabilizer Hamiltonian family. For finite temperature they analyze coupling to local Markovian thermal baths from single-site system-bath interactions obeying detailed balance with bounded rates. For zero temperature, they prove local topological quantum order (LTQO) across the multiscale hierarchy using a linearly dilated relaxation of the Bravyi-Hastings-Michalakis criteria.
AI.result: The variant is thermally stable below a critical temperature, with stretched-exponentially long memory lifetime. At zero temperature under arbitrary weak, superpolynomially decaying quantum perturbations, it retains a uniform bulk spectral gap, superpolynomially small ground-space splitting, and superpolynomially long closed-system unitary memory lifetime for quasi-locally dressed logical observables—stability along both boundary axes of the perturbation-temperature phase diagram.
AI.conclusion: The construction yields passive self-correction along the thermal and perturbative boundaries of the phase diagram. Combined with finite-temperature worldline cluster expansions (companion paper), the tools extend passive self-correction to the positive-temperature perturbed interior.

title: Loss-Tolerant Quantum Correlations Between Atomic and Photonic Qubits
summary: Quantum physics forbids cloning of a qubit. Therefore, a qubit is irreversibly lost upon loss of the information carrier. To mitigate this physical loss, it has been proposed to distribute the logical information across an entangled set of physical qubits, some of which can be lost. Previous experiments illustrated this concept, but failed to demonstrate a gain in the information-retrieval efficiency. Here we address this challenge with photons for which the total loss, from generation to detection, is below the loss-tolerance threshold of $50\%$. Using two single-atom emitters in an optical cavity, we encode information into the photons of a graph state and observe an efficiency gain for retrieving quantum correlations between the atoms and the photons for single-qubit measurements in the Pauli $X$ and $Z$ bases. Although technical errors reduce the probability to obtain the \textit{correct} result, we achieve average fidelities as high as $\gtrsim\!70\%$ without and $\gtrsim\!75\%$ with error detection, demonstrating entanglement between the atomic and encoded photonic qubits. Lowering the encoding errors is a next natural step toward loss-tolerant photonic quantum-information processing.

AI.tldr: Photonic experiment demonstrates a genuine information-retrieval efficiency gain from encoding a logical qubit in a loss-tolerant graph state, using two single-atom emitters in a cavity with total loss below the 50% threshold.
AI.motivation: A qubit cannot be cloned, so when its carrier is lost the information is irreversibly destroyed. Distributing logical information across an entangled set of physical qubits, some of which may be lost, was proposed as a mitigation, but prior experiments only illustrated the concept without showing an actual gain in information-retrieval efficiency.
AI.method: Encode information into the photons of a graph state generated with two single-atom emitters in an optical cavity, engineered so that total loss from generation to detection stays below the 50% loss-tolerance threshold. Retrieve quantum correlations between the atoms and the photons under single-qubit Pauli X and Z measurements.
AI.result: An efficiency gain for retrieving quantum correlations is observed relative to the uncoded case. Average fidelities reach ≳70% without and ≳75% with error detection, with technical errors reducing the probability of a correct result but still demonstrating atom–photon entanglement.
AI.conclusion: Loss-tolerant encoding of photonic quantum information is experimentally validated with a net retrieval gain; reducing encoding errors is the natural next step toward loss-tolerant photonic quantum-information processing.

title: Distrustful entanglement-based Quantum Key Distribution
summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) is the one of the most explored application of quantum information theory. While practical QKD systems are being deployed around the world, a major issue of these setups are that one has to trust the measurement devices of both parties. On the other hand, the most secure among such schemes are called device-independent (DI) QKD protocols, where no component of the setup is assumed to be trusted. However, due to their high technological demand, their loophole-free version currently remain out of practical reach. Inspired by the real world, we consider the traditional QKD in a distrustful measurement setting, that is, the measurement devices can only be trusted upto some level of confidence, which might still be large but not completely trusted. We then derive a general lower bound on the asymptotic key rate in this scenario. Then considering perfect detectors and source, and the entanglement-based BB84 (BBM) protocol, we show that to obtain secure keys one needs to trust their devices more than 82 %. However, we observe that such a protocol can not be realised with any level of distrust using the realistic detectors and sources at the current technology. Finally, we also consider the BBM protocol with arbitrary dimensional systems and observe that they are more robust to distrust than qubit systems. Consequently, with the same level of distrust, along with same detector and source efficiences, one can get better key rates with high-dimensional systems.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes entanglement-based BB84 (BBM) QKD under partially trusted measurement devices, deriving a general lower bound on the asymptotic key rate and quantifying how much device trust is required for secure keys.
AI.motivation: Practical QKD requires trusting both parties' measurement devices, while fully device-independent (DI) QKD removes this assumption but is technologically impractical and remains out of reach for loophole-free implementations. The authors seek a realistic middle ground where measurement devices are trusted only to some (possibly high but incomplete) level of confidence.
AI.method: The authors model a distrustful measurement setting with partial device trust, derive a general lower bound on the asymptotic key rate, and then specialize to ideal detectors and sources in the entanglement-based BBM protocol. They also examine the BBM protocol with arbitrary-dimensional systems and compare robustness to distrust under realistic detector and source efficiencies.
AI.result: For perfect detectors and sources in the qubit BBM protocol, secure keys require trusting the devices more than 82%. With realistic detectors and sources at current technology, the protocol cannot be realized under any level of distrust. High-dimensional BBM systems are found to be more robust to distrust than qubit systems, yielding better key rates at the same distrust level and detector/source efficiencies.
AI.conclusion: Partial-trust QKD offers a practical intermediate between fully trusted and device-independent schemes, but qubit BBM demands very high trust (above 82%) and is infeasible with current realistic components; higher-dimensional systems mitigate distrust and enable improved key rates.

title: AI Scientist Discovered Robust Quantum Control
summary: Protecting quantum coherence is a central theme of modern quantum technologies. Carefully designed control pulses can extend coherence by suppressing disorder and unwanted interactions. However, designing robust pulse sequences remains challenging in interacting multi-level systems, where multiple independent error channels must be controlled in the presence of experimental imperfections. Here we introduce QORA, a multi-agent artificial intelligence framework that integrates theoretical reasoning, automated experimental calibration and control for closed-loop discovery of quantum control sequences. Applied to a dense ensemble of spin-1 nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond, QORA discovers AID-ROD, a series of AI-discovered sequences that nearly double the measured spin coherence time relative to the state-of-the-art human-designed sequence DROID-C3PO. Subsequence analysis by human researchers reveals a hierarchy of error suppression: 18-pulse blocks suppress linear and quadratic onsite disorder and common-mode drive-amplitude errors, while their arrangement over a longer cycle reduces dipolar interactions, providing a physical explanation for the observed improvement and robustness in AID-ROD. These results demonstrate AI-guided experimental discovery of robust quantum control and identify a design strategy for protecting coherence in interacting multi-level systems beyond qubits.

AI.tldr: QORA, a multi-agent AI framework combining theoretical reasoning with automated experimental calibration, discovers pulse sequences (AID-ROD) that nearly double spin coherence time in dense spin-1 NV ensembles versus the human-designed DROID-C3PO.
AI.motivation: Protecting quantum coherence is central to quantum technologies, but designing robust control pulses in interacting multi-level systems with multiple independent error channels and experimental imperfections remains challenging.
AI.method: A multi-agent AI framework (QORA) integrating theoretical reasoning, automated experimental calibration, and closed-loop control discovery, applied to a dense ensemble of spin-1 nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond.
AI.result: QORA discovers AID-ROD sequences that nearly double measured spin coherence time relative to DROID-C3PO; subsequence analysis reveals hierarchical error suppression: 18-pulse blocks suppress linear/quadratic onsite disorder and common-mode drive-amplitude errors, while their longer-cycle arrangement reduces dipolar interactions.
AI.conclusion: AI-guided experimental discovery yields robust quantum control and a design strategy for protecting coherence in interacting multi-level systems beyond qubits.

title: Quantum Reference Frames, Locality, and Microcausality in Quantum Field Theory
summary: As a consequence of the relativistic spectrum condition, quantum reference frames for translations on Minkowski space are never described by projection-valued measures, and in many cases fail a weaker spacetime localisation property known as the norm-$1$ condition. This has several implications for the local and observable structure of quantum field theories described relative to even the best available frame: for a large class of frame states, strict locality is replaced by almost locality, and microcausality by commutators that decay rapidly with increasing separation, corresponding to an effective smearing of the light cone by the localisation density of the frame state. Operations built from finitely many almost local Kraus operators, for example nonselective measurements of relativised local observables, satisfy an approximate no-signalling bound, with a residue attributable to the localisation uncertainty of the frame. Whether causality in its strongest operational form -- non-disturbance under all physically realisable operations -- survives relativisation is left open. An upshot of our finding is that quantum field theories formulated relative to a quantum reference frame cannot rest on the traditional axioms, and some general relational axiomatisation must replace at least some of them by taking into account physically realistic properties of the frame.

AI.tldr: Quantum reference frames for translations on Minkowski space cannot be described by projection-valued measures and often violate the norm-1 condition, which weakens strict locality and microcausality in relativised quantum field theory to approximate versions.
AI.motivation: The relativistic spectrum condition constrains how quantum reference frames for translations can be localised, yet standard QFT axioms assume sharp spacetime localisation. The paper examines what happens to the local and observable structure of QFT when described relative to such frames.
AI.method: Analysis of quantum reference frames for Minkowski translations under the relativistic spectrum condition, examining PVM descriptions, the norm-1 condition, almost locality, decay of commutators (microcausality), Kraus operators for relativised local observables, and approximate no-signalling bounds.
AI.result: For a large class of frame states, strict locality is replaced by almost locality; microcausality becomes commutators decaying rapidly with separation, matching an effective smearing of the light cone by the frame's localisation density. Operations from finitely many almost local Kraus operators (e.g. nonselective measurements of relativised local observables) obey an approximate no-signalling bound with residue from frame localisation uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: Whether causality in its strongest operational form (non-disturbance under all physically realisable operations) survives relativisation remains open. QFTs formulated relative to a quantum reference frame cannot rely on traditional axioms; a general relational axiomatisation must replace at least some of them, incorporating realistic properties of the frame.

title: Transient State Preservation of a Dissipative Qubit via Lyapunov Control
comment: Accepted for presentation at IEEE URUCON 2026
summary: Preserving quantum states in the presence of environmental decoherence remains a fundamental challenge for quantum information processing. This work investigates whether Hamiltonian Lyapunov feedback can transiently preserve the state of an open qubit by reshaping its trajectory under Markovian dissipation. A state-error Lyapunov function is adopted to derive an analytical feedback law for Lindblad dynamics, ensuring a nonincreasing Lyapunov function whenever the control sensitivities are nonzero. The analysis identifies the geometric conditions under which the feedback becomes ineffective, showing that control authority vanishes when the current and target Bloch vectors are collinear. Numerical simulations are performed for amplitude damping and pure dephasing using selected target states. Performance is evaluated through fidelity, accumulated infidelity, dwell time above a fidelity threshold, coherence, and control effort. The results demonstrate that the proposed feedback cannot eliminate irreversible dissipation or achieve universal asymptotic stabilization, but it can provide transient benefits for selected target-channel combinations. In particular, under amplitude damping, the controller significantly reduces accumulated infidelity and substantially extends the interval during which the system remains above a prescribed fidelity threshold. In the pure dephasing cases examined, improvements in fidelity are generally limited, although transient coherence preservation is observed for the oblique target considered, revealing a trade-off between coherence and state fidelity. These findings indicate that Lyapunov-based Hamiltonian feedback is best suited as a transient preservation mechanism and motivate its application to gate operations and preservation of prepared states during finite time intervals before their use or readout.

AI.tldr: Hamiltonian Lyapunov feedback is analyzed for preserving an open qubit under Markovian dissipation; it yields no universal asymptotic stabilization but provides transient fidelity/coherence benefits, notably under amplitude damping.
AI.motivation: Environmental decoherence threatens quantum information processing, so the paper asks whether Hamiltonian Lyapunov feedback can transiently preserve an open qubit's state by reshaping its trajectory under Markovian dissipation.
AI.method: A state-error Lyapunov function is used to derive an analytical feedback law for Lindblad dynamics, guaranteeing a nonincreasing Lyapunov function when control sensitivities are nonzero. Geometric conditions for control failure are identified (authority vanishes when current and target Bloch vectors are collinear). Simulations cover amplitude damping and pure dephasing for selected target states, evaluated by fidelity, accumulated infidelity, dwell time above a fidelity threshold, coherence, and control effort.
AI.result: The feedback cannot eliminate irreversible dissipation or achieve universal asymptotic stabilization, but gives transient gains for selected target-channel pairs. Under amplitude damping it significantly reduces accumulated infidelity and lengthens the interval above a prescribed fidelity threshold. Under pure dephasing, fidelity improvements are limited, though transient coherence preservation occurs for the oblique target, revealing a coherence-fidelity trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Lyapunov-based Hamiltonian feedback is best suited as a transient preservation mechanism, motivating its use for gate operations and for protecting prepared states over finite intervals before use or readout.

title: Microwave-optical quantum transduction with quantum-well exciton polaritons
summary: Linking superconducting quantum processors over optical fiber requires microwave-optical quantum transducers that are efficient, high-bandwidth, and low-noise. This combination has been out of reach because of the weak nonlinearities of conventional electro-optic (EO) materials. We propose a transducer with an engineered, strong EO nonlinearity using the quantum-confined Stark effect (QCSE) of quantum-well excitons. The QCSE transducer leverages the strong light-matter interactions and extreme polarizability of quantum well excitons. Strong coupling to an optical cavity forms exciton-polaritons whose vacuum EO coupling is up to five orders of magnitude larger than in a typical thin-film lithium niobate device. We describe a GaAs/AlGaAs stepped-quantum-well transducer design with predicted transduction efficiencies above 60% and fewer than 0.01 added noise quanta over a $\sim$60 MHz bandwidth, using pump powers below 10 $μ$W and loaded optical and microwave quality factors of only $3\times10^4$ and $10^3$. We further show that the cavity protection of the polariton provides robustness against inhomogeneous broadening of the quantum well excitons.

AI.tldr: A microwave-optical transducer using the quantum-confined Stark effect (QCSE) of quantum-well excitons achieves strong engineered electro-optic coupling, predicting >60% transduction efficiency and <0.01 added noise quanta over ~60 MHz bandwidth.
AI.motivation: Fiber-linking superconducting quantum processors requires efficient, high-bandwidth, low-noise microwave-optical transducers, but conventional electro-optic (EO) materials have weak nonlinearities that make this combination unattainable.
AI.method: Engineer strong EO nonlinearity via the QCSE of quantum-well excitons, exploiting their strong light-matter interaction and extreme polarizability. Strong coupling of excitons to an optical cavity forms exciton-polaritons whose vacuum EO coupling is up to five orders of magnitude larger than thin-film lithium niobate. A GaAs/AlGaAs stepped-quantum-well design is proposed.
AI.result: Predicted transduction efficiencies above 60% and fewer than 0.01 added noise quanta over ~60 MHz bandwidth, using pump powers below 10 μW and loaded optical/microwave quality factors of only 3×10^4 and 10^3. Cavity protection of the polariton yields robustness against inhomogeneous broadening of the quantum-well excitons.
AI.conclusion: QCSE-based exciton-polariton transducers offer a promising route to efficient, high-bandwidth, low-noise microwave-optical conversion for superconducting quantum interconnects, with tolerance to exciton inhomogeneous broadening.

title: Charge self-consistent DFT+QDMFT framework with a Krylov-based quantum impurity solver
summary: We integrate a quantum impurity solver into a charge self-consistent density functional theory (DFT) plus quantum dynamical mean-field theory framework. The solver optimizes adaptive circuits to approximate the ground state of the impurity model and its particle and hole excitations, and reconstructs the impurity Green's function from their Hamiltonian moments. Higher-order moments are predicted from low-order ones using a machine-learning model, while regularized optimization mitigates violations of causality in the resulting self-energy. The latter is used to update the charge density until self-consistency is achieved. We demonstrate the framework through body-centered cubic lithium calculations and compare the results with a reference one using a continuous-time quantum Monte Carlo solver. These calculations converge with root-mean-square charge-density residuals below $\boldsymbol{2\times10^{-3}}$ and yield a nearly vanishing impurity self-energy, consistent with the noninteracting limit used for weakly correlated lithium.

AI.tldr: A quantum impurity solver based on adaptive variational circuits is integrated into charge self-consistent DFT+DMFT and validated on bcc lithium, converging to small charge-density residuals with a near-vanishing impurity self-energy.
AI.motivation: Quantum computers offer a route to impurity solvers for DFT+DMFT, but existing quantum solvers have not been embedded into a fully charge self-consistent loop that maintains a physically admissible (causal) self-energy while reconstructing the impurity Green's function accurately.
AI.method: The solver optimizes adaptive circuits to approximate the impurity ground state plus particle and hole excitations, then rebuilds the impurity Green's function from Hamiltonian moments of these states. Higher-order moments are extrapolated from lower-order ones via a machine-learning model, and a regularized optimization suppresses causality violations in the resulting self-energy. This self-energy updates the charge density iteratively until self-consistency. Demonstrated on bcc lithium and benchmarked against a continuous-time quantum Monte Carlo solver.
AI.result: The self-consistent calculations converge with RMS charge-density residuals below 2×10^-3 and yield a nearly vanishing impurity self-energy, in agreement with the noninteracting limit expected for weakly correlated lithium and with the CT-QMC reference.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive-circuit impurity solvers with moment-based Green's function reconstruction and ML moment extrapolation can be embedded in charge self-consistent DFT+DMFT, providing a viable quantum-computing pathway for materials calculations while preserving causality.

title: Infrared fluctuations and collective entanglement modes in harmonic lattices
summary:
We investigate how infrared fluctuations and spatial separation shape vacuum entanglement between two finite regions in the relativistic harmonic chain and its Lifshitz generalizations. At fixed lattice spacing and finite geometry, we establish that logarithmic negativity remains uniformly bounded as the mass approaches zero, while mutual information diverges. Infrared-enhanced total correlations therefore do not provide an unbounded distillable-entanglement resource. Using local symplectic consolidation, we identify the collective canonical modes carrying the negativity and follow their evolution with separation. Their participation crosses over from localization near the facing boundaries to a collective distribution within each region. Expansion in the adjacent-state canonical basis connects this evolution to progressively weaker, more extended reference modes, including adjacent-halo directions.
  Building on the established concentration of long-distance logarithmic negativity into a single canonical pair, we show that its spatial participation is smooth and infrared-dominated despite its ultraviolet canonical structure, a distinction also present in pure-state entanglement modes. These results refine the ultraviolet mode picture by resolving the long-wavelength organization of the oscillators participating in the surviving entanglement. Across the massless dispersions studied, the normalized participation approaches a universal long-distance profile when separation is scaled by the negativity radius. Its detailed form and the entanglement range nevertheless remain sensitive to ultraviolet deformations. Together, these findings distinguish infrared-enhanced correlations from distillable entanglement and reveal the collective spatial organization underlying its persistence at large separation.

AI.tldr: Infrared-enhanced total correlations do not imply unbounded distillable entanglement: in relativistic and Lifshitz harmonic chains, logarithmic negativity between two finite regions stays uniformly bounded as mass vanishes, while mutual information diverges; the surviving negativity is carried by a collective canonical mode whose spatial participation is smooth and infrared-dominated.
AI.motivation: Long-wavelength (infrared) fluctuations are known to generate divergent total correlations such as mutual information, and it is often assumed that such correlations constitute a growing entanglement resource. The paper asks whether infrared-enhanced correlations actually translate into unbounded distillable entanglement, and how the oscillators sustaining the surviving entanglement are spatially organized.
AI.method: Study of the relativistic harmonic chain and its Lifshitz generalizations, with fixed lattice spacing and finite geometry, in the massless (vanishing-mass) limit. Entanglement is quantified via logarithmic negativity and mutual information. A local symplectic consolidation procedure identifies the collective canonical modes carrying the negativity, and expansion in the adjacent-state canonical basis (including adjacent-halo directions) is used to track these modes as a function of region separation.
AI.result: Logarithmic negativity remains uniformly bounded as the mass goes to zero, whereas mutual information diverges. The negativity-carrying collective mode's participation crosses over from localization near the facing boundaries to a collective distribution across each region, corresponding to progressively weaker, more extended reference modes. Its spatial participation is smooth and infrared-dominated despite an ultraviolet canonical structure, a distinction also found in pure-state entanglement modes. For massless dispersions, the normalized participation approaches a universal long-distance profile when separation is scaled by the negativity radius, though its detailed shape and the entanglement range remain sensitive to ultraviolet deformations.
AI.conclusion: Infrared-enhanced correlations must be distinguished from distillable entanglement: divergent total correlations do not supply an unbounded entanglement resource. The persistence of long-distance negativity is underlain by a collective spatial organization of oscillators that is smooth and long-wavelength in character, refining the ultraviolet mode picture and clarifying which degrees of freedom remain entangled at large separation.

title: Quantum-Classical Separation in Probability Distribution Transport via Nonlocal Games
summary: In many-body physics and generative artificial intelligence, locality provides a natural notion of phase equivalence: two quantum states or classical probability distributions are regarded as in the same phase when local dynamics can reversibly transform one into the other. This raises a fundamental question: can local quantum dynamics transport classical probability distributions in ways that local classical dynamics cannot? We establish a quantum-classical separation in distribution transport: two classical distributions can be connected exactly and reversibly by a constant-depth local quantum circuit, whereas classical stochastic transport requires a substantially larger spatial range. We demonstrate this separation explicitly on a one-dimensional chain and develop a general construction principle on graphs, based on nonlocal games. Moreover, the source distribution can itself be generated by a simple local classical process, establishing a quantum advantage in distribution generation as well. Our results reveal a fundamental distinction between classical and quantum local reversibility, even when both the initial and final states are entirely classical.

AI.tldr: Constant-depth local quantum circuits can reversibly interconvert two classical distributions that no constant-range classical stochastic process can connect, establishing a quantum-classical separation in both distribution transport and generation.
AI.motivation: Locality is used as the notion of phase equivalence for quantum states and classical distributions: two objects are in the same phase if local dynamics reversibly maps one to the other. The paper asks whether local quantum dynamics can transport classical probability distributions in ways local classical dynamics provably cannot, even when both endpoints are fully classical.
AI.method: The authors construct an explicit separation on a one-dimensional chain: two classical distributions connected exactly and reversibly by a constant-depth local quantum circuit, while any classical stochastic transport needs substantially larger spatial range. They then generalize to arbitrary graphs via a construction principle rooted in nonlocal games, and show the source distribution is itself preparable by a simple local classical process.
AI.result: A quantum-classical separation in distribution transport is established on 1D chains and generalized to graphs using nonlocal-game-based constructions. The separation also yields a quantum advantage in distribution generation, since the input distribution admits a simple local classical preparation.
AI.conclusion: Classical and quantum local reversibility are fundamentally distinct even when initial and final states are entirely classical: local quantum dynamics achieves reversible transport/generation of classical distributions beyond constant-range classical stochastic reach.

title: Quantum Fisher information matrices for time-evolved bosonic Gaussian thermal states
summary: Quantum Fisher information (QFI) is a fundamental quantum metrological quantity arising from the second order term in a Taylor expansion of a smooth divergence evaluated at nearby quantum states. The $α$-$z$ information matrix is a QFI measure arising from the $α$-$z$ Rényi relative entropy, and QFI measures corresponding to various underlying smooth divergences may be recovered from the $α$-$z$ information matrix, including the standard symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) QFI. Bosonic Gaussian states are common probe states for quantum metrological tasks and admit a complete characterization in terms of their first and second moments. In this work, we consider the quantum metrological task of estimating parameters that characterize a Gaussian unitary time evolution of a faithful bosonic Gaussian thermal state. We establish a formula for the $α$-$z$ information matrix of faithful bosonic Gaussian thermal states that have undergone a Gaussian unitary time evolution. As an example, we calculate entries of the $α$-$z$ information matrix for a two-mode Gaussian thermal state that has undergone a beam splitting operation. For a parametrized family of time-evolved bosonic Gaussian states, we also derive a formula for the SLD operator, which is known to provide a measurement scheme that saturates the quantum Crámer-Rao bound and thus achieves the ultimate precision for single parameter estimation.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a formula for the α-z information matrix (a family of QFI measures from α-z Rényi relative entropy) for faithful bosonic Gaussian thermal states under Gaussian unitary time evolution, computes entries for a two-mode beam-splitter example, and derives the SLD operator for parametrized time-evolved Gaussian states to attain the quantum Cramér–Rao bound.
AI.motivation: Quantum Fisher information (QFI) underpins quantum metrology as the second-order term of smooth divergence expansions, and the α-z information matrix unifies QFI measures (including SLD-QFI) from the α-z Rényi relative entropy. Bosonic Gaussian states are ubiquitous probe states fully characterized by first and second moments, yet a general treatment of the α-z information matrix for time-evolved Gaussian thermal states was lacking, motivating a systematic formula for estimating parameters of Gaussian unitary evolutions.
AI.method: The authors consider estimating parameters that characterize a Gaussian unitary time evolution of a faithful bosonic Gaussian thermal state. Exploiting the first- and second-moment characterization of Gaussian states, they establish a closed-form expression for the α-z information matrix of faithful bosonic Gaussian thermal states that have undergone such evolution, and derive the corresponding SLD operator for a parametrized family of time-evolved bosonic Gaussian states.
AI.result: A general formula for the α-z information matrix of time-evolved faithful bosonic Gaussian thermal states is established. As an illustrative case, entries of the α-z information matrix are explicitly computed for a two-mode Gaussian thermal state subjected to a beam-splitting operation. Additionally, an SLD operator formula is derived, yielding a measurement scheme saturating the quantum Cramér–Rao bound and thus achieving the ultimate single-parameter estimation precision.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a unified, moment-based framework for evaluating the α-z information matrix and SLD operator of time-evolved Gaussian thermal states, enabling optimal measurement schemes for estimating parameters of Gaussian unitary dynamics and recovering standard SLD-QFI as a special case.

title: A Geometric Framework for Local-to-Global Symmetry: Global Constraints on Local Dynamics
summary: Aggregate molecular systems are routinely understood by decomposing them into local structural units, such as monomers in J/H-aggregates, chemical moieties, motifs, and functional groups. Implicit in such decompositions is the assumption that these local structures remain meaningful within the aggregate. Here, we ask how the symmetries of constituent structures relate to aggregate symmetry, and how this relation determines the constraints that global symmetry imposes on transitions between local symmetry sectors. We construct a covariant local-to-global representation from framed local symmetry data and show that its reconstruction map intertwines with a global quantum representation. By identifying which global symmetry sectors overlap each local symmetry sector, we resolve symmetry-enforced dynamical exclusions into site-resolved pathways. Through Frobenius reciprocity, these exclusions can be determined from standard character tables of the local and global symmetry groups, with the character values in the inner product paired according to the relative positions and orientations of local structures within the aggregate. Although motivated by molecular aggregates, the construction is formulated for arbitrary geometries modeled by a homogeneous space of an ambient transformation group.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes how local symmetry data of constituent structures (monomers/moieties) reconstruct into global symmetry of an aggregate, via a covariant local-to-global representation from framed local symmetry data, and uses Frobenius reciprocity with standard character tables to determine site-resolved dynamical exclusions imposed by global symmetry.
AI.motivation: Aggregate molecular systems are typically decomposed into local structural units (monomers in J/H-aggregates, moieties, motifs, functional groups), implicitly assuming these local structures stay meaningful within the aggregate. The paper asks how the symmetries of constituent structures relate to aggregate symmetry and how this relation constrains transitions between local symmetry sectors under global symmetry.
AI.method: A covariant local-to-global representation is constructed from framed local symmetry data; its reconstruction map is shown to intertwine with a global quantum representation. Global symmetry sectors overlapping each local symmetry sector are identified, resolving symmetry-enforced dynamical exclusions into site-resolved pathways. Frobenius reciprocity is used so exclusions follow from standard character tables of local and global groups, with character values in the inner product paired according to relative positions and orientations of local structures. The construction is formulated for arbitrary geometries modeled by a homogeneous space of an ambient transformation group.
AI.result: Symmetry-enforced dynamical exclusions can be resolved into site-resolved transition pathways; these exclusions are computable from standard character tables of local and global symmetry groups, with pairing determined by relative positions and orientations of local structures within the aggregate.
AI.conclusion: Local structural decompositions of aggregates can be made symmetry-covariant: constituent symmetry data reconstructs into a global representation, and global symmetry constraints on local-sector transitions are determined by representation-theoretic (Frobenius) methods using ordinary character tables, generalized beyond molecular aggregates to homogeneous-space geometries of an ambient transformation group.

title: Probing the real-time decoding accuracy bounds in trapped ion architectures
summary: Fault tolerant quantum computers will rely on real-time decoders that process syndromes faster than the QEC cycle duration. The millisecond cycle times offered by trapped ion platforms relax low-latency decoding demands, but simulations and experiments have not yet exploited this time budget to reach maximum logical error suppression. We show how a hybrid sliding window decoding scheme composed of a lower-accuracy and a higher-accuracy decoder can yield substantially improved logical error rates, while preserving low latency. All windows are handled by the lower-accuracy decoder, with some windows being infrequently switched to the higher-accuracy decoder. We extract soft-output information from the lower-accuracy decoder efficiently for any QLDPC code, which allows us to identify decoding windows of low confidence. We simulate memory experiments of bivariate bicycle (BB) codes, using trapped-ion informed noise models. Depending on the physical error rate and BB code, we find up to 3-4 orders of magnitude logical error rate reduction compared to the $\texttt{BP-LSD}$ decoder, and up to 2-3 orders of magnitude lower logical error rate compared to the $\texttt{Beamsearch}$ decoder. By leveraging available classical processing time, our decoding protocol significantly boosts decoding accuracy, ultimately reducing the demands on increasing code size.

AI.tldr: A hybrid sliding-window decoding scheme for trapped-ion QLDPC codes that routes low-confidence windows to a high-accuracy decoder, achieving up to 3-4 orders of magnitude lower logical error rate than BP-LSD while preserving low latency.
AI.motivation: Real-time decoders must process syndromes faster than the QEC cycle time, but trapped-ion platforms offer relatively relaxed millisecond cycle times. Prior simulations and experiments have not exploited this available time budget to push logical error suppression to its maximum, leaving decoding accuracy on the table.
AI.method: The authors propose a hybrid sliding-window decoder combining a low-accuracy and a high-accuracy decoder. All windows are processed by the low-accuracy decoder, while a subset of low-confidence windows is infrequently rerouted to the high-accuracy decoder. Soft-output information is extracted efficiently from the low-accuracy decoder for arbitrary QLDPC codes to identify low-confidence windows. The scheme is evaluated via simulated memory experiments on bivariate bicycle (BB) codes using trapped-ion-informed noise models.
AI.result: Depending on the physical error rate and the BB code, the protocol reduces logical error rates by up to 3-4 orders of magnitude relative to the BP-LSD decoder and by up to 2-3 orders of magnitude relative to the Beamsearch decoder.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting spare classical processing time through selective escalation to a higher-accuracy decoder substantially improves decoding accuracy and reduces the demand for larger code sizes, while retaining low latency.

title: Simplifying models of noisy stabilizer QEC on leakage qubits by Pauli twirling
summary: The growing capabilities of quantum error-correction (QEC) experiments make it increasingly important to develop methods that predict or assess logical performance over many QEC cycles. Prior work has shown that a stabilizer QEC cycle subject to Pauli-stochastic noise can be modeled by a classical Markov process over syndrome states, with a logical Pauli channel attached to each syndrome transition. Here, we extend this framework to systems in which physical qubits are subject to leakage. We first develop the theory of leakage-dephased Pauli twirling and show that twirled processes can be expressed in terms of Pauli maps on the computational subspace, conditioned on transitions between leakage patterns. We apply this theory to noisy stabilizer QEC with leakage, demonstrating that a QEC cycle with leakage can be modeled by a classical Markov process over the joint syndrome and leakage patterns, with a logical Pauli channel attached to each joint transition. Finally, we derive a transfer-matrix description of repeated QEC cycles and an exact transfer-matrix expression for the success probability of a QEC memory experiment. This framework connects leaky error models of the individual components of the QEC cycle to many-cycle logical performance and provides a foundation for logical characterization and benchmarking methods that can account for leakage.

AI.tldr: A transfer-matrix framework modeling repeated stabilizer QEC cycles under leakage as a classical Markov process over joint syndrome–leakage patterns with attached logical Pauli channels.
AI.motivation: QEC experiments now run many cycles, so methods to predict/assess logical performance over many cycles are needed; prior Markov-process models of stabilizer QEC cover Pauli-stochastic noise only, not leakage.
AI.method: Develops leakage-dephased Pauli twirling, expressing twirled processes as Pauli maps on the computational subspace conditioned on leakage-pattern transitions; applies this to noisy stabilizer QEC with leakage, yielding a classical Markov process over joint syndrome and leakage patterns with a logical Pauli channel per joint transition; derives a transfer-matrix description of repeated cycles and an exact transfer-matrix expression for QEC memory success probability.
AI.result: A QEC cycle with leakage is shown to be modelable by a classical Markov process over joint syndrome–leakage patterns with logical Pauli channels per joint transition; an exact transfer-matrix expression for QEC memory success probability is obtained.
AI.conclusion: The framework links leaky error models of individual QEC components to many-cycle logical performance and provides a foundation for logical characterization and benchmarking methods that account for leakage.

title: Complexity and precision in quantum associative retrieval
summary: We show that efficient and high-precision quantum associative retrieval is possible with an exponential complexity advantage with respect to the classical brute force approach and with a polynomial capacity advantage with respect to classical neural network implementations for any number of patterns scaling polynomially in the number of qubits. Both classical neural and quantum associative memories store the patterns in a Hamiltonian; in the classical case the dynamics is irreversible relaxation toward attractors, in the quantum case it is unitary transformations generating an effective thermal distribution, followed by a measurement.

AI.tldr: Quantum associative retrieval achieves an exponential speedup over classical brute force and polynomial capacity gain over classical neural networks for patterns scaling polynomially in qubit number.
AI.motivation: Associative memory retrieval classically relies on either brute-force search (costly) or neural network implementations with limited storage capacity; the authors seek a quantum approach that improves both retrieval complexity and pattern capacity.
AI.method: Patterns are encoded in a Hamiltonian, as in classical neural associative memories. Unlike the classical case of irreversible relaxation toward attractors, the quantum scheme uses unitary transformations to generate an effective thermal distribution over stored patterns, followed by a measurement to retrieve the target.
AI.result: The protocol yields high-precision retrieval with an exponential complexity advantage over classical brute-force search and a polynomial capacity advantage over classical neural network implementations, for any number of patterns scaling polynomially in the number of qubits.
AI.conclusion: Quantum associative memory offers a provable advantage in both efficiency and storage capacity, establishing unitary thermal-distribution generation plus measurement as an effective retrieval mechanism.

title: Quantum Information Transfer in Molecular Polaritonic Networks: A Van Vleck Effective-Hamiltonian Approach
summary: Achieving high-fidelity transfer of an arbitrary quantum state between spatially separated qubits is a central challenge for reliable quantum hardware. We address this question within a polaritonic framework by introducing Projected-Block Van Vleck Perturbation Theory (PB-VVPT). Based on quasidegenerate perturbation theory, this approach describes a molecular network coupled to an optical cavity and local phonons through a generalized Holstein--Tavis--Cummings Hamiltonian. Quantum information is encoded in a coherent superposition of exciton-cavity states, while phonons constitute a weakly coupled environment. In the nonadiabatic regime of weak exciton-phonon coupling, the method incorporates phonon-induced renormalization of polaritonic states and their dynamics while reducing the Hamiltonian to independent fixed-phonon-number sectors and coupled polaron-polariton subblocks. This structure provides efficient access to the coherence and population propagators governing quantum-state transfer without invoking a Markovian approximation. We benchmark the approach against exact dynamics for a molecular wheel network, considering both molecule-to-molecule and molecule-to-cavity transfer. PB-VVPT accurately reproduces short- and long-time transfer dynamics, including thermal decoherence and fidelity revivals consistent with non-Markovian memory effects, with prediction errors below $1\%$ over most of the simulated time intervals. This accuracy is achieved with an estimated diagonalization cost more than two orders of magnitude lower than that of the exact reference calculations. These results establish PB-VVPT as an accurate and computationally efficient approach to quantum information transfer in molecular polaritonic networks.

AI.tldr: PB-VVPT, a quasidegenerate perturbation scheme for a cavity-phonon-coupled molecular network, reproduces non-Markovian quantum-state transfer dynamics with sub-1% error at over 100x lower diagonalization cost than exact methods.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity transfer of arbitrary quantum states between spatially separated qubits is a central requirement for reliable quantum hardware; exact dynamics for molecular polaritonic networks coupled to cavities and phonons are prohibitively expensive.
AI.method: Projected-Block Van Vleck Perturbation Theory (PB-VVPT), built on quasidegenerate perturbation theory, for a generalized Holstein-Tavis-Cummings Hamiltonian describing a molecular network coupled to an optical cavity and weakly coupled local phonons. It includes phonon-induced renormalization of polaritonic states, reduces the Hamiltonian to fixed-phonon-number sectors and coupled polaron-polariton subblocks, and yields coherence/population propagators without a Markovian approximation.
AI.result: Benchmarked against exact dynamics on a molecular wheel network for molecule-to-molecule and molecule-to-cavity transfer, PB-VVPT reproduces short- and long-time dynamics, including thermal decoherence and non-Markovian fidelity revivals, with errors below 1% over most intervals and an estimated diagonalization cost more than two orders of magnitude lower than exact references.
AI.conclusion: PB-VVPT is an accurate and computationally efficient method for quantum information transfer in molecular polaritonic networks.

title: An alternate proof of the QMA lower bound for set-size estimation
summary: In the set-size estimation query task, a query algorithm decides whether an $N$-bit input has Hamming weight $\ge B$ or $\le A$ (with $\ge B$ as the yes instances and $\le A$ as the no instances). When $B = 2A$, this is sometimes called approximate counting. The query complexity for this problem with a quantum witness (i.e., $\mathsf{QMA}$ query bounds) was resolved by Aaronson, Kothari, Kretschmer, and Thaler (CCC 2020) and proved using Laurent polynomials. Here we give a morally similar but distinct proof of the lower bound using the polynomial method.

AI.tldr: A new lower bound proof for the QMA query complexity of set-size estimation (approximate counting at B=2A) is given using the polynomial method, paralleling the Laurent-polynomial proof of Aaronson–Kothari–Kretschmer–Thaler.
AI.motivation: The QMA query bounds for set-size estimation were settled by Aaronson, Kothari, Kretschmer, and Thaler via Laurent polynomials; the author seeks an alternative, conceptually similar yet distinct derivation to illuminate why the bound holds.
AI.method: Polynomial method: represent the query algorithm's acceptance behavior as a (low-degree) polynomial over the Boolean cube, and combine it with a symmetric-function / degree lower bound argument rather than Laurent polynomials.
AI.result: A lower bound on QMA query complexity for distinguishing Hamming weight >= B from <= A (with B=2A) is re-derived through the polynomial method, matching the known bound.
AI.conclusion: The polynomial method yields a morally similar but technically distinct proof of the set-size estimation lower bound, confirming the earlier Laurent-polynomial result and offering a complementary perspective.

title: Fundamental physics with quantum sensors in space
summary: Quantum sensors such as atomic clocks, atom interferometers, and atomic magnetometers can be used as sensitive probes of physics beyond the Standard Model. Space offers microgravity, long baselines, low environmental noise, access to varying gravitational potentials, and unique opportunities involving the Sun, Moon, planets, and asteroids. These proceedings of the Aspen Center for Physics workshop on "Fundamental physics in space with quantum sensors," held February 22-27, 2026, summarize the scientific case, current capabilities, and space mission concepts for investigating dark matter, testing general relativity, and detecting gravitational waves in frequency bands inaccessible from the ground.

AI.tldr: These Aspen Center for Physics workshop proceedings summarize the scientific case, current capabilities, and space mission concepts for using quantum sensors (atomic clocks, atom interferometers, atomic magnetometers) in space to probe dark matter, test general relativity, and detect gravitational waves in frequency bands inaccessible from the ground.
AI.motivation: Quantum sensors such as atomic clocks, atom interferometers, and atomic magnetometers are sensitive probes of physics beyond the Standard Model, and space provides unique advantages—microgravity, long baselines, low environmental noise, access to varying gravitational potentials, and proximity to the Sun, Moon, planets, and asteroids—that enable fundamental-physics searches not feasible on the ground.
AI.method: Workshop proceedings (Aspen Center for Physics, Feb 22–27, 2026) synthesizing the scientific rationale, present-day sensor capabilities, and proposed space mission concepts for quantum-sensor-based fundamental physics.
AI.result: The proceedings consolidate the scientific case, summarize current quantum-sensor capabilities, and describe space mission concepts for dark matter searches, tests of general relativity, and gravitational-wave detection in frequency bands inaccessible from ground-based observatories.
AI.conclusion: Space-based quantum sensors offer a distinctive and promising pathway to probe physics beyond the Standard Model, spanning dark matter, general relativity, and gravitational waves in otherwise inaccessible frequency regimes.

title: Transient Synchronization and Entanglement through Shared Dissipation in Circuit QED
summary: We propose a superconducting circuit in which two resonators couple through DC-biased SQUIDs to a common lossy auxiliary mode. Adiabatic elimination yields collective damping and correlated noise with an overlap $ξ$ whose magnitude is tuned by the flux biases and whose sign follows the relative sign of the couplings. The full three-mode dynamics confirm this reduced description. For detuned resonators, we derive the exceptional-point condition, above which the mean amplitudes lock to a common frequency. For resonant modes, unequal collective decay produces transient synchronization, antiphase or in phase depending on the relative sign of the couplings, with an analytical synchronization time set by the collective decay splitting and the initial mean amplitudes. For initially separable squeezed states, the same relaxation converts local squeezing into transient entanglement, quantified by logarithmic negativity. We obtain closed-form expressions for the squeezing threshold above which entanglement appears and for the time at which it disappears. Thermal noise suppresses entanglement without changing the mean-amplitude synchronization time at fixed parameters. For realistic circuit parameters, these effects occur within a few hundred nanoseconds and are accessible through output-field measurements. A single tunable shared channel thus produces an exceptional point, transient synchronization, and transient entanglement, and provides a controllable source of correlated noise for superconducting circuits.

AI.tldr: A superconducting circuit couples two resonators via DC-biased SQUIDs to a common lossy auxiliary mode, producing tunable collective damping and correlated noise. This single shared channel yields an exceptional point, transient (anti)phase synchronization, and transient entanglement from local squeezing, all within a few hundred nanoseconds.
