AI.motivation: The authors seek a single, flux-tunable resource that simultaneously provides collective dissipation, correlated noise, and non-Hermitian phenomena (exceptional points, synchronization, entanglement) in superconducting circuits, controllable via bias fluxes rather than requiring separate dedicated elements.
AI.method: Two resonators are coupled through DC-biased SQUIDs to a common lossy auxiliary mode. Adiabatic elimination of the auxiliary mode yields collective damping and correlated noise with overlap ξ (magnitude set by flux biases, sign by relative coupling sign); the full three-mode dynamics validates this reduced model. Detuned and resonant regimes are analyzed analytically (exceptional-point condition, synchronization time), and separable squeezed initial states are tracked via logarithmic negativity, with closed-form squeezing threshold and entanglement-decay time; thermal noise effects are included.
AI.result: For detuned resonators, an exceptional-point condition is derived above which mean amplitudes lock to a common frequency. For resonant modes, unequal collective decay gives transient synchronization—in-phase or antiphase depending on coupling sign—with an analytic synchronization time set by the collective-decay splitting and initial amplitudes. Local squeezing converts into transient entanglement with closed-form squeezing threshold and extinction time. Thermal noise suppresses entanglement but leaves the mean-amplitude synchronization time unchanged at fixed parameters. Effects occur within a few hundred ns for realistic parameters and are measurable via output fields.
AI.conclusion: A single tunable shared lossy channel in a SQUID-coupled superconducting circuit unifies an exceptional point, transient synchronization, and transient entanglement, and offers a controllable source of correlated noise for superconducting circuits, with signatures accessible through output-field measurements.

title: Generalized Schrieffer-Wolff transformation
summary: The Schrieffer-Wolff transformation (SWT) is a cornerstone of effective-Hamiltonian theory. However, the SWT is predominantly used for weak-coupling problems, while a systematic counterpart for strongly coupled regimes remains largely unexplored. A general closed-form SWT generator and a clear physical principle for gauge fixing remain elusive, obscuring the transformation's underlying structure. We introduce the dual SWT to deal with the strong-coupling problems. The generalized SWT (gSWT) is formulated for any Hermitian operator and block partition. We establish the geodesic principle for its canonical gauge. Furthermore, we derive an exact closed-form solution of the gSWT generator at every order as a finite nested-commutator sum whose only input is the active gap set. Both the geometric and algebraic aspects of the SWT physics are revealed. The gSWT framework is illustrated in two quantum many-body models, the collective spin model and the transverse-field Ising model.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a dual Schrieffer-Wolff transformation (gSWT) that works for strongly coupled regimes, provides a closed-form generator at every order as a finite nested-commutator sum, and establishes a geodesic principle for fixing the canonical gauge.
AI.motivation: The standard Schrieffer-Wolff transformation is essentially limited to weak-coupling problems, and there is no systematic strong-coupling counterpart. Moreover, a general closed-form generator and a clear physical principle for gauge fixing have been missing, leaving the transformation's underlying structure obscure.
AI.method: The authors formulate a generalized SWT (gSWT) for any Hermitian operator and arbitrary block partition, define a 'dual' SWT aimed at strong coupling, establish a geodesic principle that selects the canonical gauge, and derive an exact closed-form solution for the gSWT generator at every order as a finite nested-commutator sum whose only input is the active gap set. The framework is illustrated on a collective spin model and the transverse-field Ising model.
AI.result: A closed-form gSWT generator is obtained order by order as a finite nested-commutator sum depending solely on the active gap set, and a geodesic principle fixes the canonical gauge. The construction is demonstrated to work in two quantum many-body models, covering both geometric and algebraic aspects of the SWT.
AI.conclusion: The gSWT provides a systematic, gauge-fixed and closed-form extension of the Schrieffer-Wolff transformation valid beyond weak coupling, revealing the geometric (geodesic gauge) and algebraic (nested-commutator) structure of SWT physics, with applicability demonstrated in collective spin and transverse-field Ising models.

title: Magic state cultivation with lattice-surgery escape on superconducting hardware
summary: Magic state cultivation (MSC) is a low-overhead protocol for fault-tolerantly preparing logical magic states. In this work, we implement two MSC variants to prepare a magic state in a distance-5 code on a publicly available IBM Nighthawk processor. The first is a lattice-surgery escape, recently proposed by Hirano et al. and experimentally studied here for the first time. The second is a grafting escape, previously demonstrated by Rosenfeld et al., and extended here by incorporating a switch into a matchable code. Both protocols begin with fault-tolerant cultivation of a T state on a color code, followed by an escape into a larger code. We decode the results using minimum-weight perfect matching or Tesseract on circuit-level error models calibrated to the hardware noise. Compared with the previous experiment, our cultivated T state achieves a logical error probability of 2e-5 at the T-state injection angle, nearly 10x lower with about 3x the retainment. Moreover, our execution of the grafting escape has a 2x lower logical error rate per stabilizer round at a higher retainment. When comparing the two protocols under identical execution conditions and complementary gap postselection based on decoder confidence, lattice-surgery escape into the surface code preserves a T-state fidelity above 0.99 ten rounds after escape at about 5% retainment. By contrast, matchable-switched grafting drops below 0.95 fidelity at comparable retainment. Furthermore, the lattice-surgery escape reaches a logical error rate per stabilizer round of about 0.14% with around 11% average shot retainment. These results establish lattice-surgery escape as a practical MSC protocol that benefits from a direct transition into a surface code, and demonstrate the lowest MSC error and the highest surface-code magic-state fidelity reported to date, advancing the experimental realization of fault-tolerant non-Clifford gadgets.

AI.tldr: Magic state cultivation (MSC) variants are implemented on an IBM Nighthawk processor in a distance-5 code; a lattice-surgery escape achieves state-of-the-art logical error (≈0.14% per stabilizer round) and surface-code T-state fidelity >0.99 at ~5% retainment.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant non-Clifford resources (magic states) are the dominant overhead in fault-tolerant quantum computing. MSC reduces this overhead, but its escape-into-larger-code step lacks experimental comparison between candidate protocols, and prior demonstrations showed limited fidelity and retainment.
AI.method: Two MSC protocols are run on a public IBM Nighthawk device using a distance-5 code: (1) lattice-surgery escape (Hirano et al.), experimentally studied here for the first time; (2) grafting escape (Rosenfeld et al.), extended by embedding a switch into a matchable code. Both fault-tolerantly cultivate a T state on a color code, then escape into a larger code. Decoding uses MWPM or Tesseract on hardware-calibrated circuit-level noise models, with decoder-confidence-based complementary gap postselection.
AI.result: Cultivated T state reaches 2e-5 logical error probability at the injection angle, ~10x lower with ~3x retainment versus the prior experiment. Grafting escape achieves 2x lower logical error per stabilizer round at higher retainment. Under identical conditions, lattice-surgery escape into the surface code keeps T-state fidelity >0.99 ten rounds post-escape at ~5% retainment (grafting drops below 0.95), and reaches ~0.14% logical error per stabilizer round at ~11% average shot retainment.
AI.conclusion: Lattice-surgery escape is established as a practical MSC protocol owing to its direct transition into a surface code, delivering the lowest reported MSC error and highest surface-code magic-state fidelity to date and advancing experimental fault-tolerant non-Clifford gadgets.

title: Cantor correlations II. Synchronicity and bisynchronicity
summary: We study synchronous and bisynchronous no-signalling correlations, defined over Cantor topological spaces, from the perspectives of both continuous variable quantum information and operator algebra theories. We focus on strategies, satisfying a natural no-signalling condition across the Cantor space levels, called graded, identifying a universal C*-algebra, whose tracial states of different types characterise synchronous correlations of respective types. The universal C*-algebra for bisynchronous graded correlations is shown to coincide with the C*-algebra of a projective limit of free wreath products of quantum permutation groups, introduced by Bhowmick, Goswami and Skalski, and a type description, analogous to the one in the synchronous case, is provided. Extending results in the finite case, we show that bisynchronous graded correlations canonically give rise to factorisable maps on type I factors, defined via Cantor permutation matrices. We examine non-local games over Cantor topological spaces, with inputs/outputs that are finite words of equal length, define corresponding game algebras, and characterise the perfect strategies of the games via the respective game algebras. In the case of the Cantor graph isomorphism game, we provide equivalent descriptions of the existence of perfect strategies of quantum commuting type, in terms of bigalois correspondences, factorisable maps, Cantor permutation intertwiners and game algebra non-triviality. Our results supply a quantum information interpretation of a notion of a quantum isomorphism of locally finite graphs, introduced by Rollier and Vaes, canonically arising from Cantor graphs.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a unified operator-algebraic and quantum-information theory of (bi)synchronous no-signalling correlations over Cantor spaces, identifying universal C*-algebras whose tracial states characterise graded correlations and characterising perfect strategies of Cantor-space non-local games.
AI.motivation: Finite-dimensional synchronous/bisynchronous correlations and their game algebras are well understood, but their infinite (Cantor-space) analogues arising in continuous-variable quantum information and operator algebra remain uncharacterised; the authors aim to bridge these perspectives and give a quantum-information meaning to Rollier–Vaes' quantum isomorphism of locally finite graphs.
AI.method: They define graded no-signalling correlations across Cantor space levels and construct a universal C*-algebra whose tracial states of various types yield synchronous correlations. For bisynchronous graded correlations they identify the universal C*-algebra with the C*-algebra of a projective limit of free wreath products of quantum permutation groups (Bhowmick–Goswami–Skalski) and give a type description. Using Cantor permutation matrices they build factorisable maps on type I factors, and define game algebras for non-local games over Cantor spaces with finite equal-length word inputs/outputs.
AI.result: Graded (bi)synchronous correlations are characterised via tracial states of the universal C*-algebra; bisynchronous graded correlations canonically yield factorisable maps on type I factors; perfect strategies are characterised through game algebras; and for the Cantor graph isomorphism game, existence of perfect quantum-commuting strategies is equivalently described by bigalois correspondences, factorisable maps, Cantor permutation intertwiners, and game-algebra non-triviality.
AI.conclusion: The work extends finite-dimensional correlation theory to Cantor topological spaces and provides a quantum-information interpretation of Rollier–Vaes' quantum isomorphism of locally finite graphs, canonically arising from Cantor graphs.

title: QCap: a physics-corrected graph neural network for the capacitance matrix of any planar superconducting device layout
comment: 26 pages, 13 figures, 8 tables. Models, data and tutorials: https://lfl-lab.github.io/SQuADDS/qcap/
summary: Electromagnetic simulations of device layouts to extract capacitance are computationally intensive, a major obstacle to accurate design of circuit devices. Machine learning models can bypass these simulations, but previous approaches have been restricted to layouts using only particular components, and require thousands of simulations of those same components as training data. We present QCap, a model that accurately predicts the Maxwell capacitance matrix of an arbitrary superconducting device layout in seconds, compared to minutes to hours of Ansys Q3D simulations. We develop a novel design-embedding algorithm that converts the layout into a universal graph format, allowing the model to work with any layout created with any tool. To achieve high accuracy, we obtain a coarse physics prior from a fast method of moments simulation of capacitance, then train the model to correct this prior. On 4,009 test designs withheld from training data the model outputs agree with Q3D simulations to a median error of 0.177%, and on never-seen component families it stays below 1% error. We demonstrate the model's scaling by obtaining the capacitance matrix of a 9-superconducting-qubit device in 12 seconds on a laptop (compared to 19.9 h and 228 GB of memory in Ansys) with sub-percent error, and capacitance of a (too large to simulate) 100-qubit, 781-conductor device in 3.4 min on a laptop. We provide the open-source models and data on SQuADDS and Hugging Face. Our results provide a powerful tool for large-scale accurate circuit design and guide the development of models to bypass other physical simulations.

AI.tldr: QCap is a machine-learning model that predicts the Maxwell capacitance matrix of arbitrary superconducting device layouts in seconds with sub-percent error, using a universal graph-based design embedding and a physics prior from method-of-moments simulations.
AI.motivation: Extracting capacitance via EM simulation (e.g., Ansys Q3D) is computationally expensive (minutes to hours per layout), a bottleneck for accurate circuit design. Prior ML surrogates were limited to specific component sets and required thousands of same-component simulations for training, restricting generality.
AI.method: A novel design-embedding algorithm converts any layout (from any tool) into a universal graph format. The model first obtains a coarse physics prior from a fast method-of-moments capacitance simulation, then is trained to correct this prior, enabling layout-agnostic prediction of the Maxwell capacitance matrix.
AI.result: On 4,009 held-out test designs, predictions agree with Q3D to a median error of 0.177%; on never-seen component families error stays below 1%. A 9-superconducting-qubit device is solved in 12 s on a laptop vs. 19.9 h and 228 GB in Ansys with sub-percent error, and a 100-qubit, 781-conductor device (too large for Ansys) in 3.4 min on a laptop. Models and data are released on SQuADDS and Hugging Face.
AI.conclusion: QCap enables fast, accurate, layout-agnostic capacitance extraction, supporting large-scale circuit design and offering a template for ML models that bypass other physical simulations.

title: Commutator-guided repair and classical-accessibility boundaries for shallow quantum circuits
summary: Trainability does not guarantee low-energy arrival: a shallow quantum circuit can be optimizable yet fail, under fixed depth and evaluation budgets, to reach Hamiltonian-selected states. We introduce a commutator-guided repair for this operational failure mode. Low-order host--Hamiltonian commutators and fixed same-support companion axes define a restricted pool of local Pauli rotations, from which a compact completion layer is selected before full reoptimization. Across 189 paired six-qubit trials, unrepaired circuits achieve 0/189 strict successes, a non-deployable per-trial control envelope achieves 109/189, and two predeclared selectors achieve 133/189 and 127/189. The repair loses to matched controls for transverse-field Ising, is weak for pure-ZZ MaxCut, and remains size-limited for weighted MIS. Under fixed-depth geometric locality, repaired losses and gradients are classically computable, while corresponding ground-state targets admit low-bond-dimension tensor-network approximations through the tested sizes. The method reveals a trainability--arrival--classical-accessibility tradeoff rather than quantum advantage.

AI.tldr: A commutator-guided "repair" procedure is proposed to fix a shallow quantum circuit's failure to reach Hamiltonian-selected (e.g., ground/low-energy) states despite being trainable; it improves strict success to ~133/189 on six-qubit trials but loses to controls on some problems and offers no quantum advantage.
AI.motivation: Trainability (optimizability) does not guarantee that a fixed-depth, fixed-budget variational circuit actually arrives at Hamiltonian-selected states—an operational failure mode distinct from barren plateaus. The paper targets this trainability–arrival gap.
AI.method: Low-order commutators between the host circuit and the Hamiltonian, together with fixed same-support companion axes, are used to define a restricted pool of local Pauli rotations. A compact "completion layer" is selected from this pool and then the full circuit is reoptimized. Evaluated via 189 paired six-qubit trials against a non-deployable per-trial control envelope and two predeclared selectors.
AI.result: Unrepaired circuits: 0/189 strict successes. Per-trial control envelope: 109/189. Two predeclared selectors: 133/189 and 127/189. The repair loses to matched controls for transverse-field Ising, is weak for pure-ZZ MaxCut, and remains size-limited for weighted MIS.
AI.conclusion: Under fixed-depth geometric locality, repaired losses and gradients are classically computable, and the corresponding ground-state targets admit low-bond-dimension tensor-network approximations at tested sizes. The method exposes a trainability–arrival–classical-accessibility tradeoff rather than demonstrating quantum advantage.

title: Perturbative Recovery of Stabilizer-Subspace Correlations for Quantum Computational Chemistry
summary: Stabilizer-based subspace methods can substantially reduce the quantum resources required for electronic structure calculations, but the resulting projection neglects Hamiltonian couplings to configurations outside the retained subspace. In this work, we introduce Stabilizer-Subspace Perturbation Theory (SSPT) to recover the associated correlation contributions, using the Contextual Subspace Variational Quantum Eigensolver (CS-VQE) as a representative application. The central idea is to exploit the Pauli terms eliminated by stabilizer projection as perturbative operators that generate an external manifold from the optimized reference state. Their energetic contributions are evaluated using an Epstein-Nesbet-type second-order correction or a resolvent-based formulation that retains couplings within the external space. By exploiting the factorized structure of the stabilizer-constrained reference state, the required matrix elements can be evaluated through Pauli expectation values on the reduced contextual register without explicitly reconstructing the full-space wave function. Molecular benchmarks demonstrate substantial reductions in projection-induced energy errors, allowing chemical precision to be achieved with fewer contextual qubits in several cases. These results establish stabilizer-guided perturbation theory as a promising strategy for improving the accuracy of resource-efficient quantum chemistry calculations.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Stabilizer-Subspace Perturbation Theory (SSPT), which recovers the Hamiltonian couplings lost by stabilizer-based subspace projection in electronic structure calculations by treating the eliminated Pauli terms as perturbative operators generating an external manifold from the optimized reference state.
AI.motivation: Stabilizer-based subspace methods such as CS-VQE can substantially reduce quantum resources for electronic structure calculations, but the stabilizer projection neglects Hamiltonian couplings to configurations outside the retained subspace, introducing projection-induced energy errors.
AI.method: SSPT exploits the Pauli terms eliminated by stabilizer projection as perturbative operators that generate an external manifold from the optimized reference state. Energetic contributions are evaluated either via an Epstein-Nesbet-type second-order correction or a resolvent-based formulation retaining couplings within the external space. Leveraging the factorized structure of the stabilizer-constrained reference state, the required matrix elements are computed through Pauli expectation values on the reduced contextual register without explicitly reconstructing the full-space wave function. CS-VQE serves as a representative application.
AI.result: Molecular benchmarks demonstrate substantial reductions in projection-induced energy errors, enabling chemical precision to be achieved with fewer contextual qubits in several cases.
AI.conclusion: Stabilizer-guided perturbation theory is a promising strategy for improving the accuracy of resource-efficient quantum chemistry calculations.

title: Variational Relevance-Informed Sparsification of Term Measurements for Variational Quantum Algorithms
summary: Repeated measurements are a major bottleneck in variational quantum algorithms (VQAs). We uncover and characterize parameter-specific sparsity in the matrix of qubit-wise commuting (QWC) group contributions to parameter-shift gradients: most absolute contribution mass concentrates in a subset of groups whose relevance varies across parameters and optimization states. Building on this structure, we introduce a learned controller that predicts group relevance from Hamiltonian, circuit, light-cone, and current-state features, then selects measurements through a tunable coverage threshold. Exact contributions provide offline supervision without being required at deployment. Across 15 molecular VQE settings, our method saves 49.6% of nominal gradient-measurement shots with a mean absolute energy gap of 5.67 mHa to Full-QWC. We then ask whether large language models (LLMs) can solve the same selection problem without fine-tuning. The results reveal both promise and a clear limitation: LLMs can identify useful measurement groups, yet without guidance, local models do not consistently prioritize the physical information that matters most. Our learned controller uses these cues more effectively. This contrast points toward a broader direction for AI-assisted science: combining the flexibility of general-purpose models with explicit physical representations, task-specific objectives, and domain-grounded validation.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies parameter-specific sparsity in qubit-wise commuting (QWC) group contributions to parameter-shift gradients and exploits it with a learned controller that selects measurement groups, saving ~49.6% of gradient-measurement shots at a mean absolute energy gap of 5.67 mHa versus Full-QWC. It also probes whether off-the-shelf LLMs can solve the same selection problem.
AI.motivation: Measurement overhead is a dominant bottleneck in variational quantum algorithms. The authors observe that gradient contribution mass is unevenly distributed across QWC groups and that this relevance is non-uniform across parameters and optimization states, suggesting that full measurement of all groups is wasteful.
AI.method: Characterize sparsity in the matrix of QWC group contributions to parameter-shift gradients. Introduce a learned controller that predicts per-group relevance from Hamiltonian, circuit, light-cone, and current-state features, and selects groups via a tunable coverage threshold. Train with exact contributions as offline supervision (not needed at deployment). Separately, evaluate off-the-shelf LLMs on the same selection task without fine-tuning.
AI.result: Across 15 molecular VQE settings, the method saves 49.6% of nominal gradient-measurement shots with a mean absolute energy gap of 5.67 mHa relative to Full-QWC. LLMs identify useful measurement groups but, without guidance, do not consistently prioritize the most physically informative ones; the learned controller uses these cues more effectively.
AI.conclusion: Parameter-specific sparsity in QWC group contributions is exploitable for shot-efficient gradient estimation. The LLM comparison motivates AI-assisted scientific workflows that combine the flexibility of general-purpose models with explicit physical representations, task-specific objectives, and domain-grounded validation.

title: Two-Qutrit Quantum Battery Charging through Ising Model and Anisotropic XZ Heisenberg Interactions
comment: 16 Pages, 9 figures. Accepted for publication in AVS Quantum Science
summary: In this paper, we propose a model of a two-qutrit quantum battery composed of two spin-1 systems coupled to an external field via anisotropic Heisenberg interactions. From the Ising model, we derive an exact analytical expression of ergotropy in the parallel-charging case. However, the collective charging process offers an advantage over the parallel one. Moreover, increasing the collective exchange coupling accelerates the evolution of ergotropy and enhances the maximum average power, as measured by global coherence and mutual information. Conversely, the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction primarily acts as a detrimental mechanism, essentially reducing all of these quantities. In the XZ model, the obtained results show that the DM interaction is constructive when it cooperates with the longitudinal anisotropy and when the exchange coupling is sufficiently strong. Therefore, by optimising the maximum reachable ergotropy and maximum average power, we conclude that the Ising model without DM interaction is sufficient to maximise the ergotropy. The anisotropic XZ model allows the DM interaction to be exploited constructively to improve the maximum average power through the joint control of the exchange coupling, longitudinal anisotropy, and chiral interaction.

AI.tldr: A two-qutrit quantum battery with anisotropic Heisenberg coupling is analyzed for ergotropy and charging power, comparing parallel vs. collective charging and Ising vs. XZ models with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction.
AI.motivation: To understand how charging protocol (parallel vs. collective) and spin-spin interactions—exchange coupling, longitudinal anisotropy, and chiral DM interaction—affect the extractable work (ergotropy) and average power of a qutrit-based quantum battery.
AI.method: A two-spin-1 (qutrit) battery coupled to an external field via anisotropic Heisenberg interactions. Exact analytical ergotropy is derived for the Ising model in the parallel-charging case; collective charging is compared, with global coherence and mutual information used as quantifiers. DM effects are studied in both Ising and XZ (longitudinal anisotropy) models.
AI.result: Collective charging outperforms parallel charging. Increasing collective exchange coupling accelerates ergotropy evolution and raises maximum average power, tracked by global coherence and mutual information. In the Ising model, DM interaction is detrimental, reducing all these quantities. In the XZ model, DM becomes constructive when combined with longitudinal anisotropy and sufficiently strong exchange coupling.
AI.conclusion: The Ising model without DM interaction suffices to maximize ergotropy, whereas the anisotropic XZ model exploits DM constructively to improve maximum average power via joint control of exchange coupling, longitudinal anisotropy, and chiral interaction.

title: Exceptional-point Sensing with Quantum Advantage
summary: Exceptional-point sensors exploit singular non-Hermitian dynamics to enhance their response to weak perturbations. Recently, however, a no-go result has been established for a gain-loss-balanced dimer coupled to independent, phase-insensitive reservoirs: the exceptional-point susceptibility amplifies the signal and reservoir noise equally, precluding any quantum advantage. Here, we circumvent this limitation by engineering non-Hermitian dynamics in particle-hole Nambu space. A single common reservoir acts on modes forming a quantum-mechanics-free subsystem and generates an enhanced response protected from additional noise. We demonstrate quantum-metrological advantage for weak-signal sensing and static-parameter estimation. A continuous interpolation of the operator basis at fixed exceptional-point drift, with a singular midpoint, reveals how reservoir noise vanishes toward the protected limit. Our results provide a route to exceptional-point sensing with genuine quantum-metrological advantage through reservoir engineering.

AI.tldr: By engineering non-Hermitian dynamics in particle-hole Nambu space with a single common reservoir acting on a quantum-mechanics-free subsystem, the authors evade the exceptional-point no-go limit and achieve genuine quantum-metrological advantage for weak-signal sensing and static-parameter estimation.
AI.motivation: A no-go result showed that a gain-loss-balanced dimer coupled to independent, phase-insensitive reservoirs gains no quantum advantage at exceptional points, because the EP susceptibility amplifies signal and reservoir noise equally. The authors seek to circumvent this limitation.
AI.method: They engineer non-Hermitian dynamics in particle-hole Nambu space, coupling a single common reservoir to modes forming a quantum-mechanics-free subsystem to generate an enhanced, noise-protected response. They also interpolate the operator basis at fixed exceptional-point drift, with a singular midpoint, to track the disappearance of reservoir noise.
AI.result: Quantum-metrological advantage is demonstrated for weak-signal sensing and static-parameter estimation; the basis interpolation reveals how reservoir noise vanishes toward the protected limit.
AI.conclusion: Reservoir engineering enables exceptional-point sensing with genuine quantum-metrological advantage, providing a route beyond the gain-loss-balanced dimer no-go constraint.

title: Quantum Causal Compatibility from Spatiotemporal Correlations
summary: Which quantum causal structures can account for observed spatiotemporal correlations without access to an intervention-complete description of the underlying process? In particular, can such correlations distinguish a temporal chain, a common cause, and a common effect? Here, we address these questions using three-qubit pseudo-density operators constructed from experimentally accessible Pauli correlations. We derive necessary and sufficient conditions for pseudo-Markov compatibility with the chain, fork, and collider structures by relaxing complete positivity while preserving the corresponding quantum Markov constraints. Despite their distinct causal mechanisms, all three pseudo-Markov compatibility problems reduce to linear feasibility tests, without requiring full-rank marginal states. We further establish a unified semidefinite-programming approach to physical realizability and quantify the minimum violation of complete positivity through Choi negativity. Using a two-parameter family of pseudo-density operators, we demonstrate that different causal structures admit overlapping yet non-nested sets of correlations. Our results show that quantum causal explanations need not be unique, but experimentally accessible correlations can nevertheless distinguish and exclude candidate causal structures.

AI.tldr: Three-qubit pseudo-density operators built from Pauli correlations yield linear feasibility tests for chain/fork/collider pseudo-Markov compatibility, show overlapping non-nested sets of correlations, and quantify complete-positivity violation via Choi negativity within a unified SDP for physical realizability.
AI.motivation: Observed spatiotemporal correlations often come without an intervention-complete description of the underlying process. The paper asks which quantum causal structures can account for such correlations, and specifically whether they can distinguish a temporal chain, a common cause (fork), and a common effect (collider).
AI.method: Uses three-qubit pseudo-density operators constructed from experimentally accessible Pauli correlations. Derives necessary and sufficient conditions for pseudo-Markov compatibility with chain, fork, and collider structures by relaxing complete positivity while retaining the corresponding quantum Markov constraints. Establishes a unified semidefinite-programming approach to physical realizability with Choi negativity as the measure of minimal complete-positivity violation, and analyzes a two-parameter family of pseudo-density operators.
AI.result: All three pseudo-Markov compatibility problems reduce to linear feasibility tests without requiring full-rank marginals. The two-parameter family shows the three causal structures admit overlapping yet non-nested sets of correlations, and Choi negativity quantifies the minimal complete-positivity violation for physical realizability.
AI.conclusion: Quantum causal explanations need not be unique, yet experimentally accessible correlations can still distinguish and exclude candidate causal structures, enabling structure discrimination without an intervention-complete description.

title: Demonstration of a Qubit Control Scheme Compatible with Superconducting Digital Signals
summary: Superconducting quantum computing faces a critical scalability bottleneck arising from the escalating complexity of traditional analog control infrastructure. Single-Flux-Quantum(SFQ) systems operate at cryogenic temperatures and offer a potential route to addressing these challenges. Using microwave signals at qubit-dependent frequencies to trigger SFQ pulses requires many independent analog microwave sources, limiting the potential to reduce control wiring and increase integration density. A scalable SFQ control system therefore needs a scheme that can address qubits with different transition frequencies using a common clock. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a control scheme for implementing both single- and two-qubit gates. The scheme uses guiding waveforms to rapidly generate bipolar high-speed pulse sequences on a common clock, providing a basis for future implementation in SFQ control systems. Numerically, this scheme achieves a simulated fidelity of 99.99% for 40ns $R(\varphi, \fracπ{2})$ gates with arbitrary initial phases and 99.9% for 100ns controlled-Z(CZ) gates. Experimentally, by utilizing an arbitrary waveform generator(AWG) operated at a fixed sampling rate of 25GSa/s to deliver the bipolar high-speed pulse sequences, we successfully demonstrate 40ns single-qubit gates with an average gate fidelity of 99.94% estimated using cross-entropy benchmarking(XEB) and 120ns CZ gates with 99.63% fidelity. These results demonstrate the feasibility of common-clock encoded pulse control for both single- and two-qubit gates.

AI.tldr: The authors propose and experimentally demonstrate a common-clock control scheme that uses guiding waveforms to generate bipolar high-speed pulse sequences, enabling single- and two-qubit gates without qubit-dependent microwave sources. Simulated fidelities reach 99.99% for 40 ns R(φ, π/2) gates and 99.9% for 100 ns CZ gates; experiments on a fixed 25 GSa/s AWG yield 99.94% average single-qubit fidelity (XEB) and 99.63% CZ fidelity.
AI.motivation: Traditional analog microwave control infrastructure for superconducting qubits becomes prohibitively complex at scale, and SFQ cryogenic control could reduce wiring, but triggering SFQ pulses with qubit-dependent microwave frequencies requires many independent analog sources. A scalable SFQ control system needs to address qubits with different transition frequencies using a single common clock.
AI.method: A control scheme in which guiding waveforms rapidly generate bipolar high-speed pulse sequences on a common clock, providing a path to future SFQ-based implementation. Numerically, pulse sequences are optimized/simulated for arbitrary-phase R(φ, π/2) and CZ gates; experimentally, an AWG at a fixed 25 GSa/s sampling rate delivers the bipolar high-speed pulse sequences to implement the gates.
AI.result: Simulated fidelity of 99.99% for 40 ns R(φ, π/2) gates with arbitrary initial phases and 99.9% for 100 ns CZ gates. Experimentally, 40 ns single-qubit gates achieve an average fidelity of 99.94% by XEB, and 120 ns CZ gates achieve 99.63% fidelity.
AI.conclusion: Common-clock encoded pulse control is feasible for both single- and two-qubit gates, supporting a route toward scalable, wiring-reduced SFQ control of superconducting quantum processors.

title: Symmetry-selected entanglement death at Floquet resonances of parametrically coupled qubits
summary: Periodic modulation of a qubit--qubit coupling is a standard way to engineer quantum interactions, but a strong modulation also reorganizes the transitions through which the qubits dissipate into a comb of Floquet channels. We study two identical, strongly coupled qubits whose transverse coupling is modulated anharmonically, as by a nonlinear coupler, with each qubit damped by its own reservoir. The modulation raises the ground-state concurrence of the cycle-averaged Hamiltonian from 0.45 to above 0.8, yet the steady-state concurrence stays close to its undriven value except at Floquet resonances selected by symmetry. There it undergoes entanglement death, vanishing at all times in the drive cycle over a finite range of modulation depths. Parity and exchange symmetry split the Floquet spectrum into an even sector, whose branches anticross at multiphoton resonances, and an exactly solvable odd sector, whose branches cross. Every dissipative channel connects the two sectors, so only the even anticrossings cause entanglement death, provided their gap exceeds the damping rate, whereas the nearby odd crossings leave the concurrence unchanged. Comparing time-independent and Floquet master equations, with and without the secular approximation, we show that the basis in which the dissipator is built changes the entanglement by up to 0.2 for an Ohmic bath and 0.5 for a flat one, whereas the secular approximation matters only near anticrossings with gaps comparable to the damping. The basis matters most when the bath has spectral weight at low frequency, where the drive moves dissipative channels through zero frequency. A transverse field that breaks parity lifts the selection rule.

AI.tldr: Strong anharmonic modulation of qubit-qubit coupling reorganizes dissipation into Floquet channels. Ground-state concurrence rises from 0.45 to >0.8, but steady-state concurrence remains near its undriven value except at parity-selected Floquet resonances, where entanglement death occurs over a finite range of modulation depths.
AI.motivation: Periodic modulation is a standard tool for engineering quantum interactions, yet strong modulation also reshapes the dissipative channels (Floquet sidebands) through which qubits decay—raising the question of how drive-induced spectral reorganization affects steady-state entanglement and how master-equation construction choices (dissipator basis, secular approximation) bias predictions.
AI.method: Two identical, strongly coupled qubits with anharmonically modulated transverse coupling (nonlinear coupler), each damped by its own reservoir. Parity and exchange symmetry decompose the Floquet spectrum into an even sector with anticrossings at multiphoton resonances and an exactly solvable odd sector with crossings. Time-independent vs. Floquet master equations, with and without the secular approximation, are compared for Ohmic and flat baths.
AI.result: Cycle-averaged ground-state concurrence increases from 0.45 to above 0.8, while steady-state concurrence stays near the undriven value except at Floquet resonances, where it vanishes at all times in the drive cycle over a finite modulation-depth range (entanglement death). Only even-sector anticrossings trigger this, requiring gap > damping rate; adjacent odd crossings leave concurrence unchanged since all dissipative channels couple the sectors. Dissipator basis choice shifts entanglement by up to 0.2 (Ohmic) and 0.5 (flat) bath; the secular approximation matters only near anticrossings with gap comparable to damping. Basis effects dominate when the bath has low-frequency spectral weight, where the drive pushes dissipative channels through zero frequency. A parity-breaking transverse field lifts the selection rule.
AI.conclusion: Strong coupling modulation enhances ground-state entanglement but does not generally enhance steady-state entanglement; instead symmetry-selected Floquet resonances can drive entanglement death. Entanglement predictions are strongly sensitive to the basis used to construct the dissipator (especially for low-frequency-weighted baths) and, near anticrossings, to the secular approximation. Parity is the key selection rule, removable by a transverse field—offering a design principle for driven, dissipative entanglement control.

title: Emergence and Persistence of Maximal Atom-Field Entanglement in the Jaynes-Cummings model
comment: To be published in Physica Scripta
summary: We investigate the emergence and persistence of maximal entanglement between a two-level atom and a single-mode quantized electromagnetic field inside a cavity, whose dynamics are governed by the Jaynes-Cummings Hamiltonian. Using the von Neumann entropy as a measure of entanglement, we establish a direct connection between entanglement, atomic coherence, and atomic population inversion. This establishment shows that maximal atom-field entanglement is achieved when both the atomic population inversion and the $l_1$-norm of atomic coherence simultaneously vanish. By considering the atom initially in its excited state, we further demonstrate that the persistence of maximal atom-field entanglement strongly depends on the initial state of the field. For field states whose photon-number distributions have no two consecutive occupied photon-number levels, the local atomic coherence remains zero throughout the evolution. Consequently, complete collapse of the atomic population inversion for an extended period leads to persistent maximal atom-field entanglement. In contrast, for other field states, the interaction generates local atomic coherence, resulting in transient maximal entanglement. Our results demonstrate how the choice of the initial field state controls the temporal characteristics of entanglement in the Jaynes-Cummings system. The generation and persistence of maximal atom-field entanglement in such systems could be valuable for applications in quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: In the Jaynes-Cummings model with an initially excited atom, maximal atom-field entanglement occurs exactly when both atomic population inversion and the l1-norm of atomic coherence vanish simultaneously; whether this maximal entanglement persists or is transient depends on the initial field's photon-number distribution—specifically on whether it lacks two consecutive occupied photon-number levels.
AI.motivation: To understand what conditions generate and sustain maximal entanglement between a two-level atom and a single cavity mode, and how the initial field state controls the temporal character of that entanglement—relevant for quantum information processing.
AI.method: Analytical study of the Jaynes-Cummings Hamiltonian. Entanglement is quantified via the von Neumann entropy, which is linked to atomic coherence (l1-norm) and atomic population inversion. The atom starts in its excited state; different initial field states (photon-number distributions) are compared, tracking local atomic coherence and inversion over time.
AI.result: Maximal atom-field entanglement is achieved when population inversion and l1-norm coherence vanish together. For field states with no two consecutive occupied photon-number levels, local atomic coherence stays zero throughout evolution, so extended collapse of inversion yields persistent maximal entanglement. For other field states, the interaction generates local coherence, giving only transient maximal entanglement.
AI.conclusion: The initial field state's photon-number structure governs whether maximal atom-field entanglement is persistent or transient in the Jaynes-Cummings system. Such controllable generation and persistence of maximal entanglement is potentially useful for quantum information processing applications.

title: CHEQ: A Concurrent Hardware Evaluation Platform for QEC Decoders via Batch-Invariant Circuit-Level Noise Sampling
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. This paper has been accepted for publication in the Proceedings of DATE 2027
summary: Hardware quantum error correction (QEC) decoders require validation of logical error suppression and timing compliance before deployment. Rare logical failures and deadline violations demand extensive sampling, while algorithm-level software evaluation does not directly measure hardware response times. Circuit-level noise models contain many error mechanisms but few firings per shot at low physical error rates, making exhaustive per-shot scanning inefficient. We present CHEQ, an FPGA platform integrating on-chip sampling, concurrent decoder evaluation, scoring, and RISC-V control. Its Sampling Units use geometric skipping to sample firing locations from detector error models and amortize mechanism traversal across shots within each batch. Under independent random draws and exact geometric sampling, the shot distribution is invariant to batch size, enabling a memory-throughput tradeoff. A throughput model guides joint selection of the Sampling Unit count, batch size, and decoder count under FPGA resource constraints. Across evaluated conditions, the pooled one-sided 95% upper bound on the weighted root-mean-square relative firing-rate difference from Stim is 0.16%. At a batch size of 4,096, a Sampling Unit uses only 4.8%-11.2% of a Helios decoder's LUTs for code distances 7, 9, 11, and 13. On an AMD VCU118 FPGA at code distance 7 and physical error rate 10^-3, two Sampling Units supply 20 Helios decoders at 49.2 million shots/s, completing 10^10 shots in 3.4 minutes without host-side shot generation.

AI.motivation: Hardware QEC decoders must be validated for logical error suppression and timing compliance before deployment. Rare logical failures and deadline violations require extensive sampling, while software-level evaluation fails to measure true hardware response times. Circuit-level noise models have many error mechanisms but few firings per shot at low physical error rates, making exhaustive per-shot scanning inefficient.
AI.method: CHEQ integrates on-chip sampling, concurrent decoder evaluation, scoring, and RISC-V control on FPGA. Sampling Units apply geometric skipping to sample firing locations from detector error models and amortize mechanism traversal across shots within each batch. Under independent random draws with exact geometric sampling, the shot distribution is invariant to batch size, enabling a memory-throughput tradeoff. AI.conclusion: CHEQ enables efficient, statistically faithful, high-throughput on-chip QEC decoder validation, eliminating host-side shot generation bottlenecks and supporting scalable, resource-conscious FPGA deployment with minimal overhead relative to the decoder itself.

title: Logical error prediction and geometry selection for rectangular surface codes under biased circuit-level noise
summary: Realistic quantum hardware often exhibits biased noise, but at the circuit level this bias may affect only a subset of operations and need not be transferred uniformly to logical errors. The logical response to a given physical bias is therefore central to selecting resource-efficient surface code geometries. Here, we study unrotated rectangular surface codes under standard depolarizing and superconducting-inspired circuit-level noise models. We first construct geometry-dependent logical error rate models from unbiased circuit-level simulations. We then use logical sensitivities to compare the responses to localized idle-bias and global physical error perturbations, defining logical-error-type-dependent response coefficients from an unbiased reference circuit without fitting to finite-bias data. These coefficients are incorporated through effective error parameters, yielding a median fold error of 1.09 over the evaluated finite-bias conditions. Geometries selected by the model are validated through direct biased circuit-level simulations. At a physical error rate of 0.004 and a target logical error rate of 10^{-3}, the validated rectangular codes reduce physical qubit overhead by up to 42.4% and 26.2% under the two noise models, respectively, relative to unrotated square codes. These results provide a practical link between circuit-level bias response and resource-efficient surface code design.

AI.tldr: Unrotated rectangular surface codes are analyzed under depolarizing and superconducting-inspired circuit-level noise, with a geometry-dependent logical error model derived from unbiased simulations to predict response to biased noise and select resource-efficient code geometries.
AI.motivation: Real quantum hardware shows biased noise, but circuit-level bias may affect only a subset of operations and is not uniformly transferred to logical errors; understanding the logical response to physical bias is key for choosing resource-efficient surface code geometries.
AI.method: Geometry-dependent logical error rate models are built from unbiased circuit-level simulations. Logical sensitivities are used to compare responses to localized idle-bias and global physical error perturbations, defining logical-error-type-dependent response coefficients from an unbiased reference circuit without fitting to finite-bias data. These coefficients enter via effective error parameters.
AI.result: The model achieves a median fold error of 1.09 across evaluated finite-bias conditions. Model-selected geometries are validated by direct biased circuit-level simulations. At physical error rate 0.004 and target logical error rate 10^-3, validated rectangular codes reduce physical qubit overhead by up to 42.4% and 26.2% under the two noise models versus unrotated square codes.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a practical link between circuit-level bias response and resource-efficient surface code design, enabling overhead reduction through geometry selection informed by logical sensitivity analysis.

title: Circuit compilation in the quspect quantum SDK: selecting routings after coupling-constrained resynthesis
summary: quspect is an open-source quantum computing SDK that provides circuit construction, C++ state-vector simulation with adjoint gradients, support for variational and combinatorial-optimization algorithms, Hamiltonian simulation, control-pulse envelopes and backends for several cloud quantum processors. Here we describe and evaluate its circuit compiler. Routing and synthesis interact: inserting a SWAP can change the circuit structure that later optimization exploits. At its highest optimization level, the compiler evaluates a screened set of routing candidates by their cost after coupling-constrained resynthesis. The pipeline combines parity-state A* search for small CNOT-phase regions, heuristic synthesis for larger regions, and numerical three-qubit instantiation with a per-block 10^-9 check. For a fixed phase polynomial, A* certifies the minimum CX count when it reaches a goal within budget. On an evaluation set of 55 circuits from 41 arXiv papers on five topologies, the compiler uses 0.616 times as many two-qubit gates as Qiskit O3 (95% circuit-cluster bootstrap interval 0.555-0.679) at 0.592 times its depth. BQSKit level 2 reaches 0.853 and tket 0.930. On a 17-qubit superconducting processor, the compiled circuits had the fewest CZ gates in all six scenarios of the main run. Ablations assess the contributions within the integrated pipeline.

AI.tldr: quspect is a quantum SDK whose circuit compiler couples routing with coupling-constrained resynthesis, using parity-state A* search plus heuristic synthesis and numerical three-qubit instantiation. On 55 benchmark circuits across five topologies it reaches 0.616× the two-qubit gate count and 0.592× the depth of Qiskit O3.
AI.motivation: Routing and synthesis are interdependent: inserting a SWAP alters the circuit structure that later optimization can exploit, so treating them separately leaves optimization potential unrealized.
AI.method: The compiler is described within quspect, an open-source SDK offering circuit construction, C++ state-vector simulation with adjoint gradients, variational/combinatorial-optimization and Hamiltonian-simulation support, control-pulse envelopes, and cloud backend access. At the highest optimization level, a screened set of routing candidates is evaluated by their cost after coupling-constrained resynthesis. The pipeline combines parity-state A* search for small CNOT-phase regions, heuristic synthesis for larger regions, and numerical three-qubit instantiation with a per-block 10^-9 check. For a fixed phase polynomial, A* certifies minimal CX count when it reaches a goal within budget. Ablations isolate the contributions of individual pipeline components.
AI.result: On 55 circuits drawn from 41 arXiv papers over five topologies, the compiler uses 0.616× the two-qubit gates of Qiskit O3 (95% circuit-cluster bootstrap interval 0.555–0.679) at 0.592× its depth; BQSKit level 2 achieves 0.853 and tket 0.930. On a 17-qubit superconducting processor, compiled circuits had the fewest CZ gates in all six scenarios of the main run.
AI.conclusion: Integrating routing with coupling-constrained resynthesis yields substantial reductions in two-qubit gate count and depth relative to established compilers, validated both on a broad benchmark set and on hardware, with A* providing certified minimality for fixed phase polynomials.

title: Gradient Ascent Pulse Engineering for Multi-Time Correlations
summary: In quantum optimal control, gradient methods are often used to optimize functions of a state or propagator at a final time, while experimentally addressable observables and performance metrics may depend on multi-time correlations. We develop QRT-GRAPE, which combines the quantum regression theorem (QRT) with Gradient Ascent Pulse Engineering (GRAPE) to obtain analytic gradients for objective functions defined by multi-time correlations. The method incorporates the time evolution of an auxiliary operator in QRT into the forward propagation and backward adjoint propagation used in GRAPE. As an application, we consider the trade-off between the photon-emission probability and the conditional Bell-state fidelity in heralded remote entanglement generation among two nonidentical atom--cavity systems. Starting from a flat-top Rabi pulse pair selected by a search over pulse amplitudes and durations, QRT-GRAPE increases the photon-emission probability product from $0.2802$ to $0.3216$ and the conditional Bell-state fidelity from $0.9356$ to $0.9441$.

AI.tldr: QRT-GRAPE combines the quantum regression theorem with GRAPE to compute analytic gradients for objectives defined by multi-time correlations, and applies it to balance photon-emission probability against conditional Bell-state fidelity in heralded remote entanglement generation between two nonidentical atom–cavity systems.
AI.motivation: Standard gradient-based quantum optimal control (e.g., GRAPE) optimizes functions of a state or propagator at a single final time, but many experimentally relevant observables and performance metrics depend on multi-time correlations, which are not directly handled by conventional final-time objectives.
AI.method: The authors develop QRT-GRAPE, embedding the time evolution of an auxiliary operator arising in the quantum regression theorem into both the forward propagation and the backward adjoint propagation used in GRAPE, thereby yielding analytic gradients for objective functions defined by multi-time correlations.
AI.result: Applied to heralded remote entanglement generation between two nonidentical atom–cavity systems, starting from a flat-top Rabi pulse pair chosen by a search over amplitudes and durations, QRT-GRAPE raises the photon-emission probability product from 0.2802 to 0.3216 and the conditional Bell-state fidelity from 0.9356 to 0.9441.
AI.conclusion: QRT-GRAPE provides an efficient analytic-gradient framework for optimizing multi-time-correlation objectives in quantum control, demonstrated to jointly improve emission probability and conditional fidelity in a heralded entanglement protocol using nonidentical atom–cavity systems.

title: Optimizing interference zeros for finite-pulse transmission in waveguide quantum electrodynamics
summary: A photon pulse occupies a range of frequencies, so suppressing reflection at its carrier need not minimize the error of the transmitted pulse. We study two separated emitters coupled to a common waveguide at several contact points. Interference between the contact paths can make the coupling that drives each emitter quadratic in frequency detuning. With matched propagation and emitter resonances centered on the carrier, the reflected fields cancel once more. Their combined reflection probability is then sixth order at zero loss. Separating each local double zero into two simple zeros can nevertheless improve transmission of a finite pulse. We minimize the leading narrowband error within this common static adjustment, counting reflection, absorption, and distortion of the transmitted mode. For a Gaussian pulse without loss, the minimum is two-fifths of the error for coincident zeros. Independent emitter loss favors a smaller separation because photons entering separate reservoirs do not share the cancellation of the reflected fields. The optimum follows from the pulse spectrum and the relative weight of these two processes. Uniform and Su--Schrieffer--Heeger waveguides realize the mechanism. In the latter, coordinated contact and resonance adjustments also preserve the full ratio of complex transmission amplitudes for opposite incidence directions. Finite-band calculations determine how the benefit changes with bandwidth and contact errors.

AI.tldr: A pulse's finite bandwidth means minimizing reflection exactly at the carrier is not optimal; by tuning zero-separation of two interference-induced reflection zeros, the leading narrowband error of the transmitted pulse can be reduced to two-fifths of the coincident-zero value for a lossless Gaussian pulse.
AI.motivation: For a finite-bandwidth photon pulse, suppressing reflection at the carrier frequency does not necessarily minimize the error of the transmitted pulse, so a criterion beyond on-resonance reflection cancellation is needed.
AI.method: Two separated emitters are coupled to a common waveguide at multiple contact points; interference between contact paths makes the driven coupling quadratic in frequency detuning. Splitting each local double zero of reflection into two simple zeros is treated as a common static adjustment, and the leading narrowband error (reflection, absorption, distortion) is minimized analytically, with uniform and Su–Schrieffer–Heeger waveguide realizations.
AI.result: With matched propagation and emitters resonant at the carrier, reflected fields cancel and the combined reflection is sixth order at zero loss. Separating each double zero into two simple zeros can improve finite-pulse transmission; for a lossless Gaussian pulse the minimum error is two-fifths of that for coincident zeros. Independent emitter loss favors smaller separation, since photons entering separate reservoirs do not share the reflected-field cancellation; the optimum depends on the pulse spectrum and relative weight of the two processes.
AI.conclusion: Optimal pulse transmission through multi-contact emitter–waveguide systems follows from deliberate splitting of reflection zeros rather than exact on-resonance cancellation; in SSH waveguides coordinated contact and resonance adjustments additionally preserve the full ratio of complex transmission amplitudes for opposite incidence directions.

title: Nonlinear function regression using quantum ensemble learning
summary: Recent advances in artificial intelligence and quantum technologies have driven the emergence of quantum machine learning, yet imperfections in near-term quantum devices remain a major obstacle for achieving practical quantum advantage. In the absence of fault-tolerant machines, ensemble learning, which combines multiple imperfect quantum devices, may unlock new quantum computing applications. Here, we introduce two ensemble-learning algorithms, namely Bagging and AdaBoost, for enhancing the accuracy of nonlinear regression problems. While Bagging trains variational quantum regressors independently, AdaBoost employs a sequential training strategy and achieves significantly better prediction accuracy. By incorporating systematic feature selection into our ensemble learning algorithms, we enhance their predictive power for highly nonlinear functions. We further improve prediction accuracy through a feature-to-qubit mapping strategy based on repeated feature encoding. The performance of our ensemble-based algorithms improves with both the number of regressors in the ensemble and the size of each regressor. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using four benchmarking functions with varying degrees of nonlinearity by relying on a feature pool limited to first- and second-order polynomial terms.

AI.tldr: This work introduces Bagging and AdaBoost ensemble-learning algorithms for variational quantum regressors, combined with systematic feature selection and repeated feature encoding, to improve nonlinear regression accuracy on imperfect near-term quantum devices.
AI.motivation: Hardware imperfections in near-term quantum devices block practical quantum advantage, and fault-tolerant machines are unavailable. Ensemble learning that combines multiple imperfect quantum devices is proposed as a route to unlock new quantum computing applications.
AI.method: Two ensemble-learning algorithms are introduced for nonlinear regression: Bagging, which trains variational quantum regressors independently, and AdaBoost, which uses a sequential training strategy. Systematic feature selection is incorporated into both, along with a feature-to-qubit mapping based on repeated feature encoding.
AI.result: AdaBoost achieves significantly better prediction accuracy than Bagging. Performance improves with both the number of regressors in the ensemble and the size of each regressor. Effectiveness is demonstrated on four benchmarking functions of varying nonlinearity using a feature pool limited to first- and second-order polynomial terms.
AI.conclusion: Ensemble learning of imperfect quantum regressors, augmented by feature selection and repeated feature encoding, is a viable strategy for enhancing nonlinear regression accuracy on near-term quantum hardware, with accuracy scaling favorably with ensemble and regressor size.

title: Strong eigenstate thermalization in Singer-cycle Clifford circuits
summary: Eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH) provides a central framework for understanding thermalization in isolated quantum systems. Recently, the infinite-temperature ETH has been established for almost all Floquet eigenstates in linear feedback shift register quantum circuits. Here we introduce brickwork Clifford circuits with $L$ qubits where the induced transformation of Pauli operators is represented by an irreducible symplectic matrix over the finite field $\mathbb F_2$ of the maximal order $2^L+1$, known as a Singer cycle. For these Singer-cycle Clifford circuits, we prove a strong version of ETH: all Floquet eigenstates are thermal at infinite temperature without exceptions. We derive uniform bounds on both diagonal deviations from thermal expectation values and off-diagonal matrix elements of arbitrary observables supported on a fixed number of sites. The results indicate that long-time averages of observables approach the infinite-temperature values in the thermodynamic limit for arbitrary initial states. We also show that the temporal fluctuation of expectation values of observables is exponentially suppressed in the thermodynamic limit, implying that each observable remains close to the infinite-temperature value for almost all times.

AI.tldr: The authors prove a strong, exception-free eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH) at infinite temperature for all Floquet eigenstates of brickwork Clifford circuits generated by a Singer cycle (an irreducible symplectic matrix over F_2 of maximal order 2^L+1), with uniform bounds on diagonal and off-diagonal matrix elements and exponentially suppressed temporal fluctuations.
AI.motivation: ETH is the central framework for thermalization in isolated quantum systems, but rigorous results are scarce and typically hold only for almost all eigenstates. Prior work established infinite-temperature ETH for almost all Floquet eigenstates in linear feedback shift register quantum circuits; the goal here is to strengthen this to an exception-free statement and characterize observable dynamics.
AI.method: Construct brickwork Clifford circuits on L qubits whose induced action on Pauli operators is an irreducible symplectic matrix over F_2 of maximal order 2^L+1 (a Singer cycle). Exploit the algebraic structure of the Singer cycle to prove uniform bounds on diagonal deviations from thermal expectation values and on off-diagonal matrix elements of arbitrary observables supported on a fixed number of sites, then bound long-time averages and temporal fluctuations of expectation values.
AI.result: All Floquet eigenstates are thermal at infinite temperature without exceptions. Uniform bounds are obtained on diagonal and off-diagonal matrix elements for arbitrary fixed-support observables. Long-time averages of observables approach infinite-temperature values in the thermodynamic limit for arbitrary initial states, and temporal fluctuations of expectation values are exponentially suppressed in the thermodynamic limit.
AI.conclusion: Singer-cycle Clifford circuits provide a clean, exactly solvable setting realizing the strongest form of infinite-temperature ETH, showing that every eigenstate thermalizes and that each observable stays close to its infinite-temperature value for almost all times, thereby clarifying the mechanism of thermalization in a structured yet non-trivial Floquet setting.

title: Optimal Measurement Rounds for Perfect Encoded Fusion
summary: Encoded fusion combines probabilistic physical fusions to perform a logical Bell measurement. Adaptive choices depend on earlier measurement outcomes and therefore require multiple measurement rounds. We determine the minimum worst-case number of rounds for perfect fusion of two blocks of an irreducible [[n,1]] stabilizer code. A strategy is perfect if the logical Bell measurement succeeds on every branch containing at least one successful physical fusion. Even after fixing the past history, including measurement values, we consider all success/failure branches, including those with zero probability for a particular input state or measurement device. In a lossless model with fixed coordinate pairing, arbitrary Pauli failure bases, and each pair fused exactly once, the optimum equals the minimum root eccentricity over the local complementation orbit of rooted graphs representing the code. The lower bound applies to arbitrary perfect strategies that choose batches and bases using previous outcomes. We also characterize the batch sequences that can occur on an all-failure branch of a perfect strategy by a necessary and sufficient graph adjacency condition. A matching strategy fuses distance layers from the outside in and, after the first success, completes the remaining fusions in at most one further round by changing the failure bases along an induced path.

AI.tldr: This work determines the minimum worst-case number of adaptive measurement rounds needed to perform a perfect logical Bell measurement ("encoded fusion") between two blocks of an irreducible [[n,1]] stabilizer code, showing the optimum equals a minimum root eccentricity over the local complementation orbit of rooted graphs representing the code.
AI.motivation: Encoded fusion performs a logical Bell measurement via probabilistic physical fusions, but adaptive choices depending on prior outcomes force multiple measurement rounds. A fundamental question is how few rounds (worst case) suffice for perfect fusion, where success is guaranteed on every branch having at least one successful physical fusion.
AI.method: A lossless model with fixed coordinate pairing, arbitrary Pauli failure bases, and each pair fused exactly once is analyzed. The problem is mapped to graph theory: rooted graphs represent the code, and the optimum is characterized as the minimum root eccentricity over the local complementation orbit of that graph. Lower bounds are proven to hold even for arbitrary perfect strategies that select batches and bases from previous outcomes. Batch sequences on an all-failure branch are characterized by a necessary and sufficient graph adjacency condition. A constructive matching strategy fuses distance layers from the outside in and, after the first success, finishes remaining fusions in at most one further round by changing failure bases along an induced path.
AI.result: The minimum worst-case round count for perfect fusion equals the minimum root eccentricity over the local complementation orbit of rooted graphs representing the code. A lower bound valid for all adaptive perfect strategies is established, the all-failure batch sequences are fully characterized, and a matching strategy achieving at most one additional round after the first success is constructed.
AI.conclusion: Perfect encoded fusion of irreducible [[n,1]] stabilizer code blocks has a graph-theoretic optimum given by minimum root eccentricity on the local complementation orbit, with tight lower bounds for arbitrary adaptive strategies and a matching constructive strategy, linking adaptive fusion round complexity to rooted-graph invariants.

title: Generating Massive Mechanical Superpositions through Qubit-Mediated Interference
summary: We propose a method towards demonstrating a quantum superposition of a massive mechanical resonator without the need for exact ground-state cooling, a requirement that becomes increasingly difficult to satisfy for low-frequency resonators. Our scheme relies on coupling the resonator to a spin-qubit. Using magnetic force coupling between the motion of the mechanical resonator and the spin-qubit, the resonator is forced into attracted and repelled states as the spin-qubit is coherently controlled. Interference between the resonator states can be observed when a series of $\tfracπ{2}$-pulses is applied to the spin-qubit within the coherence time of the resonator. The protocol describes a true which-path interference experiment suitable for use at ultra-low temperatures, since it requires only three $\tfracπ{2}$-pulses, separated in time by half a mechanical period, thus minimizing the heat-load and duration of the experiment. By analysing the experimental requirements necessary to successfully execute the protocol, we show that the protocol is suitable for resonators in a broad regime of resonance frequencies, ranging from 1kHz resonators, which have the advantage of a relatively high spin-coupling, to resonators of more than 100kHz, whose mechanical mode is easier to cool. We show that interference remains visible for resonator mode occupations exceeding 10 phonons. Lastly, we observe that an implementation of the protocol with low-frequency mechanical resonators provides a promising approach towards testing objective collapse models.

AI.tldr: A spin-qubit–coupled mechanical resonator scheme creates a genuine which-path superposition via three π/2 pulses spaced by half a mechanical period, removing the need for exact ground-state cooling and working for 1 kHz–>100 kHz resonators with occupations above 10 phonons.
AI.motivation: Demonstrating quantum superposition of massive mechanical resonators traditionally requires near-ground-state cooling, which becomes prohibitively difficult for low-frequency resonators. A protocol tolerant of finite thermal occupation would therefore broaden the accessible mass/frequency regime.
AI.method: The resonator is magnetically force-coupled to a spin-qubit. Coherent control of the spin-qubit drives the resonator into attracted/repelled displaced states, and a sequence of three π/2-pulses separated by half a mechanical period realises a which-path interference measurement, all within the resonator coherence time and at ultra-low temperature with minimal heat load.
AI.result: Analysis of experimental requirements shows applicability across resonance frequencies from 1 kHz (strong spin coupling) to above 100 kHz (easier to cool). Interference visibility persists for mode occupations exceeding 10 phonons.
AI.conclusion: The protocol enables true which-path interference of a massive mechanical resonator without exact ground-state cooling, and low-frequency implementations offer a promising route to testing objective collapse models.

title: Analytical prediction of superradiant burst dynamics in extended atomic ensembles
summary: We present an open-system quantum theory of forward superradiant bursts in extended two-level atomic ensembles using coupled Heisenberg-Langevin and Maxwell propagation equations. Starting from a fully inverted state with zero mean polarization, local dipole correlations initiate emission without a prescribed tipping angle or stochastic seed. Assuming a spatially uniform population inversion while retaining longitudinal field propagation and spatially dependent atomic polarization, we derive an analytical expression for the absolute photon emission rate into the selected forward optical channel. Coupled to self-consistent inversion dynamics, the expression quantitatively reproduces the pulse waveform and absolute peak rate from spatially resolved stochastic simulations for the sample parameters considered, up to an optical depth (OD) of approximately 200. At higher OD, longitudinal inversion gradients limit the approximation, while the peak rate trends toward Dicke-like quadratic scaling and the pulse width decreases approximately inversely with OD. The framework thus connects quantum initiation, propagation, and inversion depletion while delineating the limits of a spatially reduced description.

AI.tldr: An open-system quantum theory combining Heisenberg-Langevin and Maxwell propagation equations reproduces forward superradiant burst waveforms and absolute peak rates in extended two-level ensembles up to OD≈200 without any prescribed tipping angle or stochastic seed.
AI.motivation: Existing descriptions of forward superradiant bursts often presume a tipping angle or stochastic seed and neglect propagation, leaving unclear how emission initiates from a fully inverted state with zero mean polarization and how longitudinal propagation and inversion depletion jointly set the pulse shape.
AI.method: Coupled Heisenberg-Langevin equations with Maxwell propagation are used; local dipole correlations initiate emission from a fully inverted, zero-polarization state. Under a spatially uniform inversion approximation that retains longitudinal field propagation and spatially dependent polarization, an analytical expression for the absolute photon emission rate into the selected forward optical channel is derived and combined with self-consistent inversion dynamics.
AI.result: The analytical rate quantitatively reproduces pulse waveforms and absolute peak rates from spatially resolved stochastic simulations for the sample parameters, up to OD≈200. At higher OD, longitudinal inversion gradients limit the approximation; the peak rate trends toward Dicke-like quadratic scaling and the pulse width decreases approximately inversely with OD.
AI.conclusion: The framework links quantum initiation, propagation, and inversion depletion in a single open-system description, while explicitly delimiting where a spatially reduced approximation breaks down.

title: Anti-aging Squeezed Quantum Battery
summary: Exhibiting the superiority of energy storage and conversion over its classical counterpart, quantum battery (QB) emerges as a promising platform to revolutionize traditional energy technologies. However, their practical performance is severely constrained by the ubiquitous decoherence in microscopic world, which causes rapid aging and reduced ergotropy. Here, we propose a decoherence-tolerant QB consisting of a continuous-variable bosonic mode. Acting as the quantum resource, the utilized squeezing endows the QB with unprecedented energy capacity and ergotropy. Through investigating the non-Markovian decoherence effect on the QB, we find that such squeezing enhanced performance can be persistently preserved under the influence of decoherence as long as a bound state is present in the energy spectrum of the total system formed by the QB and the environment. This decoherence-tolerance feature is even maintained under moderate finite-temperature condition. Providing a useful energy storage paradigm for designing long-lived QBs, our result sheds light on the realization of anti-aging QBs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a decoherence-tolerant quantum battery (QB) built from a single continuous-variable bosonic mode, showing that squeezing enhances energy capacity and ergotropy, and that this enhanced performance persists under non-Markovian decoherence whenever a bound state exists in the QB-environment spectrum.
AI.motivation: Quantum batteries offer advantages in energy storage and conversion, but ubiquitous microscopic decoherence causes rapid aging and reduced ergotropy, limiting practical performance.
AI.method: A continuous-variable bosonic mode serves as the QB, with squeezing as the quantum resource. The authors analyze non-Markovian decoherence of the QB coupled to an environment, tracking energy capacity and ergotropy and examining the spectrum of the total QB-environment system.
AI.result: Squeezing endows the QB with unprecedented energy capacity and ergotropy, and this enhancement is persistently preserved under decoherence as long as a bound state exists in the total system's energy spectrum; the tolerance also holds at moderate finite temperature.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a useful energy-storage paradigm for designing long-lived, anti-aging quantum batteries, highlighting bound states as the mechanism for decoherence-tolerant performance.

title: Entanglement in restricted experimental setups
