summary: Entanglement is a necessary resource for steering and Bell nonlocality, yet whether a state is separable takes no account of what an experiment can prepare or measure. We define two notions of separability relative to an experiment, one on either side of separability. Inner separability confines the local states to the preparable sets. Outer separability lets the local factors be self-adjoint operators positive on the available effects but not necessarily positive semidefinite. We find exactly when each departs from separability and that outer separability keeps the operational content of separability for the available measurements: outer separable states, entangled or not, admit local hidden variable models for every behaviour these measurements generate and, when the steered party is unrestricted, local hidden state models for every assemblage the steering party's measurements generate. Such hidden state models do not imply outer separability in general, but we identify conditions under which they do.

AI.tldr: The authors define two experiment-relative notions of separability—inner separability (local states restricted to preparable sets) and outer separability (local factors allowed to be non-positive self-adjoint operators)—and characterize exactly when each diverges from standard separability. They show outer separability preserves the operational content of separability for available measurements: outer separable states admit local hidden variable models for all behaviours these measurements generate, and local hidden state models for all assemblages when the steered party is unrestricted.
AI.motivation: Standard separability is a device-independent, all-measurement property, but actual experiments can only prepare a restricted set of states and measure a restricted set of effects. Whether a state is entangled (as theoretically defined) does not reflect what a given experiment can actually prepare or measure, so a more operational, experiment-relative notion of separability is needed to capture the genuinely observable consequences of separability.
AI.method: The paper introduces two definitions of separability relative to a fixed experiment. Inner separability constrains the local states to the set of states that can be prepared. Outer separability relaxes the requirement that local factors be positive semidefinite, allowing self-adjoint operators that are merely positive on the available effects. The authors derive exact conditions under which each notion departs from standard separability, and analyze the operational consequences in terms of local hidden variable (LHV) models for behaviours and local hidden state (LHS) models for assemblages.
AI.result: The authors determine exactly when inner and outer separability deviate from standard separability. They show that outer separability fully retains the operational content of separability for the available measurements: outer separable states—entangled or not—admit LHV models for every behaviour generated by these measurements and, when the steered party is unrestricted, admit LHS models for every assemblage generated by the steering party's measurements. They further show that such LHS models do not in general imply outer separability, but identify conditions under which they do.
AI.conclusion: Separability should be understood relative to the capabilities of a given experiment rather than as a purely device-independent property. Outer separability is the operationally relevant notion, as it guarantees LHV and LHS models for all behaviours and assemblages accessible with the available measurements, while departing from standard separability only under identifiable conditions. This reframes the role of entanglement in steering and Bell nonlocality as experiment-dependent.

title: Quantum Optimal Control of Many-Body States in an Antiferromagnetic XXZ Chain with a Single Local Magnetic Field
summary: We investigate the quantum optimal control of an antiferromagnetic XXZ spin chain with open boundary conditions, driven solely by a local time-dependent magnetic field applied to a single terminal spin. By optimizing the control field via Krotov's algorithm, we evaluate the feasibility of preparing multi-particle many-body states, including highly polarized Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ)-type states and study the mechanisms by which the control is applied. We demonstrate that global spin-flip symmetry restricts reachable state spaces, strictly confining dynamics within the parity sector of the initial ground state and requiring parity-adapted linear combinations to avoid fundamental population upper bounds. Beyond symmetry constraints, driven population transfer does not occur via direct multi-spin flips, but proceeds stepwise across intermediate magnetization sectors ($|S_{\mathrm{tot}}^z| = 0 \to 1 \to 2 \to 3$) mediated by resonant frequency components matching the internal energy gaps. To overcome optimization stagnation caused by the small overlap mechanism in gradient updates, we introduce a four-stage sequential target protocol and compared it to spectrally filtered, time-localized frequency seed pulses. Combining frequency-tailored seed fields with an extended propagation time window yields GHZ state preparation fidelities exceeding $0.927$ establishing that a single local actuator is sufficient for high-fidelity multipartite state engineering in interacting spin networks.

AI.tldr: A single local magnetic field on one terminal spin of an open antiferromagnetic XXZ chain can prepare GHZ-type multipartite states with fidelity above 0.927 when Krotov-optimized, provided parity-adapted targets and frequency-tailored seed pulses are used.
AI.motivation: To assess whether a single local actuator (one time-dependent magnetic field at a terminal spin) suffices to control and prepare highly polarized multipartite many-body states such as GHZ states in an interacting antiferromagnetic XXZ spin chain, and to understand the physical mechanisms and symmetry constraints governing such driven population transfer.
AI.method: Quantum optimal control via Krotov's algorithm on an open-boundary antiferromagnetic XXZ chain driven only by a local time-dependent field on a terminal spin. A parity-adapted target construction is used to respect global spin-flip symmetry; a four-stage sequential target protocol is introduced to counter optimization stagnation from the small-overlap mechanism in gradient updates, and compared against spectrally filtered, time-localized frequency seed pulses combined with an extended propagation time window. Mechanisms are analyzed via intermediate magnetization sectors and resonant frequency components matched to internal energy gaps.
AI.result: Global spin-flip symmetry confines dynamics to the parity sector of the initial ground state, imposing fundamental population upper bounds unless parity-adapted linear combinations are targeted. Driven population transfer does not proceed by direct multi-spin flips but stepwise through intermediate magnetization sectors (|S_tot^z| = 0 → 1 → 2 → 3), mediated by resonant frequency components matching internal energy gaps. Frequency-tailored seed fields plus an extended propagation window yield GHZ-state preparation fidelities exceeding 0.927.
AI.conclusion: A single local actuator is sufficient for high-fidelity multipartite state engineering in interacting spin networks, with symmetry-adapted targets, frequency-tailored seeding, and adequate propagation time being key enabling factors.

title: Quantum Codes for Distributed Quantum Fault Sensing
summary: Targeted recovery in modular quantum processors requires identifying the component affected by a fault. Independent qubits can monitor faults through repeated preparation and measurement. Bell-pair probes improve the guaranteed correct-site probability for unknown local channels, but require partners kept away from the fault. Can entanglement among exposed probes supply this advantage without protected storage? We establish a quantum-code criterion for optimal distributed fault sensing of one unknown local qubit channel with strength in a prescribed positive range. For one interrogation with zero false alarms and no background noise, suitable code states attain the optimal worst-case correct-site probability, improving on independent probes by 50% with every qubit exposed. Exact attainment is equivalent to mutually orthogonal input and single-qubit Pauli error subspaces. Pairwise entanglement gives no improvement, and entanglement depth at most four cannot exceed 95.54% of the optimum without protected ancillas. Approaching the optimum without protected ancillas also requires a number of probes proportional to the array size to participate in larger entangled factors. For a persistent fault under memoryless depolarizing background of fixed strength 0 < eta < 1, independent probes already attain the optimal logarithmic interrogation scaling at fixed success between zero and one and a positive false-alarm budget. In three 1000-site comparisons with specified readouts, an encoded-probe protocol certifies fewer interrogations than independent probes and only one more than optimally decoded ideal Bell pairs, while storing no protected qubits.

AI.tldr: A quantum-code criterion establishes the optimal distributed sensing of one unknown local qubit channel; suitable code states reach the optimal worst-case correct-site probability (50% better than independent probes) with all probes exposed, provided input and single-qubit Pauli error subspaces are mutually orthogonal.
AI.motivation: Targeted recovery in modular quantum processors requires identifying which component is faulty. Bell-pair probes improve guaranteed correct-site probability but need protected partner qubits kept away from the fault; the paper asks whether entanglement among exposed probes can supply the advantage without protected storage.
AI.method: Problem framed as optimal distributed fault sensing of one local qubit channel with strength in a prescribed positive range. A quantum-code criterion is derived; optimality is analyzed via orthogonality of input and single-qubit Pauli error subspaces, entanglement depth bounds, and probe-number scaling. Also treats a persistent fault under memoryless depolarizing background (0<eta<1), with three 1000-site numerical comparisons.
AI.result: For one interrogation with zero false alarms and no background noise, code states attain the optimal worst-case correct-site probability, improving on independent probes by 50% with every qubit exposed. Exact attainment is equivalent to mutually orthogonal input and single-qubit Pauli error subspaces. Pairwise entanglement gives no improvement; entanglement depth ≤4 reaches at most 95.54% of the optimum without protected ancillas. Approaching the optimum requires a number of probes proportional to array size to join larger entangled factors. Under depolarizing background, independent probes already attain optimal logarithmic interrogation scaling; in 1000-site tests, an encoded-probe protocol certifies fewer interrogations than independent probes and only one more than optimally decoded ideal Bell pairs, storing no protected qubits.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement among exposed probes can approach the optimal fault-sensing advantage without protected ancillas only via large entangled factors, while pairwise entanglement is useless; code-state orthogonality is the exact optimality condition, and encoded probes offer near-Bell-pair performance with no protected qubit storage.

title: Multilevel Effects and the Limits of the Quantum Rabi Model in Ultrastrong Coupling system
summary: The spectrum of artificial atoms coupled to resonators in the ultrastrong coupling regime have been analyzed using the quantum Rabi model over a wide range of coupling strengths. However, the accuracy of models obtained by truncating multilevel artificial atoms to two levels, as well as the correspondence between effective parameters extracted from spectral fitting and the bare parameters of the circuit Hamiltonian, depends on the multilevel structure of the system. In this study, I analyze the spectrum of an ultrastrongly coupled circuit consisting of a multilevel superconducting artificial atom and a resonator using a circuit Hamiltonian, and investigate the effects of truncating higher atomic levels on the low-energy spectrum. Based on Löwdin partitioning, I evaluate the contributions of virtual transitions through higher atomic levels and show that diagonal energy corrections reduce the errors arising from simple two-level truncation over a wide parameter range. I also show that there are parameter regimes in which readjustment of the effective Rabi parameters successfully reproduces the multilevel spectrum, while systematic deviations remain in other regimes. These results demonstrate the necessity of separately evaluating two-level truncation, perturbative corrections, and effective-parameter fitting in ultrastrongly coupled systems, and provide guidance for quantitative spectral analysis of multilevel quantum circuits.

AI.tldr: Analyzes the low-energy spectrum of an ultrastrongly coupled multilevel superconducting artificial atom-resonator circuit using a full circuit Hamiltonian, and uses Löwdin partitioning to quantify how virtual transitions through higher atomic levels correct simple two-level truncation.
AI.motivation: The quantum Rabi model is widely used to describe artificial atoms coupled to resonators in the ultrastrong coupling regime, but it relies on truncating a multilevel artificial atom to two levels. The accuracy of this truncation, and whether effective parameters from spectral fitting correspond to the bare circuit parameters, depends on the multilevel structure—issues that require systematic investigation.
AI.method: Spectrum of an ultrastrongly coupled circuit Hamiltonian comprising a multilevel superconducting artificial atom and a resonator is analyzed over a wide parameter range. Löwdin partitioning is applied to derive perturbative corrections that capture virtual transitions through higher atomic levels, and the resulting diagonal energy corrections and effective (renormalized) Rabi parameters are compared with the exact multilevel spectrum.
AI.result: Diagonal energy corrections from Löwdin partitioning reduce the errors of simple two-level truncation over a wide parameter range. Effective-parameter readjustment reproduces the multilevel spectrum in some parameter regimes, while systematic deviations persist in others.
AI.conclusion: Two-level truncation, perturbative corrections, and effective-parameter fitting must be evaluated separately in ultrastrongly coupled systems. The results provide guidance for quantitative spectral analysis of multilevel quantum circuits.

title: Predicting Quantum Mpemba Effects from Quantum Speed Limits
summary: Can anomalous Quantum Mpemba Effects be anticipated before a system comes close to its stationary state? We employ Quantum Speed Limits as geometric indicators of Quantum Mpemba Effects, arguing that Mpemba physics is already imprinted in speed limits by benchmarking dissipative qubits and open spin chains. Our results show that short-time speed limits can predict Quantum Mpemba Effects at low cost and with reasonable precision over broad parameter regimes. This predictive power implies a useful application of speed limits for open many-body quantum systems.

AI.tldr: Short-time quantum speed limits can be used as geometric indicators to predict anomalous Quantum Mpemba Effects in dissipative qubits and open spin chains, before the system approaches its stationary state.
AI.motivation: Anomalous Quantum Mpemba Effects (QME) are typically diagnosed only near the stationary state, so anticipating them early is non-trivial; the authors ask whether QME can be foreseen before the system comes close to stationarity.
AI.method: Quantum Speed Limits (QSLs) are employed as geometric indicators of QME, benchmarked on dissipative qubits and open spin chains; short-time speed limits are compared against the emergence of Mpemba physics across broad parameter regimes.
AI.result: Short-time speed limits predict Quantum Mpemba Effects at low cost and with reasonable precision over broad parameter regimes, indicating that Mpemba physics is already imprinted in the speed limits.
AI.conclusion: Speed limits offer a practical, predictive diagnostic for QME in open many-body quantum systems, extending the usefulness of QSLs as an early-warning tool for anomalous relaxation phenomena.

title: Local distinguishability of five six-partite orthogonal product states
summary: The local distinguishability of a set of orthogonal quantum states can be used to reduce the amount of quantum state transmission in quantum protocols and lower system operational costs and quantum resource overhead. In this paper, we investigate the local distinguishability of five six-partite orthogonal product states (OPSs), where any two states are orthogonal on only one subsystem. We classify all feasible sets of five six-partite OPSs into five categories with 249 cases in total, and prove that these sets can be perfectly distinguished by local operations and classical communication, except for two cases. For five six-partite OPSs corresponding to these two exceptional cases, we further discuss their local distinguishability. Our work fully characterizes the local distinguishability of all feasible sets of five six-partite OPSs.

AI.tldr: This paper fully characterizes the local distinguishability of all feasible sets of five six-partite orthogonal product states under the restricted orthogonality structure where any two states are orthogonal on exactly one subsystem.
AI.motivation: Local distinguishability of orthogonal quantum states reduces quantum-state transmission in protocols and lowers system operational cost and quantum resource overhead, yet the multipartite case with limited orthogonality (one-subsystem orthogonality) is not fully understood.
AI.method: The authors classify all feasible sets of five six-partite orthogonal product states (OPSs) into five categories totaling 249 cases, then analyze each case under local operations and classical communication (LOCC).
AI.result: All 249 cases are proven perfectly LOCC-distinguishable except for two exceptional cases; the local distinguishability of these two exceptions is further examined.
AI.conclusion: The work completely characterizes the local distinguishability of all feasible sets of five six-partite OPSs, giving a near-complete LOCC distinguishability result with only two unresolved exceptions analyzed separately.

title: Entanglement Lower Bounds for Symmetric Quantum Circuits
summary:
Symmetric circuits require every symmetry of the input to extend to an automorphism of the circuit. In the classical setting, their connection to descriptive complexity yields strong unconditional lower bounds. We extend this approach to the quantum model of symmetric computation defined by Castro-Silva, Gur, and Strelchuk (ITCS 2026), proving a tradeoff between circuit size and entanglement width (the smallest $b$ such that, on every computational-basis input, the state after each layer factors into states on at most $b$ qubits each).
  Our main result identifies a graph property decidable in classical polynomial time that no polynomial-size family of symmetric quantum circuits on $n$-vertex graphs with entanglement width $o(n/\log n)$ can compute. The bound holds for circuits with arbitrary one-qubit and two-qubit gates and unrestricted depth, and remains valid under the weaker notion of symmetry with respect to even permutations of vertices. Our proof is based on a new quantum pebble game based on the partial trace. The resulting indistinguishability theorem transfers classical pebble-game lower bounds to quantum circuits with restricted entanglement.
  By contrast, without entanglement restrictions, we show that every graph property in BQP can be computed by a uniform family of polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits. Restricting to circuits with no entanglement at all, we show that polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits with entanglement width 1 can compute every graph property definable in fixed-point logic with counting. Finally, we give an efficient symmetric implementation of QAOA for MAX 3XOR, providing a starting point for studying entanglement lower bounds in quantum optimization algorithms.

AI.tldr: Symmetric quantum circuits exhibit a size versus entanglement-width tradeoff: a polynomial-time-decidable graph property cannot be computed by polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits of entanglement width o(n/log n), while unconstrained symmetric circuits capture all of BQP.
AI.motivation: Classical symmetric circuits connect to descriptive complexity and yield strong unconditional lower bounds; the authors aim to transfer this program to the quantum model of symmetric computation recently defined by Castro-Silva, Gur, and Strelchuk (ITCS 2026).
AI.method: The proof introduces a new quantum pebble game built on the partial trace, yielding an indistinguishability theorem that lifts classical pebble-game lower bounds to quantum circuits with restricted entanglement. The model uses symmetric quantum circuits with arbitrary one- and two-qubit gates, unrestricted depth, entanglement width b (state after each layer factors into blocks of at most b qubits on every computational-basis input), and symmetry under even vertex permutations.
AI.result: Main result: a graph property decidable in classical polynomial time that no polynomial-size family of symmetric quantum circuits on n-vertex graphs with entanglement width o(n/log n) can compute. Conversely, without entanglement restrictions every BQP graph property is computable by uniform polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits; entanglement width 1 captures all properties definable in fixed-point logic with counting (FPC). An efficient symmetric QAOA implementation for MAX 3XOR is also given.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement width acts as a genuine resource separating symmetric quantum circuit classes, mirroring classical descriptive-complexity lower bounds; the framework opens a route toward entanglement lower bounds in quantum optimization.

title: Quantum speed limits from symmetries: A numerical analysis
summary: Target-specific quantum speed limits (QSLs) bound the minimal time required to realize a given operation. Recent theoretical work derives these limits directly from the symmetries of the dynamical Lie algebra of the control system and a symmetry-restoring perturbation, bypassing the need to solve the equations of motion. In practice, however, identifying a suitable symmetry and a perturbation that restores it demands strong physical intuition and offers no guarantee of tightness. We show that, for any given symmetry, the minimal restoring perturbation is the solution of a convex semidefinite program, which can be solved to global optimality and thus yields the tightest achievable speed limit for that symmetry. This semidefinite program is one building block of our numerical method, alongside an explicit computation of the space of admissible symmetries and a search over this space. Since this search is non-convex, it is addressed with gradient-based optimization, black-box heuristics, or the injection of physically motivated candidate symmetries. We apply the method to three examples: a two-qubit CNOT gate, a SWAP on a spinless-particle chain, and a Dicke state preparation on a qubit ring. Our results improve on previously known symmetry-based bounds, most notably for the SWAP, where solving the semidefinite program for the known analytical symmetry tightens the bound by a factor of approximately 2.5. For the Dicke state preparation, however, the bounds decrease with system size, which we trace back to a symmetry-independent perturbation ceiling. This work provides a reproducible numerical procedure for constructing target-specific quantum speed limits directly from the system Hamiltonians and the target operation.

AI.tldr: A reproducible numerical procedure constructs tight target-specific quantum speed limits (QSLs) by expressing the minimal symmetry-restoring perturbation as a convex semidefinite program, combined with symmetry-space computation and a non-convex search over candidate symmetries.
AI.motivation: Prior symmetry-based QSL derivations require physically intuitive guesses of a symmetry and its restoring perturbation, with no guarantee that the resulting bound is tight. The authors seek an automated, reproducible way to obtain the tightest bound achievable for any given symmetry directly from the system Hamiltonian and target operation.
AI.method: The minimal restoring perturbation for a fixed symmetry is formulated as a convex semidefinite program (SDP) solvable to global optimality. This SDP is one building block, alongside explicit computation of the space of admissible symmetries and a search over that space. Because the symmetry search is non-convex, it is handled by gradient-based optimization, black-box heuristics, or injection of physically motivated candidate symmetries.
AI.result: The method is applied to a two-qubit CNOT gate, a SWAP on a spinless-particle chain, and Dicke state preparation on a qubit ring. It improves previously known symmetry-based bounds, notably for SWAP, where solving the SDP for the known analytical symmetry tightens the bound by a factor of about 2.5. For Dicke state preparation, bounds decrease with system size, traced to a symmetry-independent perturbation ceiling.
AI.conclusion: The work delivers a reproducible numerical pipeline for constructing target-specific QSLs from system Hamiltonians and the target operation, replacing intuition-driven symmetry selection with an optimization-based, globally optimal construction of symmetry-restoring perturbations, while revealing a perturbation ceiling limiting scalability for certain targets.

title: Measurement-Conditioned Bloch-Sphere State Steering with a Continuous-Variable Pointer
summary: We investigate measurement-conditioned state steering of a qubit coupled to a continuous-variable pointer through a state-dependent displacement interaction. A position measurement on the pointer induces a nonunitary conditional transformation of the qubit, allowing its post-measurement state to move along a trajectory on the Bloch sphere. We derive the conditional state, the measurement-outcome distribution, and the corresponding Bloch-sphere coordinates. For a real Gaussian pointer, the conditional state follows a meridian, whereas a phase-engineered Gaussian pointer produces a trajectory with a measurement-dependent azimuthal angle. We further describe outcome-dependent unitary feedback for preparing a prescribed target state from a known initial qubit state. We distinguish this state-preparation task from implementing a universal deterministic single-qubit gate, which does not follow from the proposed interaction and measurement alone. Finally, we derive the quantum Fisher information of the joint qubit--pointer state for estimating the displacement-generating parameter and discuss the implications of pointer squeezing, phase engineering, and experimental implementation. The results provide a framework for analysing conditional Bloch-sphere steering using continuous-variable measurement resources.

AI.tldr: Measurement-conditioned steering of a qubit coupled to a continuous-variable pointer via a state-dependent displacement is analyzed, yielding conditional Bloch-sphere trajectories and quantum Fisher information for parameter estimation.
AI.motivation: To establish a framework for controlling qubit states using continuous-variable measurement resources, clarifying how pointer measurement induces nonunitary qubit transformations and distinguishing state preparation from universal gate implementation.
AI.method: A qubit interacts with a continuous-variable pointer through a state-dependent displacement; a position measurement on the pointer induces a conditional nonunitary qubit transformation. The authors derive the conditional state, outcome distribution, and Bloch coordinates, comparing real versus phase-engineered Gaussian pointers, and compute the quantum Fisher information of the joint state for the displacement-generating parameter.
AI.result: For a real Gaussian pointer the conditional state follows a meridian; a phase-engineered pointer yields a measurement-dependent azimuthal angle. Outcome-dependent unitary feedback prepares a prescribed target state from a known initial state. Pointer squeezing and phase engineering affect estimation precision via the quantum Fisher information.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a framework for conditional Bloch-sphere steering with continuous-variable measurement resources, and clarifies that the scheme enables state preparation but not universal deterministic single-qubit gates.

title: A Quantum Support Vector Regression Framework for Missing Data Imputation in Ship Performance Data
summary: The Internet of Ships enables vessels to generate vast amounts of data, yet missing values remain a persistent issue. To the best of the authors' knowledge, existing imputation techniques in this domain rely exclusively on classical machine learning. This study investigates quantum support vector regression (QSVR) for imputing missing values in ship performance data. Classical support vector regression and QSVR models based on different quantum feature maps are compared for estimating marine fuel consumption under varying levels of data availability. The case study uses real-world data from a Panamax bulk carrier, covering 37 variables across six categories. Three experiments are conducted: exploratory analysis with three input features, scalability analysis with increasing dimensionality (3 to 18 features), and comparative evaluation under a selected representative configuration. Across all scenarios, both classical and quantum approaches captured the relationship between the inputs and the main-engine fuel-flow rate, maintaining strong imputation performance even under severe data scarcity. ZZFeatureMap_1 achieved the highest average R2 (0.991 in the performance comparison conducted with 60% of the dataset, 90% missing data, and 14 input features, for instance) and the lowest aggregate imputation errors, while the radial basis function kernel was the strongest classical baseline, delivering highly competitive results.

AI.tldr: This study investigates quantum support vector regression (QSVR) for imputing missing values in ship performance data, comparing it against classical SVR across varying data-availability scenarios.
AI.motivation: The Internet of Ships generates large volumes of data, but missing values persist, and existing imputation techniques in this domain rely exclusively on classical machine learning.
AI.method: Classical SVR and QSVR models built on different quantum feature maps are compared for estimating marine fuel consumption. A case study uses real-world data from a Panamax bulk carrier covering 37 variables in six categories, via three experiments: exploratory analysis (3 input features), scalability analysis (3 to 18 features), and comparative evaluation under a representative configuration.
AI.result: Both classical and quantum approaches captured the input–fuel-flow relationship and maintained strong imputation performance even under severe data scarcity. ZZFeatureMap_1 achieved the highest average R² (e.g., 0.991 with 60% of the dataset, 90% missing data, and 14 features) and lowest aggregate errors; the RBF kernel was the strongest classical baseline.
AI.conclusion: QSVR with an appropriate quantum feature map offers a viable, competitive approach to imputing missing ship performance data, outperforming the best classical baseline, though classical RBF-based SVR remains highly competitive.

title: Resonance-induced quantum non-Gaussian states below criticality
summary: The Quantum Rabi Model (QRM), consisting of a single qubit coupled to a harmonic oscillator, provides a paradigmatic platform for exploring critical phenomena investigated for their applications in quantum technologies. In the superradiant phase of the QRM with coupling strength above the critical point, the bosonic ground state exhibits temporally stable quantum non-Gaussian features. However, the quantum non-Gaussian features of such superradiant ground states can be fragile against loss during preparation. Here, we show that persistent quantum non-Gaussian features can instead be realized below the critical point through weak periodic qubit modulation. We analyze an adiabatic ramp protocol in which the modulation amplitude is gradually increased, allowing the system to approximately follow the instantaneous Floquet state. When the modulation period is tuned close to Poincaré-Birkhoff resonances, the resulting state exhibits pronounced quantum non-Gaussian features in the directly measurable Wigner function with a complex phase-space structure that is considerably more robust against loss than that of the superradiant ground state. The protocol of adiabatic ramps provides an attractive route for generating long-lived quantum non-Gaussian effects below the critical point.

AI.tldr: Weak periodic qubit modulation below the critical point of the Quantum Rabi Model generates persistent, loss-robust quantum non-Gaussian features via an adiabatic ramp protocol near Poincaré-Birkhoff resonances.
AI.motivation: Superradiant ground states of the QRM above the critical coupling exhibit temporally stable quantum non-Gaussian features useful for quantum technologies, but these features are fragile against loss during state preparation, motivating a more robust alternative.
AI.method: The authors propose an adiabatic ramp protocol in which the amplitude of a weak periodic qubit modulation is gradually increased, so the system approximately tracks the instantaneous Floquet state. The modulation period is tuned close to Poincaré-Birkhoff resonances.
AI.result: Below the critical point, the resulting states display pronounced quantum non-Gaussian features in the directly measurable Wigner function, with a complex phase-space structure that is considerably more robust against loss than that of the superradiant ground state.
AI.conclusion: Adiabatic ramps with weak periodic modulation offer an attractive route for generating long-lived quantum non-Gaussian effects below the critical point of the QRM, avoiding the fragility of superradiant ground states.

title: Complex quasiprobabilities as measurable temporal interference
summary: Quantum dynamics can encode interference information that conventional correlation functions leave unresolved. Here we show that the imaginary component of the extended Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability reveals dynamical distinctions absent from out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) formed from two repeated Hermitian observables at infinite temperature. We interpret its real and imaginary components as complementary quadratures of interference between many-body echo amplitudes. We prove that the imaginary component vanishes for every unitary evolution if either projective measurement has two outcomes, whereas nonreal values arise for generic unitary dynamics when it has at least three (e.g., spin-1 systems). We develop an algorithm to reconstruct the full quasiprobability from covariances of local probe signals over repeated preparations of randomised initial states, using forward evolution and probe readout only. In a spin-1 chain, a nonzero imaginary signal distinguishes a real Hamiltonian $H$ from $-H$ despite identical corresponding OTOCs, and identifies opposite sides of a pair-conversion resonance at short times while dipolar and quadrupolar OTOCs remain nearly unchanged. These results show how temporal interference resolves dynamical ambiguities and provides additional constraints for Hamiltonian inference.

AI.tldr: The imaginary part of the extended Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability captures quantum interference that OTOCs miss, distinguishing H from -H and locating resonances in a spin-1 chain.
AI.motivation: Conventional correlation functions, including OTOCs built from two repeated Hermitian observables at infinite temperature, fail to resolve certain dynamical/interference information encoded in quantum dynamics. The authors seek a finer diagnostic that resolves these ambiguities.
AI.method: They use the imaginary component of the extended Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability, interpreting real and imaginary parts as complementary quadratures of interference between many-body echo amplitudes. They prove vanishing of the imaginary part when either projective measurement has two outcomes, nonreal values for generic dynamics with at least three outcomes. They give a reconstruction algorithm using covariances of local probe signals over randomised initial states, with forward evolution and probe readout only.
AI.result: In a spin-1 chain, a nonzero imaginary signal distinguishes H from -H despite identical OTOCs, and identifies opposite sides of a pair-conversion resonance at short times, while dipolar and quadrupolar OTOCs remain nearly unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Temporal interference resolves dynamical ambiguities beyond OTOCs and provides additional constraints for Hamiltonian inference.

title: Quantum Random Number Generators: principles, practical challenges and mainstream implementations
summary: Quantum random number generators have become a cornerstone technology for modern digital cryptography, including key generation, quantum key distribution, and post-quantum cryptographic systems. While existing reviews typically concentrate on specific entropy sources or implementation platforms, a comprehensive perspective encompassing the complete QRNG pipeline remains largely absent. This work addresses this gap by providing a unified review of the theoretical foundations, practical methodologies, and technological developments that underpin modern QRNGs. We examine randomness from both classical and quantum perspectives and survey the principal discrete-variable and continuous-variable entropy sources, together with entropy estimation, randomness certification, extraction techniques, randomness enhancement protocols, and statistical validation methods. Beyond the fundamental components, we review representative implementations reported in the literature, comparing performance metrics, architectural trade-offs, integration strategies, and attainable generation rates across different technological platforms. Practical deployment challenges, including scalability, trust assumptions, hardware integration, and cryptographic adoption, are also discussed. By complementing the discussion with a broad survey of state-of-the-art implementations and applications, this review provides researchers with a comprehensive reference on the current landscape, open challenges, and future directions of quantum random number generation.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive, pipeline-wide review of quantum random number generators (QRNGs) covering theory, entropy sources, estimation and certification, extraction and enhancement, statistical validation, implementations, and deployment challenges.
AI.motivation: QRNGs are foundational to modern cryptography (key generation, QKD, post-quantum systems), yet existing reviews focus narrowly on specific entropy sources or implementation platforms; a unified perspective spanning the full QRNG pipeline is missing.
AI.method: Survey and synthesis of the field: randomness viewed from classical and quantum perspectives; coverage of discrete- and continuous-variable entropy sources; entropy estimation, randomness certification, extraction techniques, randomness enhancement protocols, and statistical validation; comparative analysis of representative implementations by performance metrics, architectural trade-offs, integration strategies, and generation rates.
AI.result: A consolidated reference mapping the current QRNG landscape: a unified treatment of pipeline components plus a broad survey of state-of-the-art implementations and applications, with cross-platform comparison of rates, architectures, and integration approaches.
AI.conclusion: The review closes the gap of a holistic QRNG reference and outlines practical deployment challenges—scalability, trust assumptions, hardware integration, cryptographic adoption—alongside open challenges and future research directions.

title: Proven optimality for LABS with quantum-classical branch and bound
summary: Low autocorrelation binary sequences (LABS) are the phase codes of pulse compression radar and the synchronization words of digital communication, and finding the sequence of a given length whose aperiodic autocorrelations have the smallest sum of squares is a hard binary optimization problem. The quantum optimization methods tested on LABS so far return good sequences, but they cannot show that a sequence is optimal or bound how far from optimal it may be. We show that a quantum optimization algorithm can deliver proven optimality. In our quantum-classical branch and bound, fixed-angle QAOA samples the Hamiltonians of the nodes of the search tree, its samples supply candidate sequences and the branching choice, and classical bounds prune the tree, so that the algorithm returns either a proof of optimality or, if it is stopped early, the best sequence found with a certified lower bound and gap. It works on the native quartic Hamiltonian without penalty terms, and its correctness does not depend on the sampler. With QAOA at depth p= 12 and at p= 1 and 1,000 shots per node, it proved the optima of all lengths from 2 to 30, where from length 27 on the root node is split without being sampled. Every run records both bounds against time, and its primal-dual integral measures its convergence. We claim no speedup.

AI.tldr: A quantum-classical branch-and-bound algorithm using fixed-angle QAOA sampling on the native quartic LABS Hamiltonian provides proven optimality (or certified bounds) for low autocorrelation binary sequences, solving all lengths 2-30 exactly with no claimed speedup.
AI.motivation: Prior quantum optimization methods on LABS return good sequences but cannot prove a sequence is optimal or bound how far from optimal it is. The goal is a quantum optimization algorithm that can deliver proven optimality or, at minimum, a certified lower bound and optimality gap.
AI.method: A quantum-classical branch-and-bound framework. Fixed-angle QAOA samples the Hamiltonians of the nodes of the search tree; its samples supply candidate sequences and the branching choice, while classical bounds prune the tree. The algorithm operates directly on the native quartic Hamiltonian without penalty terms, and its correctness is independent of the sampler. Used QAOA at depth p=12 and p=1 with 1,000 shots per node; from length 27 on, the root node is split without being sampled.
AI.result: The algorithm proved the optima of all lengths from 2 to 30. Each run records both bounds against time, and its primal-dual integral measures convergence. When stopped early, it returns the best sequence found with a certified lower bound and gap.
AI.conclusion: A quantum optimization algorithm can deliver proven optimality for LABS, returning either an optimality proof or a certified bound with gap, without relying on penalty terms or on sampler-specific correctness. The authors explicitly claim no speedup.

title: Tomographic reconstruction of non-Markovian Gaussian noise in continuous-variable photonic systems
summary: Memory effects in continuous-variable (CV) photonic systems can make standard Markovian Gaussian noise models inaccurate, even when the average noise strength is correctly calibrated. We propose a theoretical and simulation-based tomography framework for reconstructing such memory effects directly from time-resolved homodyne data. The method estimates an effective time-local Gaussian generator, represented by drift and diffusion matrices, using a regularized maximumlikelihood procedure constrained by complete positivity (CP) of the finite-time Gaussian channel. This description covers any Gaussian-preserving noise dynamics for which a well-defined time-local generator exists, rather than being restricted to particular noise mechanisms. Non-Markovianity is then diagnosed at the generator level through temporary violations of local CP-divisibility, rather than from time dependence alone. This distinction is important because ordinary nonstationary noise can remain CP-divisible, whereas genuine memory can produce a non-CP-divisible reduced generator while the accumulated channel remains physical. Numerical benchmarks covering memorydependent loss, nonstationary thermal excitation, and pseudomode-mediated memory show that the reconstruction distinguishes CP-divisible time-dependent noise from genuine non-CP-divisible dynamics and captures the corresponding signatures in the Gaussian covariance evolution. The framework therefore provides a practical route for diagnosing non-Markovian Gaussian noise in CV photonic quantum systems.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a regularized maximum-likelihood tomography framework that reconstructs an effective time-local Gaussian generator (drift and diffusion matrices) from time-resolved homodyne data, constraining it by complete positivity of the finite-time Gaussian channel, and diagnoses non-Markovianity via violations of local CP-divisibility rather than mere time dependence.
AI.motivation: Standard Markovian Gaussian noise models become inaccurate in continuous-variable photonic systems exhibiting memory effects, even when average noise strength is correctly calibrated. There is a need to reconstruct and diagnose such memory effects directly from measurable data, and to distinguish genuine memory from ordinary nonstationary (but CP-divisible) noise.
AI.method: A theoretical and simulation-based tomography framework reconstructing memory effects from time-resolved homodyne data. It estimates an effective time-local Gaussian generator characterized by drift and diffusion matrices, using a regularized maximum-likelihood procedure constrained by complete positivity of the finite-time Gaussian channel. The approach is general for any Gaussian-preserving noise dynamics admitting a well-defined time-local generator. Non-Markovianity is diagnosed at the generator level through temporary violations of local CP-divisibility.
AI.result: Numerical benchmarks on memory-dependent loss, nonstationary thermal excitation, and pseudomode-mediated memory show that the reconstruction distinguishes CP-divisible time-dependent noise from genuine non-CP-divisible dynamics and captures the corresponding signatures in the Gaussian covariance evolution.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a practical route for diagnosing non-Markovian Gaussian noise in CV photonic quantum systems, correctly separating genuine memory effects (non-CP-divisible reduced generators with physical accumulated channels) from ordinary nonstationary noise.

title: Catalytic imaginarity transformations
summary: State conversion is a central problem in quantum resource theories. In this work, we investigate catalytic state transformations within the resource theory of imaginarity. Catalytic imaginarity transformations enable otherwise impossible state transformations using only real operations, assisted by an auxiliary system with imaginarity that is not consumed. For deterministic catalytic conversion, we show that a maximally imaginary pure state is the unique catalyst. This result contrasts with the resource theories of entanglement and coherence, where maximally entangled and maximally coherent catalysts cannot enable such deterministic conversions under their respective free operations. For stochastic-approximate catalytic conversion, if we do not require catalyst recovery upon failure, any pure state with imaginarity can serve as a catalyst, and we derive the optimal success probability. If the catalyst is required to be recovered exactly regardless of whether the catalytic state transformation succeeds or fails, the optimal success probability coincides with that without a catalyst, and thus no advantage arises from catalysis. If exact catalyst recovery upon failure is relaxed, we find a tradeoff relation between the success probability of a single conversion and the catalyst's residual imaginarity after transformation. When the initial state is re-prepared and the catalyst's residual imaginarity can be reused after failure, the success probability can be further improved over $N$ ($N \geq 2$) rounds of catalytic conversion, and we obtain the corresponding maximum overall success probability.

AI.tldr: This paper studies catalytic state transformations in the resource theory of imaginarity, showing that a maximally imaginary pure state is the unique deterministic catalyst, and characterizing optimal success probabilities for stochastic-approximate catalytic conversions under various catalyst-recovery regimes.
AI.motivation: State conversion is central to quantum resource theories, and catalysis—using an auxiliary system that is not consumed—can enable otherwise impossible transformations. While catalysis has been studied for entanglement and coherence, its role in the resource theory of imaginarity remains unexplored, motivating a systematic investigation of catalytic imaginarity transformations under real operations.
AI.method: The authors analyze deterministic and stochastic-approximate catalytic transformations of quantum states under real operations (free operations of the imaginarity resource theory). They examine several cases distinguished by catalyst-recovery requirements: exact recovery, no recovery upon failure, relaxed recovery with a tradeoff, and multi-round (N ≥ 2) reuse of residual catalyst imaginarity with re-prepared initial states, deriving optimal success probabilities in each setting.
AI.result: For deterministic catalytic conversion, a maximally imaginary pure state is the unique catalyst—contrasting with entanglement and coherence theories where maximally entangled/coherent catalysts cannot enable such conversions. For stochastic-approximate conversion without catalyst recovery upon failure, any pure imaginary state can act as a catalyst, and the optimal success probability is derived. With exact catalyst recovery regardless of success or failure, the optimal success probability equals the catalyst-free case, yielding no catalytic advantage. Relaxing exact recovery upon failure yields a tradeoff between single-conversion success probability and the catalyst's residual imaginarity. When the initial state is re-prepared and residual imaginarity reused over N rounds, the success probability improves, and the maximum overall success probability is obtained.
AI.conclusion: Catalysis in the imaginarity resource theory exhibits distinctive features relative to entanglement and coherence, with a maximally imaginary pure state serving as the unique deterministic catalyst. The results delineate regimes where catalysis provides advantage (no exact recovery upon failure) versus none (exact recovery), and quantify tradeoffs and multi-round success-probability gains, clarifying the role of catalysts in imaginarity-based state conversion.

title: Finite-key security of BB84 with passive receivers via reduction to active measurements
summary: In BB84 with passive receiver basis choice (passive BB84) and threshold detectors, the distribution of detection bases can depend on the incoming photon number. Its relation to BB84 with active receiver basis choice (active BB84), in which the basis is chosen using independent randomness, is therefore nontrivial. We establish a reduction theorem that expresses the secret-key-length formula for passive BB84 in terms of an active BB84 formula. The theorem allows a passive key-length formula to be obtained by simple substitutions into an existing active formula, without constructing a passive-specific security proof from scratch. It applies to key-length formulas derived using the Shor--Preskill, Koashi, and Renner approaches, because the reduction uses only properties shared by these approaches. Our result illustrates a modular approach that separates receiver analysis from the security proof and allows the proof of a common reference protocol to be reused for different implementations.

AI.tldr: The paper proves a reduction theorem that converts the secret-key-length formula for passive BB84 (passive basis choice, threshold detectors) into that of active BB84, enabling passive security-key formulas to be derived by simple substitution into existing active formulas.
AI.motivation: In passive BB84 with threshold detectors, the distribution of detection bases depends on the incoming photon number, so its relation to active BB84 (independent randomness for basis choice) is nontrivial. Constructing a passive-specific security proof from scratch is burdensome, motivating a way to reuse existing active proofs.
AI.method: Establish a reduction theorem expressing the passive BB84 secret-key-length formula in terms of an active BB84 formula. The reduction relies only on properties shared by the Shor–Preskill, Koashi, and Renner security-proof approaches, so it applies to key-length formulas derived from any of them. This modularizes the analysis, separating receiver analysis from the security proof.
AI.result: Passive key-length formulas can be obtained by simple substitutions into an existing active formula, without building a passive-specific security proof. The theorem applies to formulas derived via the Shor–Preskill, Koashi, and Renner approaches.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a modular approach that separates receiver analysis from the security proof, allowing the proof of a common reference protocol to be reused across different implementations.

title: Double-Bracket Quantum Algorithms for Preparing Multiple Excited States
summary: Many problems in quantum chemistry, many-body physics, and optimization require excited states of a Hamiltonian. Double-bracket quantum algorithms compile circuits recursively from evolutions under the Hamiltonian and a second operator, without a parameterized ansatz. They have been proposed for several tasks, such as diagonalization and the preparation of ground and thermal states. In this work, we extend this framework to excited states. Combining the ensemble approach with double-bracket flows, we introduce the Double-Bracket quantum algorithm for Multiple EXcited states (DB-MEX), which evolves $p+1$ orthonormal states toward low-lying eigenstates of the Hamiltonian with a single recursively compiled quantum circuit, so they remain orthonormal by construction. The circuit approximates a double-bracket flow of a weighted sum of projectors onto the evolving states, whose number and weights are design parameters. The number of states sets the highest targeted excited state, and the weights determine whether the algorithm prepares the $p+1$ lowest eigenstates, only the $p$-th excited state, or only the span of the $p+1$ lowest eigenstates. In the latter case, a post-processing step recovers the individual eigenstates from their span. We show that the double-bracket flow and, for small step sizes, its discretization converge to the target for almost all initial states, with explicit local rates given by products of weight and energy gaps.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce DB-MEX, a double-bracket quantum algorithm that evolves p+1 orthonormal states in a single recursively compiled circuit toward low-lying eigenstates of a Hamiltonian, with convergence guarantees for almost all initial states.
AI.motivation: Many problems in quantum chemistry, many-body physics, and optimization require excited states of a Hamiltonian. Existing double-bracket quantum algorithms compile circuits recursively without a parameterized ansatz and have been proposed for diagonalization and ground/thermal state preparation, but had not been extended to excited states.
AI.method: The ensemble approach is combined with double-bracket flows to construct DB-MEX, which evolves p+1 orthonormal states with a single recursively compiled circuit, preserving orthonormality by construction. The circuit approximates a double-bracket flow of a weighted sum of projectors onto the evolving states, where the number of states and their weights are design parameters: the number of states sets the highest targeted excited state, and the weights select whether to prepare the p+1 lowest eigenstates, only the p-th excited state, or only the span of the p+1 lowest eigenstates (with a post-processing step recovering individual eigenstates from the span).
AI.result: The double-bracket flow, and its discretization for small step sizes, is shown to converge to the target for almost all initial states, with explicit local convergence rates given by products of weights and energy gaps.
AI.conclusion: DB-MEX extends double-bracket quantum algorithms to excited-state preparation, offering a flexible, ansatz-free framework whose target states are controlled by design parameters and whose convergence is theoretically guaranteed with explicit rates.

title: Time-Travel Paradox in a Bohmian Extension of Deutsch's Approach: Mandatory Tunneling as the "Banana Peel Mechanism"
summary: We consider a self-prevention paradox in which a particle travels through a wormhole into its own past, encounters its younger version, and blocks its movement. In a specially constructed one-dimensional model, this collision rules out a classically self-consistent history. Deutsch's quantum approach can resolve such contradictions by imposing a self-consistency condition on the density matrix. The physical interpretation of this approach, however, remains debated. In particular, Dunlap argues that Deutsch's model presupposes the existence of interacting parallel worlds. Here we extend Deutsch's approach within de Broglie-Bohm theory by supplementing the self-consistency condition on the quantum state with a self-consistency requirement for the particle's ontic configuration. This allows us to consider the self-consistent evolution of an individual particle. In a two-channel, narrow-band Gaussian approximation, we find a self-consistent solution in which quantum tunneling is mandatory, despite its arbitrarily small probability in an ordinary scattering process. This realizes the "banana peel mechanism": to avoid a contradiction during a journey into the past, an event that would ordinarily be extremely unlikely occurs nonetheless.

AI.tldr: The authors extend Deutsch's self-consistency approach to a self-prevention (grandfather-type) paradox within de Broglie-Bohm theory by adding a self-consistency condition on the particle's ontic configuration, and find that a self-consistent history requires improbable quantum tunneling—realizing the "banana peel mechanism."
AI.motivation: The Deutsch model resolves self-prevention paradoxes by imposing a self-consistency condition on the density matrix, but its physical interpretation is contested—Dunlap argues it presupposes interacting parallel worlds. The authors seek an interpretation that avoids this commitment and permits analysis of an individual particle's self-consistent evolution.
AI.method: A specially constructed one-dimensional model is used in which a particle travels through a wormhole into its past, meets its younger self, and blocks its motion, ruling out a classically self-consistent history. Deutsch's self-consistency condition on the quantum state is supplemented, within de Broglie-Bohm theory, by a self-consistency requirement on the particle's ontic configuration. The analysis is carried out in a two-channel, narrow-band Gaussian approximation.
AI.result: A self-consistent solution is found in which quantum tunneling is mandatory, even though its probability in ordinary scattering is arbitrarily small.
AI.conclusion: The extended de Broglie-Bohm formulation yields a self-consistent single-particle history realizing the "banana peel mechanism": to avoid a contradiction during a journey into the past, an ordinarily extremely unlikely event occurs nonetheless. This offers a physical interpretation of self-consistency without invoking interacting parallel worlds.

title: How can every physicist become a Bohmian
summary: The Bohmian interpretation of quantum mechanics is controversial because it attributes deterministic trajectories to microscopic particles. We propose a reformulation that sidesteps this controversy: rather than applying Bohmian mechanics at the microscopic level, we recast it as an effective deterministic description of the macroscopic pointer of a measuring apparatus, with no claims about the fundamental nature of the microscopic world. In this form, the Bohmian trajectory becomes a practical tool for visualizing the emergence of a definite measurement outcome, broadly acceptable to physicists who would otherwise reject the Bohmian program.

AI.tldr: Bohmian mechanics is reframed not as microscopic fundamental physics but as an effective deterministic description of the macroscopic pointer of a measuring apparatus, making Bohmian trajectories a practical visualization tool for the emergence of definite outcomes.
AI.motivation: The Bohmian interpretation is controversial because it assigns deterministic trajectories to microscopic particles, a claim many physicists reject. The authors seek a formulation that avoids this controversy while retaining the interpretive and practical benefits of Bohmian trajectories.
AI.method: Rather than applying Bohmian mechanics at the microscopic level, the authors recast it as an effective deterministic description operating at the level of the macroscopic pointer of a measuring apparatus, making no claims about the fundamental nature of the microscopic world.
AI.result: In this reformulation, the Bohmian trajectory becomes a practical tool for visualizing the emergence of a definite measurement outcome.
AI.conclusion: By restricting Bohmian mechanics to an effective macroscopic description, the framework becomes broadly acceptable to physicists who would otherwise reject the Bohmian program.

title: Depth-Dependent Collapse and Warm-Start Limits of a Symmetry-Preserving VQE for the J$_1$--J$_2$ Heisenberg Ring
summary: Increasing circuit depth is expected to improve a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE). We show that this expectation can fail, and that curing the failure does not guarantee the exact ground state. We study a symmetry-preserving ansatz of SingleExcitationMinus gates, started from the Néel state, on the frustrated spin-$1/2$ $J_1$--$J_2$ Heisenberg ring with $N=10$ and $12$ sites. With random initialization the fidelity, energy error, half-chain entropy and total spin change abruptly at intermediate depth ($L\approx 9$ for $N=10$, $L=10$--$12$ for $N=12$), giving improvement, degradation and recovery, a double-descent-like shape. The circuit family is nested and the gradient stays finite, so this is an optimization failure, not a loss of expressibility or a barren plateau. A chained warm start, which extends an optimized shallow circuit with identity layers, removes the collapse and improves energy error and fidelity almost monotonically for most frustration values. However, near $J_2/J_1=0.60$ ($N=10$) and over $J_2/J_1=0.60$--$1.00$ ($N=12$) the warm start stalls at a fidelity of $\approx 0.50$--$0.58$, although the energy error is small and the total spin stays in the $S=0$ sector. Removing the non-monotonic depth dependence is therefore not the same as reaching the ground state, and low energy and a singlet-like state are not sufficient: the fidelity, entropy and total spin must be satisfied together. The conclusions are limited to the system sizes and frustration values studied.

AI.tldr: Deeper VQE circuits can hurt, not help: a symmetry-preserving ansatz shows a double-descent-like collapse at intermediate depth, and while a chained warm start removes it, the optimization can still stall well short of the exact ground state.
AI.motivation: The common assumption is that increasing circuit depth monotonically improves VQE performance. The authors test whether this expectation holds for a frustrated quantum spin system and whether fixing depth-related non-monotonicity is sufficient to reach the true ground state.
AI.method: Symmetry-preserving ansatz of SingleExcitationMinus gates initialized from the Néel state, applied to the spin-1/2 J1–J2 Heisenberg ring with N=10 and 12 sites. Performance tracked via fidelity, energy error, half-chain entropy and total spin, with random initialization versus a chained warm start that extends optimized shallow circuits with identity layers.
AI.result: With random initialization, metrics change abruptly at intermediate depth (L≈9 for N=10; L=10–12 for N=12), showing improvement, degradation and recovery (double-descent-like). The family is nested and gradients stay finite, so this is an optimization failure, not loss of expressibility or a barren plateau. The chained warm start removes the collapse and yields near-monotonic improvement for most frustration values, but stalls at fidelity ≈0.50–0.58 near J2/J1=0.60 (N=10) and over 0.60–1.00 (N=12), despite small energy error and total spin remaining in the S=0 sector.
AI.conclusion: Removing non-monotonic depth dependence does not guarantee reaching the exact ground state. Low energy and a singlet-like state are insufficient; fidelity, entropy and total spin must be satisfied together. Conclusions are limited to the system sizes and frustration values studied.

title: Molecular energies from sparse quantum prolate diagonalization on a trapped-ion quantum processor
summary: We introduce sparse quantum prolate diagonalization (sparse QPD), which combines the original formulation of QPD [Phys. Rev. Res., 8(3), 033177, (2026)] with compressed sensing to exploit Hamiltonian spectrum sparsity for molecular systems. We show that sparse sampling reduces the sample complexity of QPD from $\mathcal{O}(N_s)$ to $\mathcal{O}(\log N_s)$, where $N_s$ is the number of sampled points of the autocorrelation function (i.e.\ distinct circuits), without increasing circuit depth at chemical accuracy. With a two-orbital active-space-embedded Hamiltonian for an interacting arginine--tryptophan residue pair in water as an example, we show that on the Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum computer, sparse QPD resolves the Hamiltonian energies to chemical accuracy with circuits of up to 448 two-qubit gates. For a suitably large quantum processor, we demonstrate numerically in the weakly correlated regime that the method extends to larger systems.

AI.tldr: Sparse QPD combines quantum prolate diagonalization with compressed sensing to exploit Hamiltonian spectrum sparsity, reducing sample complexity from O(N_s) to O(log N_s) without increasing circuit depth, validated on a trapped-ion device.
AI.motivation: Original QPD requires O(N_s) sampled points of the autocorrelation function, making it costly in circuit count. Molecular Hamiltonians, however, have sparse spectra, which can be exploited to reduce sampling overhead.
AI.method: Sparse quantum prolate diagonalization (sparse QPD): merge the QPD formulation (Phys. Rev. Res., 8(3), 033177, 2026) with compressed sensing to exploit Hamiltonian spectrum sparsity. Benchmarking uses a two-orbital active-space-embedded Hamiltonian for an interacting arginine–tryptophan residue pair in water on the Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum computer, plus numerics for larger systems in the weakly correlated regime.
AI.result: Sample complexity drops from O(N_s) to O(log N_s) over distinct circuits with no increase in circuit depth at chemical accuracy. On Helios, sparse QPD resolves Hamiltonian energies to chemical accuracy with circuits of up to 448 two-qubit gates; numerical simulations show scalability to larger weakly correlated systems.
AI.conclusion: Compressed-sensing-based sparse sampling makes QPD substantially more sample-efficient while preserving depth and accuracy, and is experimentally viable on current trapped-ion hardware with a plausible path to larger molecular systems.

title: Exact classical bounds of bipartite correlation Bell inequalities using improved branch-and-bound
summary: We present an improved branch-and-bound (IBB) algorithm for the exact computation of classical (local) bounds of bipartite correlation Bell inequalities. We strengthen pruning in the standard BB algorithm in two ways: a heuristic search based on see-saw iteration supplies a strong initial lower bound, and greedy row reordering of the Bell matrix reduces the tail bounds used during the exact search. An OpenMP implementation combines these improvements with shared-memory parallelism and dynamic work redistribution. Random-matrix benchmarks show substantial runtime reductions in matrix sizes, while explicit constructions demonstrate exact local-bound computations for square matrices up to $130 \times 130$ and rectangular matrices of sizes up to $81 \times 321$. Applications provide improved lower bounds on finite-order Grothendieck constants for $d=3,4,5,7$ and uniform-input XOR games with quantum-to-classical ratios exceeding $\sqrt2$. The method retains an exponential worst-case search for this NP-hard optimization problem, and its practical performance depends on matrix structure and tail-bound preprocessing depth.

AI.tldr: An improved branch-and-bound (IBB) algorithm is introduced for exact computation of local bounds of bipartite correlation Bell inequalities, using see-saw-based heuristic lower bounds, greedy row reordering for tighter tail bounds, and OpenMP parallelism, enabling exact bounds for matrices up to 130x130 and 81x321.
AI.motivation: Exact local bounds of bipartite correlation Bell inequalities are needed for quantities such as finite-order Grothendieck constants and quantum-to-classical ratios of XOR games, but the underlying optimization is NP-hard and standard branch-and-bound suffers from limited initial bounds and loose pruning tails.
AI.method: Strengthens standard branch-and-bound pruning via (1) a see-saw iterative heuristic producing strong initial lower bounds and (2) greedy row reordering of the Bell matrix to reduce tail bounds during exact search; combined with an OpenMP shared-memory parallel implementation featuring dynamic work redistribution.
AI.result: Random-matrix benchmarks show substantial runtime reductions; explicit constructions yield exact local bounds for square matrices up to 130x130 and rectangular matrices up to 81x321; applications give improved lower bounds on finite-order Grothendieck constants for d=3,4,5,7 and uniform-input XOR games with quantum-to-classical ratios exceeding sqrt(2).
AI.conclusion: The algorithm preserves exponential worst-case complexity for this NP-hard problem, with practical performance dependent on matrix structure and tail-bound preprocessing depth, while extending the reach of exact local-bound computation.

title: Development of a Discrete Variable Representation of a Field-Adaptive Hermite Basis for Accurate Modeling of Magnetically Confined Systems
summary: Accurate magnetic-field evolution of spectra requires a common wavefunction representation that consistently describes multiple states across different field regimes. Discrete Variable Representation (DVR) methods combine accurate basis-based kinetic-energy evaluation with flexible real-space potential representation, enabling arbitrary non-analytic potentials to be treated. Here, we develop a magnetic-field-dependent Hermite function-based (Hermite-B) DVR that adapts naturally to magnetic confinement, efficiently representing compressed wavefunctions across a wide range of field strengths while remaining centered in regions relevant to the scalar confinement potential. This ensures accurate treatment of the field-dependent kinetic energy while addressing two key challenges: maintaining accuracy from the Zeeman to Landau regimes and accommodating diverse confinement potentials. We also introduce a spatial restriction scheme that confines Hermite DVR grid points to a fixed-length domain, enabling compact representations for smooth potentials. The method is benchmarked for two-dimensional quantum dots in perpendicular magnetic fields against analytical models and compared with finite-grid, sine DVR, and field-free Hermite DVR calculations. The performance of field-independent DVR methods for magnetically confined systems is also investigated for the first time. Excellent agreement with exact analytical spectra and wavefunctions is obtained, with Hermite-B requiring the fewest basis functions and smaller Hamiltonian matrices, improving computational efficiency. Applications to arbitrary confinement potentials and tilted magnetic fields demonstrate its versatility beyond analytically solvable systems. The proposed method offers a robust, accurate, and efficient framework for large-scale calculations of realistic semiconductor nanostructures and molecular systems in external magnetic fields.

AI.tldr: Develops a magnetic-field-dependent Hermite-B DVR method that adapts to magnetic confinement, achieving accurate spectra across Zeeman-to-Landau regimes with fewer basis functions and smaller Hamiltonian matrices than field-independent DVR approaches.
AI.motivation: Accurate magnetic-field evolution of spectra requires a common wavefunction representation that consistently describes multiple states across different field regimes. Existing field-independent DVR methods may be inefficient for magnetically confined systems, and the challenge is to maintain accuracy from the Zeeman to Landau regimes while accommodating diverse confinement potentials.
AI.method: Introduces a Hermite function-based (Hermite-B) DVR whose basis adapts naturally to magnetic confinement, remaining centered in regions relevant to the scalar confinement potential. Adds a spatial restriction scheme that confines Hermite DVR grid points to a fixed-length domain for compact representation of smooth potentials. Benchmarked on two-dimensional quantum dots in perpendicular magnetic fields against analytical models and compared with finite-grid, sine DVR, and field-free Hermite DVR; also tested for arbitrary confinement potentials and tilted magnetic fields.
AI.result: Excellent agreement with exact analytical spectra and wavefunctions. Hermite-B requires the fewest basis functions and smaller Hamiltonian matrices, improving computational efficiency. The performance of field-independent DVR methods for magnetically confined systems is investigated for the first time. The method generalizes to arbitrary confinement potentials and tilted magnetic fields.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Hermite-B DVR offers a robust, accurate, and efficient framework for large-scale calculations of realistic semiconductor nanostructures and molecular systems in external magnetic fields, handling non-analytic potentials and remaining valid across field regimes.

title: Entanglement cost and classical capacity of multimode Gaussian states and channels
summary: Gaussian states and operations are central to continuous-variable quantum information and communication. For systems with any finite number of modes, we prove that entanglement of formation, Gaussian entanglement of formation, and entanglement cost coincide for every finite-energy bipartite Gaussian state. Their common value is strongly superadditive and lower-bounds entanglement of formation and entanglement cost for arbitrary non-Gaussian states with the same covariance matrix. We then determine the entanglement cost of every multimode Gaussian channel as well as its classical capacity under a mean energy constraint. These quantities reduce to Gaussian covariance optimizations, and the capacity is attained by pure Gaussian signals with Gaussian displacement modulation, independently across channel uses. The proof combines geodesic convexity of entanglement for pure Gaussian states with a relative-entropy inequality for arbitrary states. We also obtain a closed formula for the entanglement cost of a family of four-mode bound entangled states.

AI.tldr: For any finite number of modes, entanglement of formation, Gaussian entanglement of formation, and entanglement cost coincide for every finite-energy bipartite Gaussian state; the common value is strongly superadditive and lower-bounds these measures for non-Gaussian states with the same covariance matrix. The authors also determine the entanglement cost and mean-energy-constrained classical capacity of every multimode Gaussian channel, showing capacity is achieved by pure Gaussian signals with Gaussian displacement modulation across channel uses.
AI.motivation: Gaussian states and operations are fundamental to continuous-variable quantum information and communication, yet the relationships among entanglement measures (entanglement of formation, Gaussian entanglement of formation, entanglement cost) for Gaussian states and the resource costs/capacities of Gaussian channels were not settled for arbitrary finite-mode systems. The paper aims to close these gaps.
AI.method: The proof combines geodesic convexity of entanglement for pure Gaussian states with a relative-entropy inequality valid for arbitrary states. This yields the coincidence of the three entanglement measures for finite-energy bipartite Gaussian states, and reduces the entanglement cost and classical capacity of multimode Gaussian channels to Gaussian covariance optimizations.
AI.result: Entanglement of formation, Gaussian entanglement of formation, and entanglement cost coincide for every finite-energy bipartite Gaussian state; their common value is strongly superadditive and lower-bounds entanglement of formation and cost for arbitrary non-Gaussian states sharing the covariance matrix. The entanglement cost of every multimode Gaussian channel and its classical capacity under a mean energy constraint are determined; capacity is attained by pure Gaussian signals with Gaussian displacement modulation, independently across channel uses. A closed formula is obtained for the entanglement cost of a family of four-mode bound entangled states.
AI.conclusion: The three entanglement measures coincide for finite-energy bipartite Gaussian states, giving a strongly superadditive quantity that bounds non-Gaussian counterparts, and the entanglement cost and energy-constrained classical capacity of arbitrary multimode Gaussian channels reduce to Gaussian covariance optimizations with Gaussian-achievable capacity; a closed formula also follows for certain four-mode bound entangled states.

title: Problem-adjusted $X$-mixer eigenstates for improved QAOA
summary: We show that the use of problem-adjusted excited eigenstates of the $X$-mixer Hamiltonian can be beneficial for the performance of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) when applied to problems with degenerate ground states. We show that this advantage persists in the presence of quantum gate and readout noise, with the problem-adjusted excited initial states achieving better optimal performance than the standard ground state initialization. The realized advantage depends on the number of QAOA layers and whether or not the initial state has a reasonable time evolution path into the ground space of the problem Hamiltonian.
