We also explain how to prepare these problem-adjusted $X$-mixer eigenstates exactly, as well as how to approximate them using a linear combination of ladder operators. Finally, we discuss how the power of these initial states can be applied to any problem Hamiltonian regardless of the degeneracy of its ground state by making use of a Grover-style mixer Hamiltonian.

AI.tldr: Problem-adjusted excited eigenstates of the X-mixer improve QAOA performance on degenerate-ground-state problems, even under gate and readout noise, compared to standard ground-state initialization.
AI.motivation: Standard QAOA initialization uses the ground state of the mixer Hamiltonian, which may be suboptimal for problems with degenerate ground states. The authors seek to leverage excited mixer eigenstates tailored to the problem to enhance optimization performance and robustness to noise.
AI.method: The authors use problem-adjusted excited eigenstates of the X-mixer Hamiltonian as initial states for QAOA. They analyze performance under gate and readout noise, characterize dependence on the number of QAOA layers and the existence of a time-evolution path from the initial state into the ground space, and provide exact preparation schemes plus approximations via linear combinations of ladder operators. They extend the approach to arbitrary problem Hamiltonians using a Grover-style mixer.
AI.result: Problem-adjusted excited initial states achieve better optimal performance than standard ground-state initialization, including in the presence of gate and readout noise. The realized advantage depends on the number of QAOA layers and whether the initial state has a reasonable time-evolution path into the ground space.
AI.conclusion: Excited X-mixer eigenstates provide a practical initialization strategy for QAOA on degenerate problems, are exactly preparable and approximable, and can be generalized to any problem Hamiltonian via a Grover-style mixer.

title: Dynamical Decoupling via Continuous Unitary Design
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures (Main text); 17 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables (Supplementary Material )
summary: Dynamical decoupling is a cornerstone of quantum control for protecting and engineering quantum systems. However, conventional schemes rely on idealized instantaneous pulses, limiting their performance under realistic finite-duration and imperfect controls. To overcome this limitation, we establish a dynamical decoupling framework based on continuous unitary designs, which intrinsically suppresses arbitrary static noise during continuous control. We further derive closed-form phase conditions to suppress Rabi-amplitude errors, unifying universal decoupling, finite-pulse compatibility, and control-error robustness within a single analytical framework. We experimentally validate our approach on a superconducting quantum cloud platform, demonstrating significantly extended coherence times and the highest robustness against Rabi-amplitude errors and detuning among the tested sequences.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a continuous dynamical decoupling framework based on continuous unitary designs that intrinsically suppresses arbitrary static noise under continuous control, and derives closed-form phase conditions to suppress Rabi-amplitude errors, unifying universal decoupling, finite-pulse compatibility, and control-error robustness.
AI.motivation: Conventional dynamical decoupling schemes rely on idealized instantaneous pulses, which limits their performance under realistic finite-duration and imperfect controls.
AI.method: Establish a dynamical decoupling framework built on continuous unitary designs to suppress arbitrary static noise during continuous control, and derive closed-form phase conditions for suppressing Rabi-amplitude errors within a single analytical framework.
AI.result: The approach was experimentally validated on a superconducting quantum cloud platform, showing significantly extended coherence times and the highest robustness against Rabi-amplitude errors and detuning among the tested sequences.
AI.conclusion: Continuous-unitary-design-based dynamical decoupling unifies universal decoupling, finite-pulse compatibility, and control-error robustness, and is experimentally verified to outperform tested sequences in coherence protection.

title: Variable-length MDI QKD under source imperfections and local randomization over horizontal links
summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) provides security guarantees that hold despite device imperfections and finite-size effects. We address these challenges in measurement-device-independent (MDI) QKD, combining its intrinsic untrusted detection with an imperfection model for Alice's and Bob's sources via fidelity bounds. We establish variable-length general security under the Marginal-constrained Entropy Accumulation Theorem (MEAT), estimating the relevant Rényi entropies through conic optimization. We evaluate our model under a horizontal channel link, reporting secret keys for blocks as small as n~3x10^4 rounds under atmosphere-free conditions, and show that compensating for unequal channel attenuation through appropriately chosen transmitted amplitudes improves performance in asymmetric configurations, enabling communication distances beyond 80 km for commercial satellite systems.

AI.tldr: A finite-size, device-imperfection-aware security analysis of MDI-QKD that combines fidelity-bounded source models with the Marginal-constrained Entropy Accumulation Theorem and conic-optimization Rényi entropy estimation, yielding variable-length keys for blocks as small as ~3×10^4 rounds and >80 km links in asymmetric satellite configurations.
AI.motivation: Practical QKD must retain security under realistic device imperfections and finite statistics. MDI-QKD removes detector side channels via untrusted detection but still requires accounting for imperfect state preparation at Alice's and Bob's sources, plus tight finite-size bounds for small block sizes and asymmetric channel losses.
AI.method: Model source imperfections with fidelity bounds relative to ideal states; derive variable-length general composable security using the Marginal-constrained Entropy Accumulation Theorem (MEAT); estimate the relevant Rényi entropies via conic optimization; evaluate under a horizontal atmospheric-free channel link, including asymmetric attenuation with optimized transmitted amplitudes.
AI.result: Reports positive secret key rates for blocks as small as n ≈ 3×10^4 rounds under atmosphere-free horizontal-link conditions; compensating unequal channel attenuation by choosing suitable transmitted amplitudes improves performance in asymmetric setups, extending operation beyond 80 km for commercial satellite systems.
AI.conclusion: The framework yields rigorous finite-size, variable-length MDI-QKD security under explicit source-imperfection models, is practical for small blocks, and amplitude optimization enables asymmetric satellite-based links over 80 km.

title: PRISM: A Logical-Physical Boundary Compiler for Dual-Rail Qubits
summary: Quantum computers can encode each logical qubit across multiple physical degrees of freedom so that errors on the physical qubits can be detected or corrected. A compiler must then translate each logical gate into native instructions, and one gate can have several equivalent realizations that interact through different wires. Routing moves those wires, so a realization chosen before routing can force SWAPs that another would avoid, making code expansion and physical routing a phase-ordering problem. PRISM therefore keeps each gate's realizations open across the logical--physical boundary and commits to one only when routing reaches a layout that can execute it. We formalize which physical circuits implement a gate, which respect the fault model, and which the compiler keeps, and define when a gate can execute under a layout. For dual-rail cavity qubits, logical $\mathrm{CR}_z$ has four loss-admissible realizations, one per rail pairing, and its logical availability graph is exactly the simple quotient of the occupied device graph by the rail pairs. Across 25 workloads with 7 to 25 logical qubits on three device graphs, PRISM reduces routing SWAPs by 20.4--30.8\% and physical depth by 8.8--10.1\% relative to a greedy search that fixes each realization before routing. On the grid and hexagonal lattice, the SWAP reductions hold through 32 logical qubits. By shortening routes, PRISM also reduces photon loss on device models and therefore needs 44.3\% fewer attempts per retained shot at 16 logical qubits, as a geometric mean over workloads and device graphs, and it lowers decoded logical error in a three-round Steane memory under skip-gate leakage.

AI.tldr: PRISM is a compiler that keeps each logical gate's equivalent physical realizations open across the logical-physical boundary and commits to one only when routing reaches an executable layout, mitigating the code-expansion/routing phase-ordering problem for quantum error-correcting codes.
AI.motivation: Logical qubits span multiple physical degrees of freedom, so a logical gate has several equivalent realizations that interact through different wires. Routing moves those wires, so fixing a realization before routing can force SWAPs that another realization would avoid—making code expansion and physical routing a phase-ordering problem.
AI.method: PRISM defers realization selection: it keeps each gate's realizations open and commits only when routing reaches a layout able to execute it. The authors formalize which physical circuits implement a gate, which respect the fault model, and which the compiler retains, and define when a gate can execute under a layout. For dual-rail cavity qubits, logical CR_z has four loss-admissible realizations (one per rail pairing), and its logical availability graph is exactly the simple quotient of the occupied device graph by rail pairs.
AI.result: Across 25 workloads (7–25 logical qubits) on three device graphs, PRISM cuts routing SWAPs by 20.4–30.8% and physical depth by 8.8–10.1% versus a greedy baseline that fixes realizations before routing. SWAP reductions persist through 32 logical qubits on grid and hexagonal lattices. Shorter routes lower photon loss, needing 44.3% fewer attempts per retained shot at 16 logical qubits (geometric mean), and reduce decoded logical error in a three-round Steane memory under skip-gate leakage.
AI.conclusion: Deferring gate-realization commitment to routing time resolves the phase-ordering conflict between code expansion and physical routing, yielding fewer SWAPs, lower depth, reduced photon loss, and lower decoded logical error.

title: Frequency Multiplexing of Purcell-Enhanced Optically Coherent NV Centers
summary: Integrating optically coherent quantum emitters into nanophotonic structures is key to scalable quantum networks. Realizing them with nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond is hindered by the degradation of optical coherence accompanying nanofabrication. Here, we overcome this challenge by integrating multiple NV centers into a monolithic diamond photonic crystal nanocavity while preserving near-lifetime-limited optical coherence. We observe linewidths as narrow as 19 MHz, enabling the frequency multiplexing of spectrally distinct NV centers within a common cavity mode, while maintaining charge-state stability over several minutes under resonant excitation. Tuning the cavity into resonance with the NV zero-phonon line enhances the optical emission, consistent with Purcell enhancement predicted by finite-element simulations. Additionally, individual cavities can be independently brought into resonance with NV zero-phonon lines on the same chip. These results combine bulk-like optical coherence with frequency multiplexing and cavity-enhanced emission, establishing a scalable nanophotonic platform for NV-based quantum network nodes.

AI.tldr: Multiple nitrogen-vacancy centers are integrated into a monolithic diamond photonic crystal nanocavity while maintaining near-lifetime-limited optical coherence (linewidths down to 19 MHz), enabling frequency multiplexing and cavity-enhanced emission for scalable quantum network nodes.
AI.motivation: Integrating optically coherent quantum emitters into nanophotonic structures is essential for scalable quantum networks, but NV centers in diamond suffer from degraded optical coherence caused by nanofabrication, which has blocked this integration.
AI.method: The authors fabricate a monolithic diamond photonic crystal nanocavity and integrate multiple NV centers into it, characterizing optical linewidths, charge-state stability under resonant excitation over several minutes, and tuning the cavity into resonance with the NV zero-phonon line. Finite-element simulations are used to predict Purcell enhancement, which is compared with measured emission. Individual cavities on the same chip are also independently tuned into resonance with NV zero-phonon lines.
AI.result: Near-lifetime-limited optical coherence is preserved, with linewidths as narrow as 19 MHz. This enables frequency multiplexing of spectrally distinct NV centers within a common cavity mode, with charge-state stability maintained over several minutes under resonant excitation. Cavity resonance with the zero-phonon line enhances optical emission, consistent with simulated Purcell enhancement, and individual cavities on the same chip can be independently brought into resonance with NV zero-phonon lines.
AI.conclusion: The work combines bulk-like optical coherence with frequency multiplexing and cavity-enhanced emission, establishing a scalable nanophotonic platform for NV-based quantum network nodes.

title: Performance of Fusion-Based Quantum Computing with Imperfect Photon Indistinguishability
summary: Fusion-based quantum computation (FBQC) is a promising route to fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing, connecting small entangled resource states through linear-optical fusion measurements. While logical encoding can substantially improve resilience to photon loss, whether these benefits extend to other noise remain an open question. In this work, we show that this is not generally the case when accounting for partial photon distinguishability during resource state generation and fusion measurement. We develop hardware-motivated noise models to capture these effects and investigate their impact on fault tolerance in the 6-ring fusion network. We compare unencoded and Shor(2,2)-encoded resource states prepared using all-photonic and emitter-assisted repeat-until-success (RUS) schemes. For the all-photonic construction, encoding reduces the distinguishability threshold from 0.136% to 0.08%. In contrast, the RUS construction tolerates more distinguishability, with comparable unencoded and encoded thresholds (0.256% and 0.271%, respectively). These results expose a fundamental limitation of evaluating logical encodings under idealized resource-state assumptions and demonstrate that resource-state generation can critically determine the fault tolerance of photonic architectures.

AI.tldr: Logical encoding in fusion-based photonic quantum computing does not universally improve resilience to partial photon distinguishability; fault tolerance depends critically on how resource states are generated.
AI.motivation: FBQC is a leading route to fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing, and logical encoding can markedly improve robustness to photon loss. However, it is unclear whether these benefits extend to other noise channels, particularly partial photon distinguishability arising during resource-state generation and fusion measurements, which is not captured by idealized resource-state assumptions.
AI.method: The authors construct hardware-motivated noise models for partial photon distinguishability during resource-state generation and fusion. They analyze the 6-ring fusion network and compare unencoded versus Shor(2,2)-encoded resource states prepared via (i) all-photonic construction and (ii) emitter-assisted repeat-until-success (RUS) schemes, extracting distinguishability thresholds.
AI.result: In the all-photonic construction, encoding degrades the distinguishability threshold from 0.136% (unencoded) to 0.08%. With RUS, both variants are far more tolerant and comparable: 0.256% unencoded versus 0.271% encoded.
AI.conclusion: Encoding does not generically enhance resilience to photon distinguishability. Evaluating logical encodings under idealized resource-state assumptions is fundamentally misleading, and the resource-state generation method can critically determine the fault tolerance of photonic architectures.

title: Causality, determinism and predictability: Probing nature through classical and quantum eyes
summary: In this article, mainly focussed on students and interested readers, we discuss how the understanding of causality, determinism and predictability is transformed as we move from the classical world view to the quantum description. We first explain how determinism and predictability operate in classical dynamics and outline the notion of causality. A paradigm shift occurs within the framework of quantum mechanics where we have to revisit, and even give up, the notions of determinism, predictability and maybe even strict causality. An engrossing and fascinating debate ensues, after the formulation of quantum mechanics among the giants of physics like Einstein, Bohr, Heisenberg, Pauli, and many others. While some questions have been settled in the last century in favour of quantum world view, there are still many open questions, most important of which is the role of gravity in shaping events within the quantum framework.

AI.tldr: An expository article tracing how the notions of causality, determinism, and predictability transform from classical dynamics to quantum mechanics, and highlighting the historical Einstein–Bohr debate and the unresolved role of gravity.
AI.motivation: To help students and interested readers understand the conceptual shift in causality, determinism, and predictability when moving from the classical world view to the quantum description.
AI.method: Conceptual and pedagogical exposition: first explaining how determinism and predictability operate in classical dynamics and outlining causality, then revisiting and potentially abandoning these notions within quantum mechanics, framed through the historical debate among Einstein, Bohr, Heisenberg, Pauli, and others.
AI.result: The article outlines that classical dynamics supports determinism and predictability, whereas quantum mechanics forces a revision or abandonment of these notions and possibly of strict causality; some questions were settled in favor of the quantum world view over the past century, but many remain open.
AI.conclusion: Understanding of causality, determinism, and predictability is fundamentally transformed by quantum mechanics; while several debates have been resolved, the most important open question is the role of gravity in shaping events within the quantum framework.

title: Non-equilibrium topological order from Floquet anyon proliferation in the toric code
summary: We analyze the dynamics of Kitaev's toric code in Floquet quenches where the drive coherently creates and propagates fermionic $f$ anyons. We show that the long-time state departs from pure-state topological order but retains long-range entanglement, thereby realizing a Floquet analog of intrinsic mixed-state topological order. As a key result enabling this analysis, we derive decompositions of the entanglement entropy and logarithmic negativity that separate the ground-state value, including topological terms, from a contribution given by the driven quasiparticles. For a drive inducing non-interacting $f$ dynamics, these decompositions allow us to leverage numerical methods for free fermions and to link the emergence of the proposed long-time ordered state to the equilibration of $f$ anyons to a periodic Gibbs ensemble. For drives inducing Floquet eigenstate thermalization of $f$, our results suggest a scenario where Floquet heating of the $f$ sector stabilizes a genuine non-equilibrium topological phase, in contrast with the usual view of heating as an obstacle to order in periodically driven systems.

AI.tldr: Floquet drives of the toric code that coherently create and propagate \(f\) anyons drive the system away from pure-state topological order but into a Floquet analog of intrinsic mixed-state topological order, characterized by long-range entanglement and analyzed via new decompositions of entanglement entropy and logarithmic negativity.
AI.motivation: Periodically driven systems are usually expected to heat toward trivial states, so it is unclear whether topological order can survive Floquet dynamics when the drive excites anyonic quasiparticles. The authors ask what long-time state results when the drive coherently creates and moves fermionic \(f\) anyons in Kitaev's toric code.
AI.method: The authors study Floquet quenches of the toric code with drives generating \(f\)-anyon creation and propagation. They derive decompositions of the entanglement entropy and logarithmic negativity that isolate the ground-state (including topological) contribution from a term set by the driven quasiparticles. For non-interacting \(f\) dynamics these decompositions permit free-fermion numerical methods; for drives producing Floquet eigenstate thermalization of \(f\), the results are interpreted through a heating/thermalization picture.
AI.result: The long-time state departs from pure-state topological order yet retains long-range entanglement, realizing a Floquet analog of intrinsic mixed-state topological order. For non-interacting \(f\) drives, the long-time ordered state is linked to equilibration of \(f\) anyons to a periodic Gibbs ensemble. For thermalizing drives, Floquet heating of the \(f\) sector appears to stabilize a genuine non-equilibrium topological phase.
AI.conclusion: Floquet heating of an anyon sector need not destroy topological order: instead it can stabilize a non-equilibrium mixed-state topological phase with long-range entanglement, in contrast to the standard view of heating as an obstacle to order in periodically driven systems.

title: Teleportation of Logical Qubits using Lattice Surgery with Superconducting Circuits
summary: Demonstrating a quantum advantage when solving large-scale computational problems on a quantum computer requires the correction of errors that occur due to limitations in control accuracy and coherence. Using the concept of quantum error correction, fault-tolerant logical qubits can be realized and manipulated with logical single- and two-qubit gates. In this paper, we experimentally analyze fault-tolerant lattice-surgery, which is a key primitive that enables operations between logical qubits realized in the surface-code. Using this primitive, we demonstrate the teleportation of logical states between two distance-three logical qubits realized in a superconducting circuit composed of 41 physical qubits. Throughout this process, we study the step-by-step transfer of logical information from a source to a target logical qubit by characterizing the time evolution of logical observables. We find that repeated execution of stabilizer measurements, after merging two surface-code patches, restores fault tolerance and yields increased fidelity of the teleported state. When optimizing the protocol in terms of gate count and sequence duration, we observe further improvements in fidelity. Our work offers new insights into the optimization of fault-tolerant lattice-surgery operations, while also providing a comprehensive description of the physical device and gate sequences used. We expect the efficient implementation of increasingly complex logical circuits to enhance the performance of future fault-tolerant quantum computers.

AI.tldr: Experimental demonstration of fault-tolerant lattice-surgery-based logical state teleportation between two distance-3 surface-code logical qubits on a 41-qubit superconducting processor, with characterization of fidelity gains from repeated stabilizer measurements and protocol optimization.
AI.motivation: Quantum advantage on large-scale problems requires error correction, but fault-tolerant logical operations—especially the key primitive of lattice surgery enabling logical multi-qubit gates in the surface code—have lacked thorough experimental characterization. The authors aim to experimentally analyze fault-tolerant lattice surgery step by step.
AI.method: Using superconducting circuits with 41 physical qubits, two distance-3 surface-code logical qubits are realized. Logical states are teleported between them via lattice surgery, with the time evolution of logical observables tracked to follow the step-by-step transfer of logical information from source to target. Fault tolerance is assessed by repeated stabilizer measurements after merging the two code patches, and the protocol is further optimized in gate count and sequence duration.
AI.result: Repeated execution of stabilizer measurements after merging two surface-code patches restores fault tolerance and increases the fidelity of the teleported logical state. Optimizing the protocol for gate count and sequence duration yields further fidelity improvements. The work also provides a detailed description of the physical device and gate sequences used.
AI.conclusion: The study offers new insights into optimizing fault-tolerant lattice-surgery operations and provides a comprehensive account of the device and sequences, supporting the expectation that efficient implementation of increasingly complex logical circuits will enhance future fault-tolerant quantum computers.

title: Integral Tensor Isomorphism via Cubic Rings and Lattice Methods
summary: We prove that isomorphism of integral $2\times3\times3$ tensors under $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z})\times\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})\times\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$ is decidable in bounded-error quantum polynomial time. For a tensor $T=(A,B)$ with nonzero determinant form $\det(xA-yB)$, we use the parametrization of Wood by balanced modules to reduce the isomorphism problem to principality tests for compatible lattices, and use the algorithms of Bley, Hofmann, and Johnston to solve this in BQP. When the determinant form vanishes identically, we get either an integral $2\times2\times2$ core, or a polynomial kernel vector of degree one or two. The linear-kernel case yields another compatible lattice problem, while the quadratic-kernel case reduces to a fixed system of polynomial congruences and unimodular lifting. A quantifier-elimination argument decides these congruences in deterministic polynomial time given the prime factorization of the modulus, which quantum integer factorization supplies. Finally, we show that zero padding preserves integral $2\times2\times2$ tensor isomorphism, yielding a polynomial-time reduction from real-quadratic principality to the identically singular $2\times3\times3$ problem.

AI.tldr: Isomorphism of integral 2×3×3 tensors under GL₂(ℤ)×GL₃(ℤ)×GL₃(ℤ) is decidable in bounded-error quantum polynomial time.
AI.motivation: Tensor isomorphism over the integers is a fundamental computational problem, but its complexity for small formats is poorly understood; the 2×3×3 case sits beyond known classical tractability and motivates a quantum algorithmic treatment.
AI.method: For tensors T=(A,B) with nonzero determinant form det(xA−yB), the authors use Wood's parametrization by balanced modules to reduce isomorphism to principality tests for compatible lattices, solved in BQP via algorithms of Bley, Hofmann, and Johnston. When the determinant form vanishes identically, they obtain either an integral 2×2×2 core or a polynomial kernel vector of degree one or two; the linear-kernel case gives another compatible lattice problem, and the quadratic-kernel case reduces to a fixed system of polynomial congruences plus unimodular lifting, decided in deterministic polynomial time by quantifier elimination given the modulus factorization supplied by quantum integer factorization. Zero padding preserves integral 2×2×2 tensor isomorphism, yielding a polynomial-time reduction from real-quadratic principality to the identically singular 2×3×3 problem.
AI.result: A BQP algorithm for integral 2×3×3 tensor isomorphism, relying on compatible-lattice principality testing and quantum factorization combined with quantifier elimination for polynomial congruences; a polynomial-time reduction from real-quadratic principality to the identically singular case via zero padding.
AI.conclusion: Integral 2×3×3 tensor isomorphism is decidable in bounded-error quantum polynomial time, establishing a quantum upper bound for this format and linking the singular case to real-quadratic principality testing through zero padding.

title: Quantum amplification with a linear quantum coupler
summary: Josephson parametric amplifiers (JPAs) are essential components for quantum-limited microwave measurement, but their dynamic range is often constrained by Kerr and other pump-induced nonlinear effects. In this work, we systematically study the performance of a parametric amplifier based on the linear inductive coupler (LINC). Starting from the driven-circuit Hamiltonian, we derive the effective three-wave-mixing amplifier model, including leading flux-driven nonlinear corrections relevant to realistic operation. We analyze the resulting gain response, saturation behavior, and intermodulation distortion, comparing them with representative state-of-the-art JPA designs. Our results show that the symmetry-protected structure of the LINC suppresses static Kerr nonlinearity. Moreover, suitable circuit-parameter optimization can further reduce the dressed-squeezing and driven-Kerr effects, leading to considerable improvements in power-handling metrics. These results identify the LINC architecture as a promising platform for high-linearity Josephson parametric amplification.

AI.tldr: Systematic theoretical study of a linear inductive coupler (LINC)-based Josephson parametric amplifier, showing that its symmetry-protected structure suppresses static Kerr nonlinearity and, with circuit-parameter optimization, improves dynamic range metrics compared to state-of-the-art JPAs.
AI.motivation: Josephson parametric amplifiers are key for quantum-limited microwave measurement, but their dynamic range is limited by Kerr and other pump-induced nonlinear effects. There is a need for JPA architectures that maintain high linearity and power handling.
AI.method: Starting from the driven-circuit Hamiltonian, the authors derive an effective three-wave-mixing amplifier model for the LINC-based parametric amplifier, including leading flux-driven nonlinear corrections relevant to realistic operation. They then analyze gain response, saturation behavior, and intermodulation distortion, benchmarking against representative state-of-the-art JPA designs, and examine the effect of circuit-parameter optimization on dressed-squeezing and driven-Kerr effects.
AI.result: The symmetry-protected LINC structure suppresses static Kerr nonlinearity. Suitable circuit-parameter optimization further reduces dressed-squeezing and driven-Kerr effects, yielding considerable improvements in power-handling metrics relative to representative state-of-the-art JPAs.
AI.conclusion: The LINC architecture is identified as a promising platform for high-linearity Josephson parametric amplification, offering improved dynamic range for quantum-limited microwave measurement.

title: Performance analysis of a Rydberg atom THz radiometer concept
summary: THz receiver technology lies between electronics and photonics; as such, its implementation is not as mature. This warrants investigation into alternative THz receivers such as Rydberg atom sensors, which are highly susceptible to electric fields. In particular, the conversion architecture has been demonstrated to coherently transduce thermal radiation. This system offers room-temperature operation and does not necessarily require a local oscillator at the frequency of the input signal. We provide an assessment of the feasibility of such sensors for THz radiometry within the context of Earth observation.

AI.tldr: This work assesses the feasibility of Rydberg-atom sensors as alternative THz receivers for radiometry in Earth observation, leveraging their high electric-field sensitivity and coherent thermal-radiation transduction at room temperature.
AI.motivation: THz receiver technology sits between electronics and photonics and is comparatively immature, motivating the search for alternative receiver architectures. Rydberg atom sensors are attractive candidates because of their extreme electric-field sensitivity, room-temperature operation, and demonstration of coherent transduction of thermal radiation.
AI.method: The authors evaluate the conversion (Rydberg-atom) architecture as a THz receiver, characterizing its coherent transduction of thermal radiation and its operational requirements—room-temperature operation and no necessary local oscillator at the input-signal frequency—then frame this within the requirements of THz radiometry for Earth observation.
AI.result: The abstract reports that the conversion architecture can coherently transduce thermal radiation and supports room-temperature operation without a necessarily required local oscillator at the signal frequency; a feasibility assessment for THz radiometry in Earth observation is provided.
AI.conclusion: Rydberg-atom sensors are a promising, viable candidate for THz radiometry in Earth-observation contexts, pending further validation.

title: Nonlinearity-preserving quantum simulation of flows in the early fault-tolerant regime
summary: Ensemble prediction of nonlinear dynamics propagates a probability density whose linear transport equation retains the nonlinear drift, but grid-dependent circuit costs leave end-to-end feasibility in early fault-tolerant quantum computing unresolved. We couple polynomial reduced-order models fitted by sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics to Walsh-synthesized Koopman-von Neumann (KvN) transport and surface-code resource estimation. At fixed model dimension and drift degree, per-step transport rotation counts scale polylogarithmically with cells per reduced coordinate. Balancing model accuracy against circuit costs makes reduced-model polynomial degree a design variable for early fault-tolerant quantum simulation. For a cylinder wake approaching saturation, preparation, propagation and sampling to 1% relative root-mean-square field error against the radial model are estimated to take 1.62 h on about 560,000 physical qubits. Estimated three-coordinate wake runtimes span hours to weeks below one million qubits. IBM hardware experiments demonstrate nonlinear radial KvN transport for this wake, using reference circuits to mitigate noise.

AI.tldr: The paper couples SINDy-fitted polynomial reduced-order models with Walsh-synthesized Koopman-von Neumann transport and surface-code resource estimation to show that ensemble prediction of nonlinear dynamics is feasible in early fault-tolerant quantum computing.
AI.motivation: Ensemble prediction propagates a probability density via a linear transport equation that retains the nonlinear drift, but grid-dependent circuit costs have left end-to-end feasibility in early fault-tolerant quantum computing unresolved.
AI.method: Polynomial reduced-order models fitted by sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics (SINDy) are coupled to Walsh-synthesized Koopman-von Neumann transport, with surface-code resource estimation. At fixed model dimension and drift degree, per-step transport rotation counts scale polylogarithmically with cells per reduced coordinate; hardware experiments on IBM devices demonstrate nonlinear radial KvN transport for a cylinder wake using reference circuits for noise mitigation.
AI.result: For a cylinder wake approaching saturation, preparation, propagation and sampling to 1% relative root-mean-square field error against the radial model are estimated at 1.62 h on about 560,000 physical qubits; three-coordinate wake runtimes span hours to weeks below one million qubits.
AI.conclusion: Balancing model accuracy against circuit costs makes the reduced-model polynomial degree a design variable for early fault-tolerant quantum simulation of nonlinear dynamics.

title: Local interference algorithms for observables in large random circuits
summary: In quantum dynamics, it is generally believed that interference effects lead to a sign problem for classical Monte Carlo sampling methods, rendering sampling ineffective. In this paper we show that this is generically not the case for the task of simulating the evolution of observables in random instances of circuit dynamics. Specifically, we consider two examples of observables which give large signals despite the randomness of the dynamics: first order out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) in unstructured random circuits without conservation laws and time-ordered charge-charge correlators (TOCs) in particle number-preserving random circuits. We show that these observables can be approximated by classical stochastic processes and that these approximations can be systematically improved with a series expansion that incorporates coherent corrections associated with clusters of gates. We design and implement algorithms that combine Monte Carlo sampling and tensor network methods to approximate the series. We observe numerically that the computational complexity of approximating TOCs and OTOCs scales polynomially in the circuit size and in the target precision. We study the accuracy of these algorithms by directly mapping their ensemble-averaged errors to partition functions of replica statistical models, allowing for perturbative analysis and numerics in $1$d brickwork geometries. Our theoretical analysis explains the empirical observation of polynomial complexity of these algorithms and is consistent with polynomial complexity extending to arbitrarily small precision and to the thermodynamic limit.

AI.tldr: Despite the conventional belief that quantum interference causes a Monte Carlo sign problem, the authors show that simulating certain observables in random circuit dynamics (first-order OTOCs and charge-charge TOCs) admits efficient classical approximation via stochastic processes plus clustered coherent corrections, with polynomial scaling in circuit size and target precision.
AI.motivation: Interference effects are widely assumed to induce a sign problem that defeats classical Monte Carlo sampling of quantum dynamics. The paper challenges this assumption specifically for observables in random circuit dynamics that produce large signals, and seeks to understand when classical stochastic approximations remain accurate and efficiently improvable.
AI.method: Treats two observable classes—first-order OTOCs in unstructured random circuits without conservation laws, and time-ordered charge-charge correlators in particle-number-preserving random circuits. These are approximated by classical stochastic processes, systematically corrected by a series expansion incorporating coherent contributions from clusters of gates. Algorithms combine Monte Carlo sampling with tensor-network methods to evaluate the series. Accuracy is analyzed by mapping ensemble-averaged errors to partition functions of replica statistical models, enabling perturbative analysis and numerics in 1d brickwork geometries.
AI.result: Numerics show the computational complexity of approximating TOCs and OTOCs scales polynomially in circuit size and target precision. The replica-model mapping reproduces this empirical polynomial complexity theoretically and is consistent with polynomial complexity persisting to arbitrarily small precision and to the thermodynamic limit.
AI.conclusion: The sign problem is not generically fatal for simulating these observables in random circuit dynamics; clustered coherent corrections yield controllable, polynomially scaling classical algorithms. The replica partition-function framework explains the observed efficiency and suggests broader regimes of classical simulability.

title: Modeling quantum information scrambling in realistic protein NMR experiments
summary: Out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) are important probes of operator spreading and information scrambling, and have recently been proposed as a means of extracting molecular structural information through nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR). Realizing this potential requires accurate modeling of OTOCs in complex molecular environments within experimentally relevant settings. Here, we develop an end-to-end computational pipeline connecting molecular structures to OTOC dynamics in protein systems. Our framework incorporates molecular motion through molecular dynamics simulations, orientational averaging appropriate for powder samples, and spin-network truncation, using an experimentally realizable double-quantum effective Hamiltonian. We apply this framework to a dataset of over 350 carbon-carbon spin pairs across 10 protein systems, spanning interspin distances of 5-17 A. We find that OTOC arrival times scale approximately linearly with interspin distance, revealing system-dependent operator-spreading velocities that enable correlations to propagate over extended distances within milliseconds. Our sensitivity analysis further shows that individual OTOCs predominantly constrain a single structural parameter, primarily associated with interspin distance. Together, these findings highlight the potential of OTOCs to probe spatially extended spin correlations on timescales compatible with solid-state NMR experiments.

title: Expressivity of two-dimensional Gaussian fermion tensor network states
summary: Tensor network states (TNS) provide a family of efficiently compressed approximations to physically relevant many-body quantum states. An important quantity that characterizes the computational resources required by a TNS is its bond dimension. While in one dimension an area law for the Renyi-0 entropy guarantees an exact matrix product state representation with a bond dimension independent of the system size, an analogous statement does not hold for general states in two dimensions (2D). This leaves open the question of how the expressivity of 2D TNS is related to the entanglement properties of the states they represent. In this work, we focus on two families of 2D translation-invariant Gaussian fermionic states: single-band BCS superconductors and half-filled two-band insulators (including semimetals). For each family, we prove that an area law for the Renyi-0 entropy is equivalent to having an exact Gaussian fermionic TNS representation with a finite bond dimension determined by the Renyi-0 entropy. We also establish equivalent characterizations in terms of compactly supported Wannier-type orbitals and the momentum-space wavefunction, relating the spatial extent of these orbitals and the structure of the wavefunction to the required bond dimension.
